Mutation, stated so a later refactor cannot silently pass: replacing `declinedItems` with a local copy of the
bullet regex fails criterion 1 (the absence-opener); reading the population from the treatment fails criterion 3;
replacing the gross flow with a net fails criterion 4; comparing claim 3 to `5.0%` as a point value fails
criterion 7 on the flow `5.05%` in the fixture.

### 13.149.8 The rule this adds

**A treatment that can only fire on questions already scored wrong has a countable numerator and no denominator,
so its population's own conversion rate is the reading and the roster mean is not.** The corollary is the one
this campaign needed earlier: for such a treatment, **the counterfactual is the same questions without the
treatment**, and any comparison against `0` is comparing against a number the reader does not obey.

## 13.150 The retrieval ceiling is 44 questions, not five: §13.126 measured permutations and called it retrieval

§13.126 priced the retrieval axis at five questions and used that number to retire three registered increments and
to warn off a fourth. The arithmetic in it is correct and the question it answers is not the question the plan
needed answered. This section prices the other one, offline, from the artifact that was already on disk.

The ceiling of a mechanism that changes **which region** of the pool is delivered is **44 of 83 wrong questions,
8.80 points of the roster.** The ceiling of a mechanism that changes the **order** of what was delivered is 5. The
two are not the same number and they were not the same mechanism, and §13.126 read the second as a statement about
both.

### 13.150.1 Why the two counts came apart

`goldRanks` is a list with one entry per eligible gold turn. `carried` is how many of those turns reached the
reader. §13.126's count is the questions whose **best** rank is at ten or beyond -- and "best" is the operative
word:

| question                                              | golds | carried | best rank | §13.126                       | this section               |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----: | ------: | --------: | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `0a995998` (MR, wrong)                                |    17 |      17 |         8 | the reader had what it needed | nothing left to deliver    |
| a hypothetical with 17 golds, 12 carried, best rank 8 |    17 |      12 |         8 | the reader had what it needed | **five golds undelivered** |

The first row is real and the second is why the count cannot be read as retrieval. A question can have its first
gold near the top and five others the delivery dropped, and no permutation of a list produces a turn the list does
not contain. §13.126.1 says as much in one sentence -- "no permutation of a list improves the position of an element
that is already first" -- and then applies the count to mechanisms that are not permutations.

### 13.150.2 The ledger, over the control's 83 wrong questions

`tools/expand-resolution.mjs --artifact 40751394094`:

| capability |  wrong | carried = total | missing gold | of the missing: deep in pool | outside pool | region ceiling | in points |
| ---------- | -----: | --------------: | -----------: | ---------------------------: | -----------: | -------------: | --------: |
| IE         |     10 |               5 |            5 |                           16 |            2 |              5 |      3.33 |
| **MR**     | **34** |          **20** |       **14** |                        **0** |       **25** |         **14** | **11.57** |
| KU         |     11 |               0 |           11 |                           51 |           10 |             11 |     15.28 |
| **TR**     | **27** |          **14** |       **13** |                        **0** |       **21** |         **13** | **10.24** |
| ABS        |      1 |               0 |            1 |                            5 |            0 |              1 |      3.33 |
| **roster** | **83** |          **39** |       **44** |                       **72** |       **58** |         **44** |  **8.80** |

Three readings, and the third is the one that changes what the plan does next.

**1. Thirty-nine wrong questions are beyond every retrieval mechanism, and that number is now measured rather
than assumed.** They delivered every eligible gold they had. Whatever is wrong with them is in what the reader did
with the text, which is where §13.123's and §13.124's populations live. §13.126 reached the same conclusion from
the other side -- "the reading side owns the 78" -- and this table says 39 of them own it outright.

**2. The cheap bucket and the expensive bucket are disjoint by capability.** MR and TR have **zero** golds that the
index surfaced and the delivery dropped: every one of their 46 missing golds is outside the pool. KU is the
opposite: 51 of its 61 missing golds were surfaced and not delivered, and 51 is the largest single bucket in the
table. So "deliver more of what the index found" is a KU-and-IE mechanism and "search differently" is an MR-and-TR
mechanism, and a dispatch that does one will move the other's column by nothing.

**3. KU's 51 is a budget finding wearing a retrieval costume.** Those golds are in the pool; promoting them costs
characters and no retrieval at all. §13.139 measured the room: 468 of 500 questions render at or above 95% of the
48,000 ceiling and the tightest has 409 characters left. So the cheapest single bucket in the table is the one the
budget forbids, which is §13.147's "the denominator is the binding constraint" arriving on the retrieval axis.

### 13.150.3 The independent cross-check against the reference pipeline

§13.137.2 records the reference's single-variable pair: same day, same levers, one flag removed. MR **85.0 → 82.0**
with the reranker, so roughly **3.6 MR questions**. That is the _permutation_ axis and it lands under §13.126's
ceiling of 2 MR questions -- the two derivations agreeing on a small number is why §13.126's arithmetic is trusted.

The `--expand` movement is a different pair and it lands on the _region_ axis: MR **75.9 → 85.0 = +9.1 points =
11.0 questions**, TR **85.7 → 94.0 = +8.3 points = 10.5 questions**. Against this section's ceilings of **14** and
**13**, both numbers fit underneath, and they fit with room rather than filling it:

| axis | mechanism              | this roster's ceiling | the reference's measured movement |                                                          ratio |
| ---- | ---------------------- | --------------------: | --------------------------------: | -------------------------------------------------------------: |
| MR   | permutation (reranker) |                     2 |                               3.6 | 1.8x -- over, which is why the two runs disagree by a question |
| MR   | region (`--expand`)    |                **14** |                          **11.0** |                                                           0.79 |
| TR   | region (`--expand`)    |                **13** |                          **10.5** |                                                           0.81 |

The region rows are the useful ones. A mechanism claiming to move 11 or 10.5 questions on this roster would be
making a claim its own ledger permits, and a mechanism claiming 20 would not. That is what a ceiling is for: it does
not say a mechanism works, it says whether its claim is arithmetically possible.

It also says the two published `--expand` movements are **consistent with a per-question count**, which is the
first time this campaign has had a second derivation of that number from a source that did not know it was
computing one.

> **The third source below was read wrong, and §13.151 corrects it.** The paper's +7-11% is the effect of its
> `time-aware query expansion`, and that mechanism — read from the authors' code — is a **permutation**: an LLM
> infers a date range and the sessions inside it are moved to the front of an already-retrieved list. It is not a
> region change, so it does not belong on this axis, and citing it here as support for a per-entity retrieval was
> the same class of error §13.126 made in the other direction. The table is kept with its correction rather than
> deleted, because the coincidence it describes is real and the reason it is a coincidence is the finding.

**And there is a third source, which is what makes the interval an interval rather than a coincidence.**
LongMemEval's own paper (arXiv 2410.10813) reports time-aware query expansion at **+7-11% on temporal reasoning**.
On this roster that is **8.9-14.0 TR questions**, and the ceiling above is 13:

| source                               |   what it prices on TR | method                                                   | what it does not know                                   |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------: | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| the paper's ablation                 | **8.9-14.0 questions** | one mechanism, one benchmark, the authors' own harness   | reported on the temporal category only                  |
| this section's ceiling               |       **13 questions** | arithmetic over the control's gold ledger, no model call | an upper bound, silent on whether a rule set reaches it |
| the reference's single-variable pair |     **10.5 questions** | one flag removed, same day, same levers                  | it mixes three cue classes into one switch              |

Three derivations and three methods -- another group's ablation, a published artifact's ledger, and a
reimplementation's paired run -- and the reference's measured movement sits inside both of the other two. That is
the strongest form this campaign has for a number it has not dispatched: bounded from above by its own arithmetic,
bracketed from outside by an independent ablation, matched in the middle by a build of the mechanism it is about to
register.

The same table explains why §13.126's five was never going to agree with any of them. The paper reports a
**recall** movement at +7-11%; §13.126 counts questions whose **best** gold is already past rank ten. Both
sentences can be true, and only one of them can price a time-aware query expansion.

### 13.150.4 The first rule set measured the wrong cue, and the roster's own wording says so

§13.137.3 describes `--expand` as "rules, not a model call": it parses time cues, counting cues and comparison cues
and issues one retrieval per named thing. The first version of this tool implemented three families -- an **absolute
named period**, a cardinality word, a conjunction -- and reported that a question could be split 9 times out of the
44 reachable ones. That number was a measurement of the rule set and not of the mechanism, and reading the
questions is what showed it:

| cue family                                                                                | wrong questions it matches (of 83) |     share |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------: | --------: |
| cardinality (`how many`, `total`)                                                         |                                 34 |     41.0% |
| conjunction (`and`, `or`, `vs`)                                                           |                                 20 |     24.1% |
| **relative period** (`last month`, `past three months`, `two weeks ago`, `most recently`) |                             **16** | **19.3%** |
| ordering (`what is the order`, `earliest`, `which came first`)                            |                                 10 |     12.0% |
| magnitude (`percentage`, `discount`, `how old`)                                           |                                  8 |      9.6% |
| **absolute period** (`in March`, `on Tuesdays`, a year)                                   |                              **5** |  **6.0%** |

**The family the first version had, the absolute period, is the rarest one on this roster at 6.0%.** The questions
say `How many plants did I acquire in the last month?`, `What is the total amount of money I earned from selling my
products at the markets?`, `What was the significant business milestone I mentioned four weeks ago?` -- they name a
period **relative to now**, and a rule that looks for month names finds almost none of them. §13.137.3's own
description ("`analyzeQuery` resolves a named period against `now`") already said the resolution was against `now`;
the first implementation read the first half of that clause and dropped the second.

Rebuilt as six families -- adding relative period, ordering and magnitude -- the same roster reads:

| capability | wrong | decomposable |  share | reachable **and** decomposable |
| ---------- | ----: | -----------: | -----: | -----------------------------: |
| IE         |    10 |            3 |  30.0% |                              1 |
| MR         |    34 |           18 |  52.9% |                          **7** |
| KU         |    11 |            3 |  27.3% |                              3 |
| TR         |    27 |           10 |  37.0% |                              5 |
| ABS        |     1 |            1 | 100.0% |                              1 |
| roster     |    83 |           35 |  42.2% |                         **17** |

**17 of 44, up from 9.** And with that, the arithmetic against the reference stops being a contradiction: a rule set
this size reaches 7 of MR's 14, and the reference moved 11 -- still more than the rules can address and no longer
twice as much.

### 13.150.5 The holdout that keeps a hand-written rule set honest

The six families were read off the **wrong** questions' own text, so their coverage of those questions is a fitted
quantity. Citing it as evidence that the rules work would be the §13.137 error in a new place -- a number that looks
like a finding and is a description of how it was chosen. The tool therefore reports the same families against the
questions the arm got **right**, on text they were not chosen against:

| capability | wrong, split |     share | correct, split |     share |       delta |
| ---------- | -----------: | --------: | -------------: | --------: | ----------: |
| IE         |         3/10 |     30.0% |         37/140 |     26.4% |        +3.6 |
| MR         |        18/34 |     52.9% |          48/87 |     55.2% |    **-2.2** |
| KU         |         3/11 |     27.3% |          11/61 |     18.0% |        +9.2 |
| **TR**     |    **10/27** | **37.0%** |     **78/100** | **78.0%** |   **-41.0** |
| ABS        |          1/1 |    100.0% |           9/29 |     31.0% | +69.0 (n=1) |
| roster     |        35/83 |     42.2% |        183/417 |     43.9% |        -1.7 |

**The roster-level delta is -1.7 points, which is the answer that matters: the rules generalise.** 42.2% against
43.9% on 500 questions is not a rule set fitted to the 83 failures; it is a description of how this dataset writes
questions. IE, MR and KU all sit within a few points of their holdout, and ABS's +69.0 is one question and is
reported for completeness rather than read.

**TR's -41.0 is the exception, and it is the most useful number in the table.** 78% of the temporal questions the
arm answers _correctly_ are splittable, and only 37% of the ones it gets wrong are. The ordering questions --
`What is the order of the six museums I visited from earliest to latest?` -- are the splittable ones and the arm
already answers them. What it fails on is the other shape: `What gardening-related activity did I do two weeks
ago?`, `What was the life event of one of my relatives that I participated in a week ago?` -- a **single** event at
a **relative** offset, where the key is not a decomposition at all but `now - 2 weeks` resolved into a window.

So TR's ceiling of 13 and MR's ceiling of 14 are close numbers produced by **different mechanisms**, and a rule set
that raises MR's coverage does nothing for TR's:

|     | what the failures need                                      | does a per-entity decomposition help                                   |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| MR  | an item that spans sessions and has no name in the question | partly -- the period narrows it, the items still have to be enumerated |
| TR  | one event at a relative offset                              | **no** -- it needs `now` arithmetic and a windowed retrieval           |
| KU  | a fact that changed, whose current value is the answer      | no -- it needs a recency or supersession rule                          |

**That is why this section does not register a dispatch.** The three columns want three mechanisms, and the only
one of them a rule set addresses is MR's, partially. Registering "`expand`" as one increment would put all three
under one switch and one number, which is the §13.125 portfolio problem and the §13.137.2 multi-variable problem
arriving together.

### 13.150.6 What the next action is, and why it is a source read rather than a run

The rule set **is** the mechanism. §13.137.5's rule -- a number in a comparison table must be recomputable from the
other side's artifacts -- has an obvious extension: a _mechanism_ compared against must be readable as code before a
reimplementation of it is registered. Three specific things are needed from that read, and each is a number this
section cannot produce:

1. **The cue list itself.** Six families reach 17 of 44; whether the reference's list reaches more is a question
   about its source, and 11 of 14 on MR is currently explained only by "its rules are richer than mine".
2. **What it does with the resolved period.** "One retrieval per named thing" says nothing about whether a
   relative period is converted into a filter over turn timestamps, a boost, or a separate index.
3. **Whether the expansion runs before or after the top-k cut**, because that is the difference between the cheap
   bucket (72 golds the index found and the delivery dropped) and the expensive one (58 it never found), and this
   roster's two buckets are disjoint by capability.

Until then the honest statement is the one the ledger supports: **the region ceiling is 44 questions and 8.80
points, a hand-written six-family rule set reaches 17 of them, and the reference's measured MR movement of 11 sits
between the two.**

### 13.150.7 What §13.126 said next, restated

§13.126.4 wrote: "a retrieval mechanism must name its ceiling before it is dispatched, and the ceiling is computed
from the same five columns above." The four columns were wrong for the class of mechanism the paragraph was
warning off, and the reason is one word in the criterion:

> the count of wrong questions in its target capability whose best gold rank is at or beyond the cut it operates on

"best gold rank" is a permutation quantity. A mechanism that adds a delivery is not bounded by it, and a mechanism
that adds a delivery is what the reference runs for MR and TR. The corrected criterion, which is what
`tools/expand-resolution.mjs` computes:

- **A permutation mechanism** names its ceiling as wrong questions whose **best** gold is at or beyond its cut.
- **A region mechanism** names its ceiling as wrong questions with **at least one** eligible gold outside the
  delivery, split into the part the index already found (cheap) and the part it never found (expensive).
- **A mechanism that does neither** -- one that changes the instruction, the rendering or the reader -- has a
  ceiling of the wrong questions it can address at all, and §13.126's count is not it either.


Mutation, stated so a later refactor cannot silently pass: reading `carried` as `total - missing` fails criterion
1; treating an absent `pool` as zero fails criterion 5 (every missing gold becomes outside-pool); a
`Math.max(0, pool - carried)` dropped in favour of the identity fails criterion 4 with a negative; computing the
permutation ceiling from `max` instead of `min` fails criterion 7 on the `hidden` fixture; dropping the
`relative-period` family fails criterion 23 and takes the roster's decomposable count from 35 to 24; counting a
conjunction as one key instead of two fails criterion 12 (the fixture expects three).

### 13.150.9 The rule this adds

**A ceiling is priced in the unit of the mechanism, and "retrieval" is at least two mechanisms.** A count computed
from the best rank bounds permutations; a count computed from delivered versus eligible bounds region changes; and
the second is 8.8 times the first on this roster. Applying the smaller one to the larger class does not make the
larger class unreachable -- it makes the plan stop looking, which is the same outcome with worse bookkeeping.

And the corollary this section paid for twice: **a hand-written rule set is a measurement of the corpus's wording,
so it has to be read back against that wording before its coverage is quoted.** The first six-line version of the
cue table had an absolute-period family that matched 6.0% of the failures, while the relative form matched 19.3%;
the coverage it reported was a fact about the rule, dressed as a fact about the mechanism. The holdout is what makes
the difference visible: 42.2% of the wrong questions and 43.9% of the right ones means the rules describe the
dataset, and TR's 37.0% against 78.0% means one capability's failures need a different mechanism rather than a
better rule.

## 13.151 The reference's time-aware expansion is a permutation, and reading its code is what said so

§13.137.3 described the retrieval-side lever as "**rules, not a model call**": `analyzeQuery` parses cues and
issues one retrieval per named thing, costing a handful of vector searches and no extra LLM call. That
description is of `al-buddy-memory`'s `--expand` flag, which is one implementation. LongMemEval's **own**
implementation is a different mechanism, it is public (`src/index_expansion/temp_query_search_pruning.py` in
`xiaowu0162/LongMemEval`), and reading it settles three questions this campaign has been guessing at since
§13.137.

This section is the source read §13.150.6 said had to precede any registration. It changes the axis assignment of
the mechanism §13.150.3 leaned on, and it hands this arm a design it can afford.

### 13.151.1 What the code does, in five statements it can be held to

The file is 198 lines and its mechanism is five steps:

1. **An LLM call infers a date range, not a set of queries.** `infer_time_range(question, question_date)` sends a
   system prompt plus ten worked examples to `gpt-4o` at `temperature=0` and asks for `{"start", "end"}` in
   `YYYY/MM/DD`, or the literal string `N/A` when the question has no temporal reference. The system prompt says so
   explicitly: _"If the question does not have any temporal references, do not attempt to guess a time range."_
2. **The range is widened by two days at each end** before use (`increment_date(start, -2)`, `increment_date(end,
+2)`), which is a rounding for the fact that an event at the boundary may be logged under a neighbouring date.
3. **Sessions whose decomposed events fall in the range are moved to the front**, and everything else is kept in
   its original relative order: `ranked_items_new = ranked_items_new_left + ranked_items_new_right`.
4. **No retrieval is re-run.** `ranked_items_original` is read from the retrieval file, reordered, and written
   back. The corpus does not change; only the order does, and only the elements already in the list.
5. **A question with no temporal reference passes through untouched** and its metrics are recorded unchanged,
   which is why the reported effect is an average over the subset that fired rather than over the roster.

### 13.151.2 What that retires, and what it confirms

**Retired: "the reference's expansion is rules."** It is a model call, at `temperature=0`, with a ten-example
few-shot prompt. The clue-based rule decomposer §13.150.4 spent its budget on is `al-buddy-memory`'s design, not
this one. Both exist, they are different mechanisms, and §13.137.3 named one and described the other.

**Retired: this mechanism belongs on the region axis.** It is a permutation of an already-delivered list, so it
cannot produce a turn the retrieval did not return. §13.126's ceiling is the right instrument for it and §13.150's
44-question region ceiling is not. **§13.150.3 cited the paper's +7-11% as external support for a region change and
that citation was wrong** -- the number is a recall movement produced by reordering, and the section now carries the
correction.

**Confirmed, and this is the part that matters: the paper's own examples are this roster's TR failures.** The ten
few-shot examples include `Where did I attend the religious activity last week?`,
`What did I do with Rachel on the Wednesday two months ago?`, `Which pair of shoes did I clean last month?` -- and
the four `N/A` examples are `How many months ago did I book the Airbnb`, `How long have I been using my Fitbit`,
`How many bikes do I currently own`, `How many engineers do I lead ... how many now`. That is a split by **shape**,
and §13.150.5 measured the same split from the other side: TR's failures are the single-event-at-a-relative-offset
questions (37.0% decomposable) while TR's successes are the ordering questions (78.0% decomposable).

**So the two implementations are not competitors for one job. They are one mechanism each for two capabilities**,
and §13.150.4's finding that MR and TR want different things now has a published implementation on each side:

| capability | what the failures need                 | the implementation that does it                                        | axis                   | cost                                  |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| **MR**     | every item, enumerated across sessions | `--expand`: one retrieval per named thing                              | region                 | ~0 LLM (rules)                        |
| **TR**     | one event at a relative offset         | `temp_query_search_pruning`: infer the range, move it to the front     | **permutation**        | **+1 LLM call on the flagged subset** |
| KU         | the current value of a changed fact    | neither; the paper's `session-userfact` is an **index-time** expansion | region, before the cut | index-time                            |

### 13.151.3 What this arm would have to build, and what it already has

The published mechanism needs `timestamped_facts`: an index-time decomposition of each session into
`{date, event}` entries, built by `batch_expansion_session_temp_event.py` (19KB of extraction prompts). **This arm
does not need it.** Its turns already carry the timestamp in the text --
`[2023/02/15 (Wed) 01:41] user: ...` -- so a date is a prefix parse rather than an extraction, and a
"session in range" test is `any(turn date in [start-2, end+2] for turn in session)`.

That is a real advantage and it is worth stating precisely, because it is the difference between adding a mechanism
and adding a mechanism **plus** an index-time LLM pass over 500 histories:

|                       | the reference                                          | this arm                                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| date source           | `timestamped_facts`, extracted by an LLM at index time | the turn's own text prefix                                |
| granularity available | the extracted event                                    | the turn                                                  |
| what has to be built  | an extraction pass + a date→session map                | a prefix parser + the same map                            |
| risk                  | an extraction error is silent and permanent            | a malformed prefix is a parse failure, which is countable |

The prefix parser is the whole prerequisite, and the arm's own artifacts already prove the format holds: every
`turns[]` entry in `40751394094` opens with `[YYYY/MM/DD (Day) HH:MM]`.

### 13.151.4 The cost, which is why this is registrable at all

A whole-roster expansion call would add 4,000 calls per dispatch, which is **+69%** on the 5,756 this arm issues
(§13.147.1) and is not affordable. The published mechanism does not do that: it calls only on questions with a
temporal reference, and returns early on `N/A`.

The arm's own roster says how often that is. Using the two period families from §13.150.4 as a proxy for "the
prompt would not answer `N/A`":

| capability | questions with a period reference |     share |
| ---------- | --------------------------------: | --------: |
| IE         |                           5 / 150 |      3.3% |
| **MR**     |                      **30 / 121** | **24.8%** |
| KU         |                            4 / 72 |      5.6% |
| **TR**     |                      **29 / 127** | **22.8%** |
| ABS        |                            2 / 30 |      6.7% |
| roster     |                      **70 / 500** | **14.0%** |

**70 calls per pass, 560 per dispatch, +9.7%.** That is the number that makes this a candidate rather than an
aspiration: a tenth of the bill for a mechanism aimed at the capability with the second-largest region ceiling, and
the proxy is an over-estimate rather than an under-estimate, because the model answers `N/A` on some questions the
cue families match (`How many months ago did I book the Airbnb` has `ago` in it and the paper's own example output
is `N/A`).

**And it cannot lower the bill, so §8's question has an answer here too.** The mechanism is a reorder, so it adds
calls and removes none; what it can remove is the alternative -- buying a wider pool or more repetitions to reach
the same 13 questions. That trade is priced in §13.145.3 and this is the cheaper side of it.

### 13.151.5 What is registered, and the four criteria it has to meet

**Registered as the next dispatch, conditional on the prefix parser's own test passing.** It is registered against
the same control as every other read in this campaign (`40751394094`) so the ledger's cross-run mode gives the
overlap for free.

| #   | criterion                                                                                               | what would falsify it                                                                                                            |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the prefix parser resolves a date on **every** turn of every question, or names the questions it cannot | any question with an unparsed turn is excluded from the reorder and reported, never silently ranked last                         |
| 2   | the reorder is a **permutation**: the multiset of delivered turns is byte-identical to the control's    | any question whose delivered set changed means this dispatched two mechanisms                                                    |
| 3   | the range inference fires on 10-20% of the roster                                                       | outside that band the cost model in §13.151.4 is wrong and the mechanism is being administered more broadly than registered      |
| 4   | TR moves by **at least 5 of its 13 reachable questions**, and MR by at most 2                           | TR below 5 and the mechanism is a recall movement that did not reach accuracy; MR above 2 and the effect is not the temporal one |
| 5   | no question outside the flagged subset changes verdict beyond the 5.0% reader floor                     | a flow above the floor among untouched questions means the reorder perturbed something it was not supposed to touch              |

Criterion 2 is the one that makes this a clean experiment rather than an increment. §13.137.2's own warning is that
`88.4 -> 92.6` was three levers at once; a permutation by construction cannot be that, because the delivered set is
invariant and the only thing that moves is order.

> **Criteria 3, 4 and 5 are restated in §13.152.4, and the restatement is what the dispatch is registered against.**
> The three were written before the population had been counted, and counting it (§13.152.3) found two things: the
> reach is 8 TR questions rather than 13, and the range inference does not need a model call on 24% of the population
> at all. A bar quoted against a population that moved is the §13.141.5 shape, and the response there was to restate
> it once, in the registration, before the run rather than after it. That is what §13.152.4 does.

**It is not dispatched in this step**, for the reason §13.150.6 gave about the rule set and one more: the prefix
parser does not exist yet, and criterion 1 is a gate on it rather than on the model. That is a code change with a
test, not a dispatch, and it is the next step's first half.

### 13.151.6 The rule this adds

**A mechanism's axis is a property of its code, not of its description.** "Query expansion" names at least two
different things -- a rule set that issues new retrievals, and a model call that reorders an existing list -- and
they are bounded by different ceilings, cost different amounts, and address different capabilities. Reading the
description gave this campaign the region axis for a permutation mechanism and a cost model (+1 call per question)
that was 7 times the real one (+1 call per _flagged_ question). The code gave both numbers.

**Corollary, and it is the one that generalises beyond this benchmark:** when two implementations of one named
technique disagree, the disagreement is usually about which axis the technique lives on. `--expand`'s rules and
`temp_query_search_pruning`'s reorder are both called "query expansion", and one is a region change while the other
is a permutation. A campaign that registers "query expansion" as one increment would be registering two axes under
one name, and the first reading would show neither.

## 13.152 The prefix parses on all 60,438 delivered turns, and the range does not need a model on a quarter of its population

§13.151.5 made the dispatch conditional on the prefix parser existing and its test passing, and §13.151.4 priced the
range inference from a **proxy** -- the share of questions whose text carries a period reference -- at 70 calls per
pass, +9.7% per dispatch. This section reports the parser, and replaces the proxy with a measurement on the control
artifact. The measurement changes the shape of the increment: the arm already owns a deterministic window resolver, so
the reference's model call is a **fallback** here rather than the mechanism.

### 13.152.1 The parse, read on the control run's own turns

`packages/cortex-eval/src/turn-clock.ts` reads a turn's `[YYYY/MM/DD (Day) HH:MM]` prefix. On `40751394094`, over
every question's delivered turns:

| reading                                                       |                  value |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------: |
| delivered turns                                               |                 60,438 |
| turns with a readable date                                    | **60,438 (100.0000%)** |
| questions with at least one unreadable turn                   |                  **0** |
| questions with no readable turn at all                        |                  **0** |
| stamps whose weekday label disagrees with the date's calendar |                  **0** |
| distinct minutes-of-day in the corpus                         |                  1,440 |

The fifth row is why the reader validates rather than truncates. A stamp carries two encodings of one fact -- the
date and its weekday -- and they agree on all 60,438 turns, so a disagreement is not noise: it is a renderer that
moved one of the two, and a reorder acting on the moved date would front-load the wrong turns. Refusing costs nothing
(the turn stays where it was) and turns a silent misordering into a count. The other refusals are the same argument
one level down: `2023/02/30`, `2023/00/10`, `24:00` and `(Xyz)` are all shapes this renderer cannot produce, and
`Date.UTC` would silently roll the first two into a different day rather than reject them.

**§13.151.5's first criterion is met, and it is met on the artifact rather than on the dataset.** The artifact is what
the mechanism will see; a parse that held on the raw corpus and failed on the rendering would be a fact about a
dataset. The 100% is also stronger than "the pattern matched": `[2023/02/15]` and `[2023/02/15 23:59]` are refused
only if they are inconsistent with themselves, so the reader accepts the two renderings `formatStructuredContext`
already produces while still refusing a corrupted one.

### 13.152.2 The artifact could not say when its question was asked

A time qualifier resolves **against the question date** -- "last Saturday" is a different day for a question asked on
a Tuesday than on a Sunday -- and the per-question record did not carry it. `Question.questionDate` was in the type
and reached `answerTemporal`, but `QuestionRecord` had no field for it, so every window read from an archived artifact
has to substitute something. That is a recording gap of the §13.145 shape: the run knew the value and the artifact
could not report it.

The repair is three lines with a comment each -- the field on `QuestionRecord`, the field on `QuestionRecordInput`,
and one conditional spread at the arm's record construction -- and it is written **only when the dataset states a
date**, because a substituted date is this layer inventing a term of the window it is asking a reader to price.
`tools/window-reach.mjs` therefore reports the substitution rate as its own number: on this control run it is
**500 of 500**, since the run predates the field.

The substitution is sound for the _firing_ count (a qualifier either parses against a valid date or does not) and
approximate for the _window_ (the delivered span's last turn is not the question date). Every window in the tables
below is therefore a lower bound on precision, and the dispatch -- which runs with the real date -- is the exact
reading. Stated because a later section quoting these windows as exact would be quoting an approximation.

### 13.152.3 Three populations, and what the proxy got wrong

The population is defined by something the arm already owns rather than by a new grammar: `classifyTemporalQuestion`
returns `eventLookup` ("what was X at that time") or `relative` ("how long ago was that one event") for exactly the
questions answered from **one** point in time, which is the only thing a single window can express. `interval`
("between X and Y") and `ordering` are excluded by construction: one window would span both events or match one of
them, and promoting half of a two-event question is a claim the mechanism cannot make.

| capability | questions | window-wanting |  ladder-fired | fires and splits | wrong and splittable |
| ---------- | --------: | -------------: | ------------: | ---------------: | -------------------: |
| IE         |       150 |             22 |             1 |                0 |                    0 |
| MR         |       121 |             14 |             2 |                1 |                **1** |
| KU         |        72 |              8 |             1 |                0 |                    0 |
| **TR**     |       127 |         **45** |        **18** |           **14** |                **8** |
| ABS        |        30 |              1 |             0 |                0 |                    0 |
| **roster** |   **500** | **90 (18.0%)** | **22 (4.4%)** |    **15 (3.0%)** |                **9** |

**The proxy was close in size and wrong in composition.** §13.151.4 estimated 70 calls per pass from the two period
families; the measured window-wanting population is 90. But the ladder resolves 22 of those 90 with no call at all,
so the model's bill is **68**, not 90 -- and the 20-question difference is not a rounding: the cue families counted
questions the ladder already answers (`two weeks ago`, `a month ago`) and missed questions that want a window while
carrying no period reference at all (`What time did I reach the clinic on Monday?`, `What is the artist that I started
to listen to last Friday?`). A proxy built from surface cues approximates neither the population nor the cost.

**Two numbers, two different jobs, and §13.151.4 used one for both.** `window-wanting` is the _reach_; `ladder-fired`
is the _free path_; `model-fallback` is the _bill_. Only the third is a cost, and it is 68 calls per run -- 544 per
dispatch at §13.151.4's own multiplier of 8, which is **+9.5%** against 5,756 rather than the +9.7% registered. The
two-tier resolver is strictly cheaper than the mechanism §13.151 registered, and the reason is that the arm already
had half of it.

### 13.152.4 The reach, restated, and the risk the original bar did not contemplate

**Reachable** means: wrong in the control, window-wanting, and the resolved window actually splits the delivered list.
The third clause is not decoration -- a window entirely outside the delivered span reorders nothing, and counting it
as a reach is a mechanism that ran and could not have had an effect.

| id              | capability | kind        | in/out of the delivered list | window (substituted reference) |
| --------------- | ---------- | ----------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `73d42213`      | MR         | eventLookup | 36 / 192 (18.8%)             | 2023/05/29 .. 2023/05/29       |
| `gpt4_e061b84g` | TR         | eventLookup | 51 / 205 (24.9%)             | 2023/05/31 .. 2023/06/06       |
| `b46e15ee`      | TR         | eventLookup | 73 / 188 (38.8%)             | 2023/02/12 .. 2023/02/26       |
| `gpt4_d6585ce9` | TR         | eventLookup | 12 / 163 (7.4%)              | 2023/04/08 .. 2023/04/08       |
| `gpt4_1e4a8aec` | TR         | eventLookup | 17 / 172 (9.9%)              | 2023/04/04 .. 2023/04/10       |
| `gpt4_59149c78` | TR         | eventLookup | 6 / 185 (3.2%)               | 2022/12/29 .. 2023/01/04       |
| `gpt4_4929293b` | TR         | eventLookup | 6 / 177 (3.4%)               | 2023/06/05 .. 2023/06/11       |
| `gpt4_fa19884d` | TR         | eventLookup | 4 / 191 (2.1%)               | 2023/03/24 .. 2023/03/24       |
| `eac54add`      | TR         | eventLookup | 11 / 172 (6.4%)              | 2023/01/29 .. 2023/02/04       |

All nine are `eventLookup`, which is the shape the paper's own few-shot examples are written for (§13.151.2), and the
in-window share runs from 2.1% to 38.8% -- in every case a small slice of a 160-200 turn list moved to the front,
which is the mechanism's whole effect.

**The bar, restated.** §13.151.5 asked for "at least 5 of TR's 13 reachable questions". Counting the population
gives 8, not 13, and §13.141.5 is the precedent for what happens when a registered bar meets a population that
shrank: restate it once, in the registration, before the run. The registration this section dispatches against is:

| #   | criterion                                                                                | what would falsify it                                                                                                                              |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the parse resolves every delivered turn, or names the questions it cannot                | **met on the control artifact**: 60,438 of 60,438, 0 questions named                                                                               |
| 2   | the delivered multiset is byte-identical to the control's, per question                  | any question whose delivered set changed means the dispatch ran two mechanisms                                                                     |
| 3   | the mechanism administers 10-20% of the roster                                           | measured **18.0%** (90/500); the ladder's own 4.4% is a cost number and is not this criterion                                                      |
| 4   | TR converts **at least 4 of its 8 reachable questions**, and MR at most 2 of its 1       | the bar is half the reachable set, which on a population this size is far outside the reader's own churn                                           |
| 5   | no question outside the fired set moves beyond the 5.0% reader floor                     | a flow above the floor among untouched questions is a perturbation of something the reorder does not reach                                         |
| 6   | **of the 12 questions the ladder fires on that are already correct, at most 2 are sold** | this is the risk the original bar did not contemplate: 6 of those 12 split, so the reorder touches six correct verdicts as well as nine wrong ones |

Criterion 6 is the one the measurement added. §13.151.5 was written as if the firing population were the wrong
population, and on this artifact it is not: **12 of the 22 firings are on questions the control already answers**, and
6 of those 12 have a list the window splits. A front-loading that buys 4 and sells 4 would read as a mechanism with
no effect while having had two; the sell bound is what keeps the reading honest.

### 13.152.5 What fires and cannot move

Of 22 firings, 15 split and **7 do not** (6 correct, 1 wrong). A window that does not intersect the delivered span is
either the substitution of §13.152.2 -- the span's end is not the question date, so the resolved window is displaced
by however long after the haystack the question was asked -- or a resolver that picked a unit the question did not
state. Both are worth a count and neither is worth a guess: the dispatch runs with the real date, and this tool will
report the number again on the treated run.

That is also the argument for why the fire/inert/move split is three numbers rather than two: "fired but inert" is
the population where a mechanism could claim a reach it never had, and on an artifact with a substituted reference
date it is exactly the population a bad substitution lands in.

### 13.152.6 What is registered, and what is deliberately not

**Registered: the ladder-only reorder.** Zero model calls, 22 questions administered, 9 wrong-and-splittable
candidates, and a bill of nothing. Everything this section prices is in place for it: the parse (§13.152.1), the
date it resolves against (§13.152.2), the population (§13.152.3), the criteria as six numbered claims (§13.152.4),
and the tool that checks all six on a pair of artifacts (`tools/window-reach.mjs`, §13.152.7).

**Not registered in this step: the model fallback.** It is 68 calls per run for 12 wrong questions, 6 of them TR, and
it is only worth buying once the free path's conversion rate is known -- because the fallback's question set
overlaps the ladder's population and a fallback that duplicated the ladder's successes would double a bill to buy
nothing. §13.151.4's lesson was that the mechanism is affordable; this section's is that the cheaper half has to be
measured first.

**And not registered: a window on `interval`/`ordering` questions.** Fourteen wrong TR questions are
`interval`/`ordering` (`How many days passed between X and Y`, `Which three events happened in this order`). A single
window is the wrong instrument for all fourteen, and the temptation to widen the mechanism until the bar is met is
the §13.126 mistake in the other direction -- a criterion that fits the mechanism rather than a mechanism that meets
the criterion.

### 13.152.7 The tool, and what it refuses

`tools/window-reach.mjs --control <report.json> [--treatment <report.json>]` reads; it dispatches nothing. Without a
treatment it prices the mechanism; with one it also checks criteria 2 and 5 by pairing the two artifacts by question
id. Twenty-nine checks in `tools/__tests__/test_window_reach.py` hold it, and the refusals are the load-bearing half:

- exit 2 for a malformed invocation (no `--control`, two `--treatment`s, the same file as both arms, unreadable JSON,
  no `questions` array, a record with no question text, a duplicate id, a `turns` field that is not a list, a turn
  that is neither text nor `{text}`) -- each replaces a plausible number with one wrong in a direction nobody notices;
- exit 1 for a well-formed artifact that answers nothing here (no question wants a window), which is a different fix
  from a different command;
- a turn it cannot read is **refused**, never skipped: skipping shrinks the delivered span, and every window decision
  is a comparison against that span;
- the substitution rate is printed rather than hidden, because a reader who does not know the reference date was
  substituted cannot tell an approximate window from an exact one.

### 13.152.8 The rule this adds

**A free path in front of a paid one changes what the criterion is about.** §13.151.5's "fires on 10-20% of the
roster" existed to police a bill -- one call per firing -- and the arm then turned out to own a resolver that answers
24.4% of the population for nothing. Keeping the band pointed at the firing rate would have failed a mechanism that
is strictly cheaper than the one the band was written for, and pointing it at the population instead is not a
relaxation: 18.0% is inside the same band. The criterion was right about the risk (a mechanism administered more
broadly than registered) and wrong about the quantity that measures it, and only a measurement of the population
could tell the two apart.

**Corollary.** A proxy is a hypothesis about a population, so it has to be replaced by a count before it is used to
price anything. §13.151.4's 70 calls were within 3 of the truth for the wrong reason -- it counted questions the
free path already answers and missed questions that want a window without naming a period -- and a cost model that is
right by accident cannot be re-derived when the implementation changes, which is precisely what happened here.

## 13.153 The reorder is wired, and it administers 19 questions of which 9 actually move

§13.152 registered the ladder-only reorder against six criteria and priced it offline. This section is the
implementation, and the implementation changed one number and one criterion:

- **fired is not moved.** 19 questions resolve a window and **9** come back in a different order. The other
  ten promoted a block that was already at the front, so their prompt is byte-identical to the control's.
  §13.152.3 counted "the window splits the delivered list" (22) and §13.152.4 counted the splits that were
  wrong (9); both are **ceilings**, and the reach is the smaller number.
- **the population is the route, not the classifier.** At runtime a question is administered if
  `resolveTimeRange` answers, and only the route that is handed a reference date can ask. That is the
  temporal route, whose capability is TR. §13.152.3 defined its population with `classifyTemporalQuestion`
  (`eventLookup` + `relative`, 90 questions) because that was the only instrument available offline; the
  wired mechanism's gate is the resolver, and the two disagree on one question (`0bc8ad93`, whose shape the
  classifier calls `other` and whose text names a period). Three numbers, three meanings, and the table in
  §13.153.3 is the one the dispatch is read against.

### 13.153.1 What is wired, and where

Four files, and each owns one thing:

| file                                  | what it now does                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `cortex-memory/src/prompt.ts`         | `EvidenceOrdering` (a predicate: should this turn lead), `partitionLead` (a stable partition, so the result is a permutation **by construction**), and a fifth parameter on `buildPrompt` |
| `cortex-memory/src/types.ts`          | `WindowOrdering`: two readers, `dateOf(content)` and `windowOf(question, questionDate)`. The product still knows nothing about dates                                                      |
| `cortex-memory/src/memory.ts`         | `#orderingFor`, which resolves a window **per question** and returns the predicate -- or `undefined`                                                                                      |
| `cortex-memory/bench/run-ablation.ts` | builds the two readers from `cortex-eval`'s turn clock and range resolver, and records `windowReorder` in `featureConfig`                                                                 |

Two structural decisions are worth stating because the alternative was easier and wrong.

**The ordering is a fifth parameter, not a `PromptOptions` field.** `buildSessionPrompt` renders session
blocks, where the unit of order is the block: reordering turns inside a block says nothing, and reordering
the blocks would destroy the boundaries. A field on the shared options would therefore be a knob the
multi-session route accepts and ignores -- the inert configuration this file has audited the product for
twice. As a parameter it cannot reach that builder at all, so the reach is a **signature**, and the
mechanism is administered on exactly the five single-block routes.

**The product takes a predicate, not a date range.** A product that parsed `[2023/02/15 (Wed) 01:41]` would
make the product's behaviour a fact about one dataset's rendering, which is the argument `roleOfTurn` and
`relevanceFor` already settle. The consequence is the one that matters here: because the predicate is
boolean, the operation is a **stable partition**, and a stable partition of a list is a permutation of it.
Criterion 2 is therefore not a property the run has to hope for -- there is no expression of this mechanism
that changes the delivered multiset.

### 13.153.2 The promotion runs on the delivered set, and the clip path is the one place it is not exactly length-preserving

`buildPrompt` promotes `carried`, never `turns`. Before the budget, a promotion changes which turns survive
the cut: the delivered set moves and the reading can no longer be attributed to order. After it, the
promoted list is a permutation of a set the control also delivers.

The selection is also handed the **unpermuted** window, deliberately: `chooseEvidence` breaks ties by
position, so a permuted input would make the delivered set a function of the mechanism.

**The rendering is length-invariant under the permutation.** `formatEvidence` numbers turns by position,
and a permutation of `n` turns assigns the same multiset of numbers `1..n`, so the rendered length is
identical and the `prompt.length <= maxChars` decision is the same one the control takes. The fits path and
the budget path therefore cannot disagree about which branch a question is on -- which is what makes the
byte-identical claim in §13.153.4 possible for the inert ten.

**One path is not exactly length-preserving, and it is named rather than discovered.** The character clip
(`relevanceFor` absent) can end inside a turn; `carried` there is the largest prefix of **whole** turns, so
re-rendering it drops the partial tail. The delivered _turns_ are unchanged and the prompt gets strictly
shorter. The registered configuration never takes that path -- §13.27 put a ranking on every route -- but a
later dispatch could, and a byte-count difference attributed to the ordering would then be wrong.

### 13.153.3 What the product does on the control artifact

`tools/window-wired.mjs` replays all 500 questions of `40751394094` through `CortexMemory` twice, readers
absent and readers supplied, with a stub reader that never leaves the process:

| capability | questions |         fired |        moved | converted |  sold | multiset broken |
| ---------- | --------: | ------------: | -----------: | --------: | ----: | --------------: |
| IE         |       150 |             0 |            0 |         0 |     0 |               0 |
| MR         |       121 |             0 |            0 |         0 |     0 |               0 |
| KU         |        72 |             0 |            0 |         0 |     0 |               0 |
| ABS        |        30 |             0 |            0 |         0 |     0 |               0 |
| **TR**     |   **127** |        **19** |        **9** |     **7** | **2** |           **0** |
| **roster** |   **500** | **19 (3.8%)** | **9 (1.8%)** |     **7** | **2** |           **0** |

**The delivered multiset is unchanged on 500 of 500.** That is criterion 2 measured on the product rather
than on a reimplementation of it, and it is the one number in this table that a defect would move.

**Seven of the nine reorders are on questions the control answers wrong, and two are on questions it
answers right.** That is a better sell bound than §13.152.4 could estimate: it counted 12 firings on correct
questions with 6 splittable, and 6 of those 12 turn out to promote a block that is already at the front. The
risk criterion 6 exists for is real and **smaller** than the ceiling suggested -- and the ceiling is exactly
what an offline instrument can see.

**What the nine look like.** Delivered lists of 90-115 turns (this run caps each turn at 400 characters
against a 48,000-character budget), and the promoted block runs from 4 to 58 turns with a mean of 22.9:

| id              | correct | kind        | delivered | promoted |
| --------------- | ------- | ----------- | --------: | -------: |
| `b46e15ee`      | no      | eventLookup |       102 |       58 |
| `gpt4_e061b84g` | no      | eventLookup |       115 |       51 |
| `9a707b82`      | **yes** | eventLookup |        97 |       31 |
| `6e984302`      | **yes** | eventLookup |        94 |       27 |
| `gpt4_d6585ce9` | no      | eventLookup |        90 |       12 |
| `eac54add`      | no      | eventLookup |        91 |       11 |
| `gpt4_59149c78` | no      | eventLookup |       105 |        6 |
| `0bc8ad93`      | no      | other       |        93 |        6 |
| `gpt4_fa19884d` | no      | eventLookup |       111 |        4 |

**The reference date on this artifact is substituted on all 500 questions**, because the run predates
§13.152.2's field. Every window in the table is therefore displaced by however long after the haystack the
question was asked, and every count is a **lower bound**. The dispatch runs with the real date.

### 13.153.4 Fired, moved, converted: three numbers, three meanings

The campaign has now used four different quantities for "the population" of this mechanism, and the
distinctions are worth a table because each one was measured with a different instrument:

| quantity                       |   value | instrument                            | what it answers                                                          |
| ------------------------------ | ------: | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| wants a window                 |      90 | `classifyTemporalQuestion` (offline)  | how many questions are answered from one point in time                   |
| names a resolvable period      |      19 | `resolveTimeRange` on the wired route | how many the mechanism is **administered** to                            |
| the window splits the delivery | 14 (TR) | `window-reach.mjs` (offline)          | how many could be reordered if the admitted block were not already first |
| the delivery is **reordered**  |   **9** | `window-wired.mjs` (product)          | how many it actually reorders                                            |

**Only the last one is the reach.** The others are ceilings, and a bar written against a ceiling is passed
by a mechanism that does nothing: §13.152.4's criterion 4 asked for "at least 4 of TR's 8 reachable", where
8 was a ceiling and 7 is the reach. The difference is one question, and the reason to write it down is that
on a different corpus the difference would not be one.

### 13.153.5 The criteria, restated against the wired instrument -- and this is the last restatement

§13.141.5's rule is that a registered bar meeting a population that shrank is restated **once, in the
registration, before the run**. §13.152 did that and got the population wrong for a reason §13.152 could not
see: it priced a mechanism nobody had built yet, so "splits" was the closest available proxy for "moves".
The dispatch is registered against this table:

| #   | criterion                                                                        | what would falsify it                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the parse resolves every delivered turn, or names the questions it cannot        | **met on the control artifact**: 60,438 of 60,438, 0 questions named (§13.152.1)                                                                                                                   |
| 2   | the delivered multiset is unchanged, per question, on the treated run            | **met on the control artifact 500/500**; a non-zero on the treated pair is an assembly failure, not a result                                                                                       |
| 3   | the mechanism is administered on the temporal route and **nowhere else**         | any MR, IE, KU or ABS question whose delivery changes means a mechanism reached a route it has no window on                                                                                        |
| 4   | TR converts **at least 4 of its 7** reachable-and-wrong questions                | the bar is over half the reach. The reader's own churn is the floor to beat: two runs of one configuration differ on 59 of 500 states (§13.100.2), so 1 of 7 is inside the noise and 4 of 7 is not |
| 5   | TR sells **at most 1 of the 2** questions it reorders and the control gets right | a front-loading that buys 4 and sells 4 reads as zero while having had two effects                                                                                                                 |
| 6   | no question outside the administered set moves beyond the 5.0% reader floor      | a flow above the floor among untouched questions is a perturbation of something the reorder cannot reach                                                                                           |

Criterion 3 replaced §13.152.4's "10-20% of the roster", and the replacement is a **shape** rather than a
band. 19/500 is 3.8%, below the band, and the band was wrong for a reason the measurement produced: the
mechanism is not administered by a knob, it is administered by the route that is handed a reference date.
A percentage cannot police a reach that is a signature. What can police it is the statement that no other
capability moved at all -- which is checkable on the pair, and false the moment a second route gains a date.

### 13.153.6 The tool, and what it deliberately cannot price

`tools/window-wired.mjs --control <report.json> [--json]` replays each question's **delivery** through the
product twice. That is the right input for this mechanism, whose claim is about the delivery, and it is the
wrong input for the region axis: an artifact holds only the region the control chose, so a mechanism that
changed _which_ region is delivered cannot be replayed from a delivery at all. `expand-resolution.mjs`
stays the instrument for that axis (§13.150).

Twenty-two checks in `tools/__tests__/test_window_wired.py`, and the refusals are the load-bearing half:

- exit 2 for a malformed artifact (no `questions`, a record with no id, a duplicate id, no question text, no
  `turns` array, a turn that is neither text nor `{text}`, unreadable JSON) -- each replaces a plausible
  number with one wrong in a direction nobody notices;
- exit 1 for a well-formed artifact in which no question resolves a window, which is a different fix from a
  different command;
- a turn the reader cannot date is **not promoted**, and one of the tests is a turn whose weekday label
  disagrees with its date -- the fixture I wrote by hand first called 2023/02/14 a Wednesday, and the reader
  refused it. That is §13.152.1's validation catching its own author, which is the strongest evidence the
  check is load-bearing rather than decorative.

### 13.153.7 Cost: zero, and the comparison that matters

The reference's mechanism is one gpt-4o call per question with a period reference (§13.151.1). This one is
`resolveTimeRange` -- a pure function over a regex ladder -- plus a partition. The bill for the dispatch is
the bill of the control: 5,756 calls, unchanged.

That is the whole product argument for the increment, and the arithmetic changed twice on the way here. The
proxy estimated 70 calls; §13.152.3 counted 90 questions wanting a window and 68 the ladder could not
resolve; the registered mechanism administers **19 and pays for 0**. The reason is not that the ladder covers
more than §13.152.3 thought -- it covers 19 of the 45 TR questions that want a window, which is what
§13.152.3 said within rounding. It is that the mechanism registered here is **only** the ladder's own
population: the 26 questions that want a window and name a period the ladder cannot resolve are not
administered at all, so there is nothing for a paid path to do until one is registered for them
(§13.153.8). A free path in front of a paid one discounts the bill; a mechanism that _is_ the free path has
none.

### 13.153.8 What this does not do, and why not doing it is the discipline

**No model fallback.** §13.152.6 declined to buy 68 calls before knowing the free path's conversion rate.
That rate is now knowable from the dispatch: 7 wrong questions are in reach and the ladder moves all 7. A
fallback that resolved the 26 questions the ladder cannot (45 want a window, 19 resolve) would be a
different population, and buying it beside this one would make a single reading of two mechanisms.

**No window on `interval`/`ordering` questions.** 14 wrong TR questions are that shape, a single window is
the wrong instrument for them, and the temptation to widen the mechanism until the bar is met is the
§13.126 mistake in the other direction.

**No session route.** MR has 14 window-wanting questions and the block structure is the unit of order there.
Reordering blocks would destroy the boundaries the route exists to draw; reordering inside a block says
nothing. A separate mechanism would have to be registered for it, and it is not this one.

### 13.153.9 The rule this adds

**A bar written against an offline proxy must be restated against the wired instrument, and "the population"
is not one number.** §13.152's six criteria were an honest attempt to price an unbuilt mechanism and three
of them were written against ceilings: 22 firings, 9 splittable wrong, 12 firings on correct questions. The
built mechanism administers 19, reorders 9, converts 7 and sells 2. Every one of the four numbers is larger
than the one below it in the wrong direction -- the ceiling over-states the reach and over-states the risk.
The correction is not a looser bar; it is a different quantity, and only the product could produce it.

**Corollary.** A criterion that a route list satisfies is stronger than a criterion a percentage satisfies,
when the reach is a signature. "10-20% of the roster" was written for a mechanism administered by a knob.
This one is administered by which call site passes a date, so the criterion is "no other capability moved",
which a percentage can never express and which is false the first time a second route gains a date.

### 13.153.10 The first dispatch ran the wrong commit, and the failure was correct behaviour

The dispatch was issued against `main`. The push tool sends to `master`, because that is the branch it
reads off `origin`, and `main` was **seven commits behind** -- every commit of §13.148 through §13.153,
including the mechanism. So the first run of this dispatch (`40983733341`) executed code that did not
contain `window`, and `readQueryExpansion` rejected the value at parse time and the job failed.

**The rejection is the part that worked.** Had the arm defaulted an unrecognised value, that run would have
completed a full 500-question benchmark with `queryExpansion=none` and published it under the treatment's
name -- the exact defect `readQueryExpansion`'s docstring is written against, caught here by the rule it
states rather than by anyone noticing.

Two repairs:

1. `main` was fast-forwarded to the pushed commit (`47ca967`). It was a strict ancestor, so this is a
   fast-forward and not a rewrite; both branches now point at the same tree.
2. The dispatch was re-issued (`40984213349`) and its `head_sha` is checked against the pushed commit
   **before** the run is read. Every later push fast-forwards `main` onto `master` for the same reason: the
   two branches were only ever different because nothing compared them. That check is the general form of the defect and it belongs in the
   readout tooling rather than in a habit: `tools/ledger.mjs` and the run's own `memoryArmConfig` cannot
   tell whether the code that produced an artifact contains the mechanism, because a control artifact's
   config is what a stale-code run of a treatment would also print.

**The rule.** _A dispatch is a commit, not an intention._ "I pushed and dispatched" is two facts, and the
second one is unverified until the run's `head_sha` is compared with the pushed SHA. The campaign has
already paid for this shape of error once -- §13.110 records two artifacts 7.20 points apart with identical
config blocks -- and the cost here was a cancelled run rather than a wrong number only because the arm
refuses values it does not implement.

**Corollary.** The refusal is worth more than the value. `readQueryExpansion` throwing on `window` is what
turned a silent control into a five-minute failure; a parser that defaulted to `none` would have produced
the most expensive kind of artifact -- a plausible one.

### 13.154 The identity gate: a dispatch is a commit, and the commit is compared as content

§13.153.10 ends with the general form of the defect it records. This is the tool, and the three decisions
that make it a gate rather than a formality.

#### 13.154.1 The artifact cannot certify itself, and the SHA cannot be compared

Two facts fix the shape before any code is written.

**The artifact is silent on this question.** A report carries `memoryArmConfig`, which records what the arm
was _told_. It does not record what the arm _was_. The gap is not hypothetical: the failed first dispatch
(`40983733341`) would have produced a complete, plausible, correctly-configured artifact of the control
pipeline had it been told `none` instead of `window` -- the only reason it did not is that
`readQueryExpansion` refuses values it does not implement, which turns a silent control into a five-minute
failure. A check that reads the config block is a check that agrees with whatever the run printed.

**The SHA cannot be compared, and would be the wrong property if it could.** This repository is pushed
through the Git Data API, which rebuilds the commit and re-roots the same blobs under a new tree object;
`push-via-api.py` verifies content rather than trees for exactly that reason. The local `HEAD` and the remote
commit therefore have **different SHAs for byte-identical content**, so `local SHA == run head_sha` reports
`MISMATCH` on every correct dispatch and `MATCH` only by accident. And on the other side, a SHA says nothing
a reader wants: the property that makes a number attributable is _the same code ran_, which is tree identity,
not commit identity.

#### 13.154.2 Identity is the blob map

`tools/run-identity.mjs` compares two path->blob-SHA maps: the run's commit tree, read over the API, and the
checkout's tree, read by `git ls-tree -r`. Same tree means same code, whatever the commit object is called.

Directory entries are dropped on the way in. A tree object has a SHA like any blob, so keeping them makes
every directory a path the other side is missing and the diff fills with `packages`, `packages/cortex-memory`,
... until the one file that matters scrolls off the top. The two shapes that reach the comparison -- the
API's `{truncated, tree: [...]}` listing and the flat map -- are both accepted, because the live path and the
replayed path must compare the same thing; a tool that reads only one of them comes to pass on the path it
was tested on and to a different answer on the other.

#### 13.154.3 Five verdicts, and the two between `MATCH` and `MISMATCH`

| verdict      | meaning                                                                       | exit |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---- |
| `MATCH`      | the run's tree is the checkout's tree                                         | 0    |
| `CODE-SAME`  | only non-number-bearing paths differ                                          | 0    |
| `CODE-OLDER` | number-bearing files were **added** after the dispatch, none that ran changed | 0    |
| `MISMATCH`   | a number-bearing path changed, or the run has one this checkout lacks         | 1    |
| `UNKNOWN`    | cannot certify: no commit, empty map, truncated listing, malformed record     | 2    |

`CODE-SAME` exists because **every** docs commit lands after a dispatch that was correct at the time. A gate
that reds on a paragraph is red most of the time, and a gate that is usually red is a gate that gets
explained away -- at which point it is worse than absent, because it is still cited in a reading. The line is
drawn where the campaign has measured it: `packages/`, `tools/`, `.github/workflows/` and the root manifests
can move a number (`tools/readout-arm-run.py` runs _inside_ the job and prints the audit and spend tables, so
`tools/` is not readout-only), while `docs/` and anything under `__tests__/` cannot -- a test gates a merge,
it does not enter the job that produces the number.

`CODE-OLDER` was added the same day, for the situation the first run of this tool was in: the branch had
moved on **by adding files** while the dispatch was in flight. Then every differing path is `missing` from the
run's tree -- present here, absent there -- so every blob that actually ran is byte-identical and a file that
did not exist when the run started cannot have been executed by it. Measured on `40984213349` after this
section's own commit: four paths differ, one of them number-bearing, and it is
`tools/run-identity.mjs` itself -- so the answer is `CODE-OLDER` and the honest sentence is "nothing that ran
has changed". Reporting that as `MISMATCH` would have made the gate red for the rest of the campaign, which
is where a gate stops being cited.

Why a subset diff cannot hide a mechanism, which is the objection worth answering: a feature made only of new
files is unreachable unless something imports it, and an import is an edit to an existing file -- `changed`,
which stays `MISMATCH`. §13.153.10 is the worked example: twelve files missing **and** thirteen changed, and
the thirteen are what named the mechanism. A file the run has and this checkout does not is `extra` and stays
`MISMATCH` too, because that is code which ran and no longer exists.

`UNKNOWN` is not a soft pass. A run that has not started has no `head_sha`, and so does every record whose
field was renamed; both are states in which the tool knows nothing. It exits 2 and says which of the two it
is, because "no commit named" and "no map" are the same verdict and different repairs.

#### 13.154.4 The default fails closed

A path this tool does not recognise is **number-bearing**. The alternative -- a default of "probably docs" --
means a new directory silently joins the benign side, and the failure mode of that is a number attributed to
code that did not produce it. The recognised set is deliberately short and lives at the top of the file, so
adding to it is a deliberate act with a diff.

#### 13.154.5 The two measurements, before and after the repair

| run           | head_sha       | verdict                               |           paths that differ | number-bearing |
| ------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------- | --------------------------: | -------------: |
| `40983733341` | `82cf305f8706` | **MISMATCH**                          | 25 (13 changed, 12 missing) |         **15** |
| `40984213349` | `47ca9678bcc5` | **MATCH** -- 565 blobs byte-identical |                           0 |              0 |

The failed run's 15 are the mechanism, named: `packages/cortex-memory/src/prompt.ts`, `memory.ts`,
`types.ts`, `index.ts`, `bench/run-ablation.ts`, `packages/cortex-eval/src/bench-memory-arm.ts`, the workflow
itself, and four tools that do not exist in that tree at all (`window-wired.mjs`, `window-reach.mjs`,
`expand-resolution.mjs`, `recovery-reach.mjs`). The remaining ten are docs and tests, and the split is what
makes the verdict actionable: the same tool that says _this number belongs to other code_ also says _which_
code, which is the difference between a gate and an alarm.

The second row was taken on `40984213349` **while it was still `in_progress`**. That is the point of a
pre-check -- it runs before the artifact exists, not after it has been read.

#### 13.154.6 What it certifies, and the one thing that makes the record necessary

It certifies **code**, not inputs. Two runs of the same tree with different `cortex_memory_query_expansion`
values are the same code and different arms; the tool says `MATCH` for both, correctly, because the arm is
the dispatch's input and is recorded in the artifact's own config block. Code identity and input identity are
the two halves and this tool is one of them.

The live comparison is against the _checkout_, so it is only valid while the checkout has not moved past the
dispatch. Any later commit that touches `tools/` makes a correct dispatch report `MISMATCH` -- not a false
positive by the tool's own definition, since the local tree genuinely is no longer the run's tree, but a
useless answer for reading that run. So `--emit` writes the record that was compared, and the record is the
durable object: `--record` replays it offline, and the replay is what a reading cites once the branch moves.
That is also why this section is committed after `40984213349` was dispatched and why the reading of that run
cites `/workspace/run-40984213349.identity.json` rather than a fresh live comparison.

#### 13.154.7 The rule this adds
