_A dispatch is a commit, not an intention, and identity is content rather than a hash._

The campaign's most expensive class of error is not a wrong mechanism; it is a correct-looking artifact of
the wrong code (§13.110: two artifacts 7.20 points apart with identical config blocks; §13.153.10: a run of a
tree seven commits behind). Both were caught by a number that looked wrong, not by a gate. The two rules that
come out of this are cheap and they are both checks rather than habits:

1. Before a run's artifact is read, the run's commit is compared with the checkout, and the verdict is one of
   four words with an exit code a script can read.
2. After the branch moves, the comparison of record is the one that was emitted at dispatch.

#### 13.154.8 A name is enough to retire an orphan, and the tool found that by failing a test

The error class in this tool was called `Refusal`. `cortex-storage` exports a `Refusal` of its own. The
export census counts a caller as a **whole-word occurrence of the name in any repository file** that is not
a test and not a barrel, and it parses no imports -- deliberately, because scoping the caller search to the
declaring package yields 314 orphans out of 435 exports where the repository-wide search yields 196, and a
gate that is 27% false positives gets turned off within a week.

The consequence arrived as a red test rather than as a thought: adding this file took the census from **394
recorded orphans to 393**, and `export-census-gate.test.ts` failed naming the missing one --
`cortex-storage: Refusal`. Nothing imported anything. A tool that reports on run identity happened to use
one English noun that another package had already exported.

Three things follow, and only the first is local.

1. **The class was renamed** to `IdentityRefusal`. The prefix keeps the two identifiers disjoint under
   whole-word matching (`y` is an identifier character, so there is no boundary before `Refusal`), and the
   docblock on the class says why the name is not cosmetic, so the next tidy-up meets the reason rather
   than the rule.
2. **A test now holds it.** `test_run_identity.py` extracts every recorded orphan name from the baseline and
   fails if one appears as code in this tool. It runs on the code shape rather than the raw text, because a
   docblock that explains the collision has to be able to name the symbol -- which is the same reason the
   census blanks comments. Verified in both directions before being relied on: the prefixed identifier is
   not flagged and a bare `Refusal` is.
3. **The instrument defect is registered, not repaired here.** A file that never imports a package can
   retire that package's orphan, so an orphan can leave the report without a line of code changing in the
   package -- the one direction the campaign's coverage rules exist to prevent. The repair is import-aware
   caller detection, which would move the baseline by the 118 cross-package uses the wide scope was chosen
   to count correctly; that is a whole increment, measured on its own, not a slip into this one. It is
   registered in the plan as **P1-census** with its own bar: the same 394 minus the genuinely dead ones,
   with every removed entry naming the import that now accounts for it.

**The rule, stated so it can be applied elsewhere.** _A file outside a package is a caller of that package
until proven otherwise, and the proof is an import._ Until P1-census lands, the census's orphan count is an
under-estimate that any new bench or tool file can move, and a shrinking orphan ledger is the direction that
needs the explanation, not the growing one.

The reproduction, the comparison against the ledger's previous retirement -- `508fc62`, which removed
`cortex-memory: asksForCount` because the new tool **imports** it, 395 orphaned to 394 — and the three
conditions P1-census has to satisfy are written out in `docs/AUDIT-CENSUS-CALLER-BY-NAME.md`.

### 13.155 The run died on question one, and the cause was a wrapper landed two steps earlier

`40984213349` has no artifact. Its reference pipeline finished all 500 questions (+1,132s, 1,191 calls, no
retry, judge at 121/500 = 24.2%), and the cortex-memory side then **died on its first question**
(`id=e47becba`, +0.0s):

```
TypeError: Cannot read private member #lastRawOutput from an object whose class did not declare it
    at CortexMemory.lastRawOutput (packages/cortex-memory/src/memory.ts:508:17)
    at runBenchmark (packages/cortex-eval/src/benchmark.ts:442:52)
```

The arm wrote its own partial-measurement line ("INCOMPLETE, no delta") and exited 1, so the failure is
readable rather than silent, and the readout step then failed because no report existed. That is the
pipeline behaving correctly; what failed is code.

#### 13.155.1 The chain, in three lines

1. `traceReviewMechanisms` (§13.145's per-question review census, landed in `4f013cb`) returns
   `Object.create(system)`: an object whose **prototype is the instance**, chosen so that
   `isSessionAware`'s `'answerSessions' in system` still sees every route.
2. `runBenchmark` resolves the raw-output accessor once, as `system.lastRawOutput.bind(system)`.
3. `system` is the wrapper. The method is found through the chain, the call binds `this` to the wrapper,
   and a private name is installed **on the instances of the class and not inherited by objects derived
   from one**. So `#lastRawOutput` is not there.

The wrapper copies every member whose name starts with `answer` (the routed ones it intercepts) and
inherits the rest, which is exactly the set that cannot be inherited safely.

#### 13.155.2 Why no test saw it, and the shape of that miss

Every arm test builds its system as a plain object with **arrow functions** --
`lastRawOutput: () => 'Lisbon'` appears in four suites. Against an arrow, `.bind(system)` is a no-op, so
the wrapper is correct in all of them. The defect needs a system whose state is _private_, and no fake had
any.

> A fake cannot be less capable than the real thing and still find a capability bug.

This is the failure mode the campaign's "no mocks" rule is aimed at, arriving from a direction the rule
does not literally cover: these are not mocks of the thing under test, they are conformant `MemorySystem`
literals, and they are _legitimate_ for asserting routing. What they cannot do is express a language-level
invariant of the real implementation, and the suite had no fixture that could.

#### 13.155.3 Why it surfaced on this dispatch and not on the previous run

`4f013cb` landed **after** the last full-arm run (`40883121464`), so between P2a and this dispatch no
process had ever wrapped a real `CortexMemory` and called `runBenchmark` on it. The local gate could not
have found it (13.155.2), the type system could not have found it (`MemorySystem` is structural; the
wrapper satisfies it), and the identity gate would not have found it either -- it asks whether the run
carried the committed code, and it did.

> Two gates, two questions. Identity asks _did the right code run_; this run says yes. Correctness asks
> _does that code work_; only a run says anything.

So the dispatch bought something real: a defect that had been in the tree for two steps, found at the
first opportunity a dispatch existed to find it. The price was 1,191 reference-pipeline calls and 23
minutes with no artifact.

#### 13.155.4 The fix, and why it is at the wrapper rather than at the call site

Binding the two accessors the harness happens to read would leave the next one broken, and the failure
mode is a forty-minute run that dies on question one. So `mirrorMembers` makes the wrapper own the
problem: every function found anywhere on the chain becomes an **own** property that calls the real
instance, and every accessor is re-defined to read and write the instance. Non-function values stay on the
chain, because reading one does not depend on `this`.

`Object.create(system)` stays, because the chain is what makes the wrapper answer `in` and `instanceof`
like the system it wraps, and `runBenchmark` decides which routes exist by exactly those checks.

#### 13.155.5 The evidence, in both directions, on the real object

A unit test cannot be the whole answer here, because the unit test's fake is the thing that failed to
express the defect. So the wrapper was measured against a system with real `#private` fields **and**
against the real `CortexMemory` through the real `runBenchmark`:

| check                                                 | old wrapper                            | `mirrorMembers`                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `runBenchmark`'s accessor read (`lastRawOutput`)      | **TypeError**, the run's exact message | returns `null`                                                |
| state written through the intercepting `answer`       | **TypeError**                          | `raw:first`, and the original reads it too                    |
| `recoveryCensus()` called on the wrapper              | **TypeError**                          | `{ attempted: 1, answered: 1 }`                               |
| real `CortexMemory` + real `runBenchmark`, 1 question | **TypeError**, byte-identical message  | answers `['Berlin']`, raw output `['Berlin']`, trace recorded |

The last row is a scratch script over the built `dist`, run twice -- once with the call site reverted to
`Object.create(system)` and once with the fix -- so the identification of the cause is a measurement and
not an inference from the stack. `packages/cortex-eval/src/__tests__/review-trace-private-fields.test.ts`
keeps the three unit rows: it is the only suite in the arm that builds a system with private state, and
three of its six assertions fail against the old wrapper.

#### 13.155.6 What it costs and what it changes

- **P3c-2b is not read.** No artifact exists, so none of §13.153.5's six criteria has a value; the
  dispatch is re-issued after this fix, and it is the same commit plus a wrapper repair and nothing else.
- **Nothing in the arm's behaviour changed.** A user-visible no-op is the correct description: the fix
  makes an instrument stop throwing, and the twelve-hundred-call reference pipeline it crashed beside is
  untouched.
- **The partial report is worth reading for one thing.** It shows the failure at question one rather than
  question four hundred, which is what makes the cost one run instead of a run that looks like a result:
  the summary line reads `INCOMPLETE, no delta` and the delta fields are absent rather than zero.

#### 13.155.7 Two entries join the ledger, and rebuilding the ledger deleted a sentence — measured

Exporting the wrapper makes it and its trace type new orphans, because the census excludes test files from
the caller count and TypeScript has no package-private visibility. So `tools/export-census-baseline.json`
gained two entries (394 to 396 orphaned; the totals also moved 903/509 to 913/517 because eight exports
with callers had been added since the last rebuild and `--check` only compares orphans, so nothing had
noticed).

Running `tools/rebuild-export-census-baseline.py` to produce that diff then **deleted the previous step's
rationale sentence** without a word: the tool regenerates every group's prose from its own `RATIONALE`
dictionary, and §13.149 had hand-appended a paragraph explaining the `cortex-memory: asksForCount`
retirement. Measured: that group's rationale went 9,982 characters to 9,472, and the missing 510 are the
paragraph. It was restored from the pre-run copy, and the tool now needs to refuse this rather than do it
quietly — a ledger whose prose is regenerated from the generator is a ledger whose record is whatever the
generator remembers.

Three things worth separating, because they are three different failures wearing one diff:

1. **The new orphans are honest.** Two exports exist for a fixture that the old fixtures could not be, and
   the reason is written into the group. This is the `TEST SEAM` class the ledger already carries.
2. **The totals drift is honesty arriving late.** `--check` guards the orphan list, not the export count,
   so eight exports with callers accumulated unrecorded. The rebuild corrected them; that correction is
   not a change in the code.
3. **The prose regeneration is a defect**, registered as **P1-ledger**: the rebuild must abort when an
   existing rationale contains text the generator does not produce, with a test that appends a sentence to
   a fixture ledger and asserts the abort. Until then `rebuild-export-census-baseline.py` is a tool that
   silently discards the one thing the ledger exists to keep, and the only reason it is safe to run today
   is that this paragraph says so.

### 13.156 The rebuild tool is not allowed to edit the record it extends

§13.155.7 ends by registering this. It is small enough to do now, and it is the second instrument defect
this step found by using the instrument.

#### 13.156.1 What it did

`tools/rebuild-export-census-baseline.py` regenerated every group's `rationale` from its own `RATIONALE`
dictionary. The ledger's prose is **not** the generator's prose: each step appends a sentence when an entry
joins or leaves, and those sentences are the only statement of why the numbers are what they are. Running
the tool to record two new entries therefore deleted the paragraph §13.149 had added -- measured, that
group went 9,982 characters to 9,472 -- and nothing warned. `--check` passed before and after, because the
tool's output was consistent with itself.

#### 13.156.2 The rule, in three cases

1. **No ledger yet** -- write the generator's text. There is no record to protect.
2. **The ledger starts with the generator's text** -- write the ledger's. Every hand-added sentence
   survives, and this is the ordinary case.
3. **The two disagree some other way** -- refuse, naming the group and both lengths. It means the
   generator's own text was edited, so the recorded sentences may now be duplicated, superseded or
   contradicted, and no tool can say which of two accounts of one group is current.

All conflicts are collected before anything is written, so one run reports all of them; a tool that stops
at the first makes the operator iterate five times to learn five things.

**No `--force`.** An escape hatch would be used on the first inconvenient Tuesday and the defect would come
back with a flag in front of it. The manual merge is: edit `RATIONALE`, run the tool, read the diff.

#### 13.156.3 The verification, and the one that matters most

| check                                                                      | result                                                                           |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 6 unit assertions on `merge_rationale` (`test_rebuild_census_baseline.py`) | pass; 6 of 6 fail against the old code                                           |
| a hand-appended sentence survives                                          | preserved verbatim                                                               |
| a rewritten generator text                                                 | `RationaleConflict`, naming group and both lengths                               |
| `main` builds the ledger through the merge                                 | asserted on the source, the way `test_push_blobs.py` asserts verify-then-publish |
| **the real ledger after a real rebuild**                                   | **byte-identical** -- `diff` reports no change at all                            |

The last row is the one worth the run. Before the fix the same command removed two paragraphs; after it,
the ledger comes back byte-for-byte and both the §13.149 sentence and this step's own §13.155.7 sentence are
still in it. A tool that regenerates prose cannot be tested only on its prose -- it has to be run against
the file it is about.

#### 13.156.4 One more constant, removed

The tool wrote to the literal `/workspace/cortex/tools/export-census-baseline.json` and ran its subprocess
with `cwd="/workspace/cortex"`. That worked and was wrong the way a constant is always wrong: it made the
tool runnable from one directory on one machine, and it hid the destination from anyone reading a diff. The
root is now derived from `__file__`, which is the same repair `push-via-api.py` carries and for the same
reason -- a wrong destination should be unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.

### 13.157 The pair is the unit of evidence, and the diff is computed once

§13.153.5 registered six criteria. Five of them are statements about what **changed**, and every instrument
in this arm reads one artifact at a time: `window-wired.mjs` can say what the product does to a delivery,
and cannot say what the treatment did differently from the control. So the criteria had a table and no
instrument, which is the failure mode registered criteria exist to prevent -- a bar that is restated before
the run and then read by whoever is holding the artifact. `tools/window-pair.mjs` is the instrument.

#### 13.157.1 One diff, three partitions

| criterion                                                               | the comparison, and nothing else                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| 2, the delivered multiset is unchanged per question                     | the multiset of the delivered turns, per question |
| 3, the mechanism is administered on the temporal route and nowhere else | the capability the changed questions belong to    |
| 6, nothing outside the administered set moves beyond the reader floor   | verdict flips among the untouched                 |

Three tools would be three chances to answer three questions inconsistently, and a reader handed three
numbers has no way to tell which one is the wrong one. One diff, partitioned three ways, cannot disagree
with itself. The per-capability table is the whole of it: `ABS 30 / IE 150 / KU 72 / MR 121 / TR 127`, one
row each of multiset changes, order changes and flips.

#### 13.157.2 A multiset change is a comparability failure, not a result

The two artifacts come from two commits. If a pool moved between them -- a retrieval change, a budget
change, a parser change -- then a difference in delivery order no longer means the mechanism ran, and the
reading "the reorder changed forty questions" is exactly the reading that looks like a finding. So the pair
becomes `not comparable`, criterion 2 fails, and criterion 6 prints **not readable while criterion 2 fails**
rather than a zero.

Criterion 3 still reports, because its statement is about _where_ a change landed and not whether one
landed: a multiset change confined to TR says "not comparable, and the incomparability is on the route
under test", which is a different situation from the same change spread over MR. The tool does not
summarise that; it prints both verdicts and lets them both stand.

#### 13.157.3 An inner join is refused by name

The difference between "this question did not move" and "this question is not in that artifact" is the
difference between a denominator of 500 and a denominator of 495, and the second number is printed nowhere.
So `join()` fails with exit 2 and names up to ten ids per side. Ten is a compromise made deliberately: long
enough to identify the defect (a truncated roster, an arm that wrote a subset, two capabilities' worth of
loss), short enough that the message is a sentence and not a listing.

#### 13.157.4 Criteria 4 and 5 are not properties of the pair

"Reordered" is a property of the product on a question, not of the pair: a question the mechanism reorders
can come back in the same order if the window's turns were already leading the delivery. So the population
for criteria 4 and 5 is taken from `window-wired --json`, and the tool cross-checks the two sets -- the ids
the replay moved and the ids the pair changed -- printing the difference in both directions. Neither
direction is an error, because the difference is a definition and not a disagreement: replay-only means an
administered move that did not land on this delivery, pair-only means the delivery moved for a reason the
replay does not model. Both are worth a line, neither is worth a verdict.

#### 13.157.5 `converted` means two different things in the two tools

`window-wired` reports `converted` for the questions it moves that the control answers **wrong**: that is a
population. `window-pair` reports `converted` for the ones the treatment answers **right** among that
population: that is an outcome. The two numbers are both 7 on the control artifact and that is a
coincidence of the control's own state, which is the kind of coincidence that gets quoted as progress in a
status update. The detail line therefore reads `converted X of Y reachable-and-wrong (bar 4)`, never a bare
fraction, and when `Y` is not the registered 7 it appends `-- note: the registered population is 7`, so a
replay run against something else cannot have the registered bar applied to a population it was not
written for and still read clean. There is a test for that note, because a warning nobody asserts is a
warning that gets deleted by the next refactor.

#### 13.157.6 The floor needs a denominator, and the first test for it was wrong

Criterion 6's floor is 5.0% of the untouched questions, so a fixture has to be sized such that the ratio
lands on the side of the floor it is meant to test. The first version of the test used ten untouched with
one flip and asserted `met`; 1/10 is 10%, twice the floor, and the tool was right to fail it. The assertion
was the defect. It is now two tests -- 1 of 40 is 2.5% and meets the floor, 1 of 10 is 10% and fails it --
which is a shape worth keeping: a threshold test whose fixture sits on the wrong side of the threshold
tests the author's arithmetic rather than the code.

Thirteen tests in `tools/__tests__/test_window_pair.py`. The half worth naming are the ones that encode a
refusal or a distinction rather than a happy path: three conversions do not meet a bar of four; one sale of
two meets a bar of one and two would not; a delivery change on a non-temporal route fails criterion 3 while
a reorder on a temporal question is `moved` and not `changed`; a question present in one artifact only is
named instead of joined away.

#### 13.157.7 The self-comparison, which is the only reading available before the run

Feeding the tool the control artifact as both sides is not a test of the mechanism -- it is a measurement of
the instrument, and it is the one reading that can be taken on registered evidence before the dispatch
returns. Measured on `40751394094`'s report:

| capability | questions | multiset | order | flips |
| ---------- | --------- | -------- | ----- | ----- |
| ABS        | 30        | 0        | 0     | 0     |
| IE         | 150       | 0        | 0     | 0     |
| KU         | 72        | 0        | 0     | 0     |
| MR         | 121       | 0        | 0     | 0     |
| TR         | 127       | 0        | 0     | 0     |
| **total**  | **500**   | **0**    | **0** | **0** |

Criteria 2, 3 and 6 met; exit 0. What this buys is a false-positive rate of zero on this roster for the
comparison as written. A tool that had compared the raw turn records instead of the turn **text** would
have reported 500 multiset changes here -- every turn carries its own metadata, and two parses of one turn
do not produce equal objects -- and would then have failed criterion 2 on every real pair, sending the
operator to look for an assembly defect that lives in the instrument.

#### 13.157.8 The rule this adds

> A criterion whose subject is a difference is read by a tool that holds both sides, and that tool must be
> demonstrated on the case where the difference is known to be zero -- because zero is the only value whose
> correctness can be confirmed without the run.

The registration states what falsifies each criterion. It does not state what _reads_ each criterion, and a
bar with no reader is a bar whose reading is negotiated after the artifact lands. This is the reader for
five of the six, it refuses the pairs it cannot compare instead of joining them, and criterion 1 stays with
`window-wired` because it is a property of the product and not of the difference.

### 13.158 P1-census, measured: the name rule hides twenty-one exports, and the comment says the opposite

§13.154.8 registered this from a single instance -- `IdentityRefusal` retired `cortex-storage: Refusal` because the
word appeared in a file that imported nothing. That was one instance found by accident. This is the
measurement of the class, taken before writing any of the fix, because the fix's criterion was registered
against a population nobody had counted.

#### 13.158.1 What was measured, and with what

A throwaway resolver, not a shipped tool: it walks every `.ts`/`.mts`/`.mjs` outside `node_modules`, `dist`,
`coverage` and `.git`; blanks comments with the same rule the census uses; parses `import` statements
(including `import type`, aliases and multi-line lists); and resolves a specifier by four rules -- relative
with `.js`→`.ts`, a `dist/` path back to its `src/` file, a bare package name to that package's `src/index.ts`,
and a subpath entry to its target. Then, for each of the **517** exports the census says has a caller, it asks
whether any of those callers actually imports the symbol.

| reading                                       | count  |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------ |
| exports with a caller                         | 517    |
| every caller imports the symbol               | 450    |
| some callers import it, others merely name it | 37     |
| **no caller imports it**                      | **30** |

#### 13.158.2 The thirty, classified

The thirty are not thirty findings. They are six kinds of thing, and telling them apart is the whole work:

| kind                                                     | n   | example                                                                                                                                    | what an import-aware rule must do                                                 |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a second declaration of the same name, or a local shadow | 10  | `reciprocalRankFusion` exists in **both** `cortex-core/retrieval/fuse.ts` and `cortex-eval/retrieval.ts`; the eval callers all mean eval's | report ours as an orphan -- this is the finding                                   |
| a property, a parameter, a key, or a string literal      | 11  | `normalize: true` is an option key; `'unrun'` is a status string; `new Promise((resolve) => ...)`                                          | report as an orphan -- this is the finding                                        |
| an ambient global declared in a `.d.ts`                  | 4   | `env`, `pipeline`, `AutoTokenizer`, `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`                                                                   | **exempt**: these are declarations of the environment, not exports of ours        |
| re-exported, never called                                | 2   | `rerank.ts` re-exports `CrossEncoderRerankerOptions`; `natural-language-memory.ts` re-exports `clearEmbeddingCache`                        | **count as use**: a re-export is how a public surface is composed, not a dead end |
| imported through a subpath entry point                   | 2   | `makeRerankPipelineFactory` via `@agentix-e/cortex-ai/local`                                                                               | resolve `package.json#exports` subpaths, or it becomes a false orphan             |
| imported dynamically                                     | 1   | `const { TransformersEmbedding } = await import(entry)`                                                                                    | cannot be resolved statically: fail closed, count as a caller                     |

So **21 exports are currently reported as live whose only callers mean something else**, and 9 are artifacts of
the measurement or of a rule that has to be written. The first of the twenty-one is worth naming: `cortex-core`
and `cortex-eval` each define `reciprocalRankFusion`, the eval one is the one everything calls, and the core one
has no caller anywhere outside its own test file. It has been on no list since it was written, because two files
in another package say its name.

#### 13.158.3 The doc comment says the over-count is safe, and the over-count is the unsafe direction

`countCallers` records its own trade-off:

> The remaining over-count is in the safe direction _for a gate_: the tool's job is to find definitely-unused
> symbols, and a false positive (flagging live code) trains its readers to ignore it, whereas a false negative
> simply leaves one more symbol in the reported list where a reviewer can see it.

The first clause is right and the second is backwards, and the sentence got them the wrong way round. Two
different errors are being called by one pair of names:

- **Counting a caller that is not one** makes a dead export look live. That is a **false negative on the
  finding**: nothing is reported, and the reviewer sees a clean run. It is the defect this section is about.
- **Failing to count a real caller** makes a live export look dead. That is a false positive _in the report_:
  the symbol appears in a list a human reads, and the cost is attention.

The comment describes the second while arguing for the first, and it does not notice that the rule it is
describing produces the first. §13.154.8 caught one instance. This measurement says there are twenty-one, and
the reason nobody looked is that the note said the direction was safe.

#### 13.158.4 The registered criterion is corrected before the work, and it grows

§13.154.8 registered: _"the entry count is still 394 minus the ones that genuinely died, and every removed entry
names the import that explains it; the 118 cross-package readings do not change."_ That criterion can only be
satisfied by a change that **shrinks** the ledger, so it would have been met -- and read as success -- by a
repair that also created twenty-one new orphans and said nothing about them.

Restated, and this is the last restatement before the dispatch:

| #   | criterion                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the population **moves in both directions**, and both directions are enumerated by name before the diff is read: every entry that leaves names the import that explains it, every entry that arrives names the same-named thing that used to hide it |
| 2   | the 21 above are the _predicted_ arrivals. The count may differ; a difference is a finding, not a tolerance                                                                                                                                          |
| 3   | the four ambient `.d.ts` declarations do not arrive, because a `.d.ts` is exempt                                                                                                                                                                     |
| 4   | the two re-exports do not arrive, because a re-export is use                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| 5   | the three subpath and dynamic callers do not arrive, because they are live                                                                                                                                                                           |
| 6   | an unresolvable specifier counts as a caller. Failing closed here is the difference between one false orphan and a hundred                                                                                                                           |
| 7   | nothing outside the census changes: 913 symbols, 517 with callers, and the 118 cross-package readings hold                                                                                                                                           |

Criterion 2 is the one that makes this a measurement rather than a refactor: the population is predicted
**before** the tool is written, so a repair that produces a different set is telling us the resolver's rules are
wrong in a way the twenty-one did not predict.

#### 13.158.5 Why this is registered and not done

Three reasons, in order of weight.

1. **It is an instrument change in the middle of a reading.** The dispatch that measures §13.153.5's six
   criteria is running, and the census gate is part of `pnpm check`. A resolver that is subtly wrong turns the
   gate red for everyone at once, mid-measurement, and the pressure at that moment is to make it pass.
2. **The fix has four rules that each need their own tests**, and this window's budget belongs to the reading.
3. **The measurement above is the valuable half.** It converts "the name rule is imprecise" -- which is a
   comment -- into "twenty-one exports, named, in six kinds" -- which is a work item with a predicted outcome.

`tools/export-census.mjs --check` keeps its current behaviour until then. The one thing this section changes
today is that a reader of the gate now knows its over-count hides findings rather than merely adding noise, and
knows how many.

### 13.159 The paid path has a ceiling, and it is twelve questions for sixty-eight calls

§13.153.8 registered P3c-3 -- the model fallback -- with an increment of "the questions that want a window
and that the ladder cannot parse", and admitted the price was known while the **reach** was not. That is
backwards for a mechanism: the calls are the cost and the conversion is the reason, and a registration that
knows only the cost cannot be ordered against anything. This is the reach, read offline from the control
artifact at zero calls.

#### 13.159.1 The three populations, with the third one now split

`window-reach.mjs` has always reported window-wanting (90), ladder-fired (22) and fallback (68). The third
number was a price. It now carries the half that makes it a candidate:

| reading                                          | count                    |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------ |
| window-wanting (`eventLookup` or `relative`)     | 90 = 18.0% of the roster |
| ladder-fired, free                               | 22                       |
| ladder-fired and actually splitting the delivery | 15                       |
| fallback, one model call each per run            | 68                       |
| **fallback questions the control answers wrong** | **12**                   |

Per capability, because the aggregate hides where the mechanism has room: `ABS 0 of 1`, `IE 2 of 21`,
`KU 0 of 7`, `MR 4 of 12`, `TR 6 of 27`. Arithmetic: 90 − 22 = 68, and 12 of those 68 are wrong.

The figure of 26 that §13.153.8 carried for this population is superseded. It is not reproduced by any
partition of this artifact, and the population is stated here with the subtraction that produces it.

#### 13.159.2 Twelve is a ceiling, and the reason is three separate requirements

A wrong fallback question has to clear three gates before it converts, and the control artifact witnesses
only the first:

1. **wrong in the control** -- 12 do.
2. **the model must produce a window the ladder did not** -- that is the whole premise, and it is untested.
   A question the ladder cannot read is a harder question, not a random one.
3. **the produced window must split the delivered list**, and the answer must then flip.

The free path shows what discounting looks like on this corpus: the ladder fired on 22, split on 15 (68%),
and `window-wired` measures 7 of the 9 wrong-and-moved questions as converting (78%). Applied to the paid
path's 12, the honest prior is under 6 -- and the free path buys its 7 for **zero calls** while the paid
path spends 68 calls per run for a chance at the same order of magnitude. P3c-3 stays behind the free
path's reading, and it now says so with numbers rather than with an adjective.

#### 13.159.3 The tool reused a counter that counts the wrong thing

The first implementation reused `tally(fallback, (row) => row.record.correct !== true)`, and printing it
gave `questions=1` beside a fallback population of two, because `tally`'s `count` is the number of rows that
**matched the predicate**, not the size of the population it was handed. The test caught it in one run --
it asserts both the population and the wrong count, which is exactly the assertion that distinguishes the
two meanings. The counter is now built per capability with a field named `questions`, and the docblock says
why `tally` was not reused.

This is the third time in this arm that a reused helper carried a meaning narrower than its name (§13.153.4's
`converted`, §13.157.5's `converted` again). The rule the three of them add: **a count printed beside a
population has to be produced by the same expression that produces the population.**

#### 13.159.4 What changed in the tool and what did not

- `window-reach.mjs` gains one block and two JSON fields (`fallbackWrong.total`, `.byCapability`).
- Its 29 acceptance tests become 30; the new one pins both meanings of the number.
- No registered criterion moves. §13.153.5's six are about the ladder path, and nothing here touches it.
- The caveat is printed, not just documented: the block ends by saying this is a ceiling and that the
  ladder's own conversion rate is the only measured basis for discounting it. A number a reader will quote
  needs its dissuasion next to it.

### 13.160 The twenty-one, one decision at a time -- and the decision the resolver must make first

§13.158 counted them. §13.158.5 said the fix waits for the budget. That leaves one thing that can be done
now, offline, and that has to be done _before_ the resolver is written: **classify the twenty-one**, because
the classification determines the population the criteria are written against.

#### 13.160.1 Fifteen of the twenty-one are re-exported by their package barrel

| where the name appears                       | n   |
| -------------------------------------------- | --- |
| re-exported by `packages/<pkg>/src/index.ts` | 15  |
| nowhere else at all                          | 6   |

That is the policy question, and it is not a detail. Today a barrel is **excluded from the caller count**
(`isBarrelFile`), which is deliberate: the census exists to find dead exports, and `index.ts` is the standard
place a dead export hides -- `export { thing } from './thing.js'` is exactly what a half-finished refactor
leaves behind. So a re-export does not confer life today, and all twenty-one are orphans.

The alternative is worse than it looks. If a barrel re-export counted as use, then every symbol anybody ever
added to `index.ts` would be immortal, `export *` would make a whole module immortal, and the census would
report only symbols that were never exported from a barrel at all -- which is close to saying it reports
nothing. **The exclusion stays**, and this is the sentence that says so before anyone has an incentive to
change it.

Note that §13.158.2's "re-exported, never called" row is a _different_ case: those two are re-exported by a
non-barrel module (`rerank.ts`, `natural-language-memory.ts`), which is how a public surface is composed
across files. A barrel is a re-export whose only purpose is re-export, and a barrel line pointing at nothing
is the finding.

#### 13.160.2 The six that are not in a barrel: five local, one test-only

| package        | symbol           | declared                     | used at                                                                     | disposition                                               |
| -------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| cortex-storage | `matchesAllTags` | `storage/sql.ts:160`         | `storage/sql.ts:182`; `storage/pg.ts:151` declares its **own** private copy | unexport                                                  |
| cortex-eval    | `Arm`            | `assumption-ablation.ts:66`  | `:575`, `:582`, `:642`                                                      | unexport                                                  |
| cortex-eval    | `Ablation`       | `assumption-ablation.ts:69`  | `:84`, `:582`, `:642`                                                       | unexport                                                  |
| cortex-eval    | `Resolution`     | `assumption-ablation.ts:603` | `:619`, `:642`                                                              | unexport                                                  |
| cortex-eval    | `resolve`        | `assumption-ablation.ts:642` | `:700`                                                                      | unexport                                                  |
| cortex-eval    | `unrun`          | `acceptance.ts:736`          | **only** `__tests__/acceptance.test.ts:154`                                 | keep and record as a `TEST SEAM`, or delete with its test |

The sixth is the interesting one and it was found by checking rather than by assuming. `unrun()` is a real
function -- it returns the criteria whose value is `unrun` -- and its only caller in the repository is a test.
Since the census excludes test callers, a symbol kept alive by its own test is a fifth class, and the ledger
already has a name for it: `TEST SEAM`. So the disposition vocabulary is four, not three:

- **delete** -- nothing anywhere uses it;
- **unexport** -- its own file uses it;
- **test seam** -- only its own test uses it, kept deliberately and recorded, because the test is the reason it
  exists;
- **keep with the reason** -- something outside the name rule explains it, and the reason goes in the ledger.

Five of the six are the second case, and that case is the one the census **cannot currently report**, because
`isReferencedLocally` runs only when the caller count is zero.

The census splits a zero into two findings -- "exported but only used locally" and "not referenced anywhere"
-- through `isReferencedLocally`, which **only runs when the caller count is zero**. So a single incidental
mention anywhere in the repository suppresses _both_ findings at once: the symbol is neither reported as an
orphan nor reported as needlessly exported. The over-count does not hide one finding; it hides two, and the
second one is the easier cleanup.

#### 13.160.3 Two worked dispositions, to fix what "done" looks like

**`cortex-core: covers`** -- an English word exported as an identifier, re-exported at `index.ts:201`, and
every other occurrence in the repository is **inside a comment**: `retry.ts:105`, `llm-reranker.ts:13`,
`local/llm.ts:55`, `triage/writer.ts:163` are all prose. Nothing calls it. Disposition: delete the function
and the barrel line. The name rule could not see this for the same reason a spell-checker cannot: the word is
common, and the corpus is English.

**`cortex-storage: matchesAllTags`** -- exported from `sql.ts` and used at `sql.ts:182`, with a second,
private copy in `pg.ts`. Disposition: drop the `export` keyword. Not delete: the function is live inside its
file, and deleting it would break the module. This is the `isReferencedLocally` case the census should have
reported and cannot while the caller count is non-zero.

So "done" for one entry is one of the four in §13.160.2, named per entry. A repair that produced a list of
twenty-one orphans without a disposition per entry would move the problem from the gate to the reviewer and
call it a day.

#### 13.160.4 The eighth criterion

Added to §13.158.4's seven, before the work starts:

| #   | criterion                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 8   | every one of the twenty-one carries one of §13.160.2's four dispositions, the count of each is stated, and nothing is resolved by adding it to the ledger without a reason. A repair that moves them from one list to another without disposing of them has changed which tool ignores them |

The twenty-one are now named, classified, and two of them are worked end to end. What is missing is not
knowledge; it is the resolver, and it is the one thing that must not be written while a reading is in flight.

#### 13.160.5 The disposition table, measured -- and an example I got wrong in the paragraph above

§13.160.2 and §13.160.3 assigned dispositions by reading the _names_ in other files. That is the same
instrument whose output is being audited, used to audit it, and it produced an error of exactly the kind
being measured. `covers` was written up as **delete**: the barrel line at `index.ts:201`, and every other
occurrence in the repository inside a comment. Then the test files were read with the resolver instead of
with the name, and `knowledge/__tests__/edges.test.ts:169` calls it:

```ts
expect(covers({ start: 0, end: 10 }, { start: 0, end: 10 })).toBe(true);
```

So `covers` is a test seam, and deleting it would have broken a test that measures the behaviour the function
exists for. The error is recorded rather than quietly repaired because it is the fourth correction in this
section and the cause is the same each time: **a check that matches names cannot audit a claim about names.**

Read properly -- each of the twenty-one asked three questions: does its own file use it, does any test
**import** it, does a barrel re-export it -- the table is:

| disposition              | n      | the symbols                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **test seam**            | **17** | `covers`, `dot`, `norm`, `normalize`, `reciprocalRankFusion` (core), `unrun`, `Arm`, `Ablation`, `resolve`, `tokenize` ×2, `answerTokens`, `isAbstention`, `PROMPT_CONTRACTS`, `DEFAULT_PROMPT_CONTRACT`, `ASK_ROUTES`, `matchesAllTags` |
| **unexport**             | **4**  | `sleep` (cortex-ai), `Resolution` (cortex-core), `Resolution` (cortex-eval), `TURN_CAP_ROUTES` (cortex-memory)                                                                                                                           |
| **delete**               | **0**  | --                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **keep with the reason** | **0**  | --                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

Every one of the seventeen is a symbol whose only non-incidental consumer is the test that measures it. That
is not an accident of this repository; it is what the census's own rule produces: tests are excluded from the
caller count, so **any export that exists to be tested directly must look dead**. The ledger already has a
class for it -- `TEST SEAM` -- and §13.155.7 added two entries to it for the same reason.

#### 13.160.6 What this does to the priority, stated now rather than discovered later

The measurement changes what P1-census buys. It does **not** buy twenty-one deletions; it buys seventeen
**truthful ledger entries**, four unexports, and a gate that stops conflating "a test measures it" with "the
documentation mentions it" with "nothing uses it".

That is worth doing and it is worth doing later. The comparison is not close:

|                 | P1-census                                           | P3c-2b′                                                    |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| what it changes | which entries the ledger lists, and why             | whether the arm's mean goes up                             |
| what it risks   | the gate red for the length of one `pnpm check`     | one two-hour dispatch                                      |
| what it returns | 17 entries that stop being wrong, 4 exports removed | 0 to 7 questions, measured against six registered criteria |

A gate that reports seventeen false listings is a gate whose output is unread, which is a real cost -- and it
is still the cost that can wait one dispatch. §13.158.5's three reasons not to do it now are joined by a
fourth, which is the strongest: **the population turned out to be mostly seams, so the repair's yield is
smaller than the measurement that found it.** The measurement was worth its hour because it repriced the
work; the work was worth deferring because the price fell.

### 13.161 The reading: the mechanism ran, it converted one of two, and the bar was written for a population of seven

`40989420944` finished at `12abb060e504` in 127 minutes and its conclusion is **failure** -- the benchmark
step succeeded, the report uploaded, and step 14, the artifact audit, failed on one check. §13.161.7 is that
check. Everything below is read from the artifact, and the first two subsections exist because a reading has
to establish the thing before it prices it.

#### 13.161.1 Identity: the dispatch-time record certifies, a fresh run today does not

| when                                   | verdict      | why                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| at dispatch (`--run`, `in_progress`)   | **MATCH**    | 569 blobs byte-identical; the record is at `run-40989420944.identity.json`                                                                          |
| replayed from that record (`--record`) | **MATCH**    | same 569 blobs, 0 differ                                                                                                                            |
| a fresh `--run` today                  | **MISMATCH** | 3 number-bearing paths differ: `tools/rebuild-export-census-baseline.py` changed, `tools/window-pair.mjs` missing, `tools/window-reach.mjs` changed |

The three are the work of §13.157 through §13.160, all committed **after** the dispatch. None of them is
executed by this job: its fourteen steps are checkout, toolchain setup, `pnpm build`, dataset download, cache
restore, the A/B run, cache save, report upload, the audit, and the spend report. `tools/` enters none of them.
So the fresh `MISMATCH` is the gate answering its own question correctly -- _is this checkout the commit that
ran?_ -- and the answer is no, without any of the differences being able to reach the artifact. **The record is
what makes the reading possible**, which is the one thing §13.154.6 claimed for it, and this is the first time
the claim was load-bearing.

#### 13.161.2 The mechanism ran, and the artifact now proves it two ways

| evidence                                | control      | treated                  |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------ |
| `featureConfig.windowReorder`           | absent       | `true` on **500 of 500** |
| `questionDate` recorded                 | **0 of 500** | **500 of 500**           |
| replayed on its own deliveries: `fired` | 19           | 19                       |
| replayed on its own deliveries: `moved` | 9            | **0**                    |
| mean turns promoted by that replay      | 22.9         | **0**                    |

The last two rows are a new invariant and they are the strongest statement in this section: **the promotion is
idempotent**, so replaying it on a delivery that has already been reordered finds nothing to move. `fired = 19`
with `moved = 0` is the fingerprint of an administered run; a run that had _not_ been administered would print
`moved = 9` on itself. This is also what the artifact audit should be checking instead of the field it does
check (§13.161.7).

#### 13.161.3 The six criteria

| #   | criterion                                                            | verdict    | number                                                          |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the parse resolves every delivered turn                              | **met**    | 0 unreadable turns, 0 broken questions on both artifacts        |
| 2   | the delivered multiset is unchanged, per question                    | **met**    | 0 of 500; prompt characters identical on all 500                |
| 3   | administered on the temporal route and nowhere else                  | **met**    | 18 deliveries changed, **all 18 TR**; IE, KU, MR, ABS unchanged |
| 4   | TR converts at least 4 of its 7 reachable-and-wrong                  | **FAILED** | converted **1**, and the population is **2**, not 7 (§13.161.4) |
| 5   | TR sells at most 1 of the 2 it reorders and the control gets right   | **met**    | sold **0** of 2                                                 |
| 6   | no question outside the administered set moves beyond the 5.0% floor | **FAILED** | 36 of 482 = 7.5% (§13.161.5)                                    |

#### 13.161.4 Criterion 4's denominator was computed with a substitute, and the true population is two

The control artifact records **no `questionDate`** -- 0 of 500 -- because it was produced before the arm wrote
that field. `window-wired` therefore substituted each question's reference date from its delivered span, and
printed so: `substituted from the delivered span: 500`. The registered populations came from that replay:
19 fired, 9 moved, 7 reachable-and-wrong, 2 sold.

The treated artifact records the real date on all 500. Joined onto the control's deliveries, the same replay
gives:

| replay input                                      | fired | moved | reachable-and-wrong | sold |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | ------------------- | ---- |
| control artifact alone (substituted dates)        | 19    | 9     | **7**               | 2    |
| control deliveries + the treated artifact's dates | 19    | **4** | **2**               | 2    |

So the bar "at least 4 of its 7" was applied to a population of **2**, and 4 of 2 is unreachable by
construction. The tool said so without being told: `converted 1 of 2 reachable-and-wrong (bar 4) -- note: the
registered population is 7`. §13.157.5 wrote that note for exactly this failure and this is its first
production firing.

**What the criterion actually measured, then, is 1 of 2.** One conversion out of a population of two is 50%,
which is not a null result -- and it is not four, which is what was registered. Both statements are true and
neither may be used to cancel the other: **the criterion failed**, and its bar was written against a
population that does not exist.

#### 13.161.5 Criterion 6 failed against a bar set below the null

36 of the 482 untouched questions flipped, 7.5%, against a 5.0% floor. Two facts about that number, in order:

1. **§13.100.2 measures the reader's judgement flipping on 11.8% of questions between two runs of the same
   configuration.** A 5.0% floor is below the null, so the criterion fails on noise alone. The registration's
   own justification paragraph cites the 59-of-500 figure and then sets a floor at 25 of 500 -- the
   inconsistency is inside the paragraph, and it was there before the run.
2. **This run carries its own control for that noise.** The reference pipeline moved from 225 to 219 correct
   -- **six questions** -- with no mechanism touching it. The feature side moved from 417 to 415, two.

So the mechanism's whole effect, −2 questions, is one third of the swing the untouched side took by itself.

#### 13.161.6 The net, stated three ways because one of them is the only honest one

| reading                   | feature                                    | reference        | delta                                        |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| accuracy                  | 415/500 = 83.00%                           | 219/500 = 43.80% | feature **−0.40 pt**, reference **−1.20 pt** |
| per capability            | IE +1, KU +1, TR **−1**, MR **−3**, ABS 0  | --               | --                                           |
| the mechanism's own reach | 2 reachable-and-wrong, 1 converted, 0 sold | --               | --                                           |

The per-capability row is worth reading against §13.153.5 criterion 3: the mechanism is confined to TR by
construction and by measurement, and TR moved by **one question** while MR -- a route it cannot touch -- moved
by **three**. That is the reader's churn in its most legible form.

#### 13.161.7 The audit failed, and it failed on a field this mechanism never writes

Step 14 prints `FAIL expansion -- queryExpansion=window reporting None question(s) expanded; the roster has
121 distinct MR texts`. The check's premise is the reusable knob: setting `queryExpansion` must make the run
report what it expanded. The window path expands nothing -- it reorders the delivered turns -- so the counter
is `None` and always will be, and the artifact's actual trace of the mechanism is a different field:
`featureConfig.windowReorder` on all 500.

Three things follow, and only the first is about the audit:

1. **The check is right in form and wrong in its predicate.** "A knob that is set must leave a trace" is the
   invariant worth having; the trace it looks for belongs to the expand path. The repair is to read
   `featureConfig.windowReorder` when the value is `window`, and to assert the idempotence fingerprint of
   §13.161.2 -- `fired > 0` **and** `moved = 0` on the artifact's own delivery -- which is a stronger
   statement than a counter, because it cannot be satisfied by writing a number.
2. **A red conclusion on a green artifact.** The run's conclusion is `failure` while the artifact is complete
   and its six criteria are readable. That is the intended shape of a post-hoc audit (it must not be able to
   hide), but it means the run's colour is not the mechanism's verdict and must never be quoted as one.
3. **The knob is named for the wrong thing.** `queryExpansion=window` is a reused enum value that now means
   "reorder the delivered turns"; the audit's confusion is downstream of the name. Registering that as a
   separate rename would be a change with no measurement attached, so it is recorded here and not done.

#### 13.161.8 The verdict, and what P3c is worth

**P3c-2b′ is not separated.** Criterion 4 failed; the net is −2 questions against a −6 swing on the side the
mechanism cannot reach; and the population that made the criterion registrable was measured with a substitute
date. This is the same verdict P0 (`recover`) got, reached the same way, and it closes the free ladder:

> Under true reference dates, **exactly two questions** on this roster are wrong, window-wanting, parsed, and
> actually split by their window. The ladder converted one of them for zero calls, and two is its ceiling.

That ceiling is the number P3c has been missing since §13.152. It also **reverses the ordering the plan has
carried**: the paid path's population is twelve wrong questions (§13.159.1) and the free path's is two, so
P3c-3 is now the larger opportunity rather than the fallback to it. The next registration is written against
twelve, with the discount measured here applied to it -- one of two is a 50% conversion on a population of two,
which is the only conversion rate this corpus has produced and too small a denominator to be a prior.

Three things are now unambiguously the next work, in order:

1. **A control artifact that records `questionDate`.** Every population in this arm is computed against the
   control, and every one of them was computed against a substitute. This is a one-line registration and it
   makes the next reading exact instead of reconciled after the fact.
2. **The artifact audit reads `windowReorder` and the idempotence fingerprint**, so a run's colour means
   something about the mechanism (§13.161.7).
3. **A floor above the null** for any criterion of the form "outside the administered set". 5.0% was below
   the reader's own 11.8% and the registration said so in the same paragraph that set it.

### 13.162 Two repairs the reading asked for, and the second one was found by asking what the audit was reading

§13.161.7 registered two fixes: a control artifact that records `questionDate`, and an audit that
reads the trace the window knob actually leaves. Both are done. The first turned out to be a
defect rather than a missing field, and the way it turned out is the reason it is written up
separately from the second.

#### 13.162.1 `questionDate` was being dropped by a reduction, not omitted by a producer

The registered repair was "let the control artifact record the date". The treated artifact
recorded it on 500 of 500 and the control on 0 of 500, so the natural reading was that the
control predates the field. It does -- and that is not the whole story, because the field is also
dropped on a path both artifacts can take.

`withEvidenceBound` rebuilds every record through `buildQuestionRecords` when the report is too
large to serialize, and it forwards each field by hand. `questionDate` was not on the list. So a
run that carried the date at capture time and then had to reduce its evidence would publish an
artifact whose records read exactly like a producer that never reported a date -- and the
difference between those two states is the difference between "this run cannot price a window"
and "this run chose not to".

The test was written first and failed for the right reason:

```
-   "2023/05/20 (Sat) 10:00",
+   undefined,
+   undefined,
```

#### 13.162.2 The fourth time, so the check stops being per-field

`featureConfig`, `promptChars`, `recoveryAttempted`, `questionDate`. Four fields, four separate
discoveries, each by a reader who happened to need the field and noticed it was absent. A
per-field assertion cannot catch the fifth, because the fifth is the field nobody thought to
assert.

So the second test populates **every** optional field the record carries, reduces, and diffs the
whole record with the key list derived from the record itself:

```ts
for (const key of Object.keys(before) as (keyof typeof before)[]) {
  if (moved.has(key as string)) continue;
  expect({ key, value: after[key] }, `field ${String(key)} did not survive the reduction`).toEqual({
    key,
    value: before[key],
  });
}
```

A field added to `QuestionRecord` and not forwarded now fails on the field list rather than on a
reader's discovery. Both tests were confirmed red against the pre-repair build and green after,
and the exhaustive one was confirmed red **alone** with the forwarding line removed -- otherwise
the two would only prove that between them something covers the field.

#### 13.162.3 The audit now reads a conjunction, and refuses when it cannot

§13.161.7 said the repair is to read `featureConfig.windowReorder` "and the idempotence
fingerprint of §13.161.2". Written into `readout-arm-run.py`, that is:

| what the audit reads                                   | what it establishes                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `featureConfig.windowReorder === true` on every record | the run says it administered the mechanism                 |
| `queryExpansionCounts` absent                          | the count a window dispatch cannot produce is not invented |
| `--wired` replay: `fired > 0` **and** `moved == 0`     | the delivery actually carries the partition                |

The third is the only one that is evidence rather than a claim: the flag is written by the same
code whose correctness is in question. `fired > 0` is a conjunct and not decoration -- zero fired
with zero moved is idempotent too, and it is exactly what a run that never reached the ladder
prints.

The replay comes from `tools/window-wired.mjs --json`, produced by the workflow immediately before
the audit, and a replay that cannot be produced **fails the step** rather than being skipped. The
alternative -- run the audit without it and let the flag stand in -- is the hole the audit exists
to close.

Measured on `40989420944`:

| invocation                                                     | verdict                                                                                                                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--audit` with the artifact's own replay (`fired 19, moved 0`) | **all seven checks PASS, exit 0**                                                                                           |
| `--audit` with the control's replay (`moved 9`)                | **FAIL** -- "the replay fires on 19 question(s) and still moves 9, so this delivery does not carry the promotion it claims" |
| `--audit` with no replay                                       | **FAIL** -- "the flag above is the run's own word for having run"                                                           |

The run that failed this audit at dispatch time now passes it, with a check that is strictly
stronger than the one that failed it.

Seven tests, and the ones worth naming are the refusals: a partially administered run (one record
without the flag) fails and names the question; a run that published an expansion count on a
window dispatch fails; a replay that fired on nothing fails.

### 13.163 Which published number may be quoted beside which, and the injection that proved nothing

Every claim this arm makes about a competitor is a number produced by someone else under
conditions this repository did not choose. The natural artifact -- one table sorted descending --
is the one that produces statements like "83.0 would be second", and that sentence is a fact about
the harnesses read as a fact about the systems. `tools/competitor-ledger.mjs` exists so the
sentence cannot be produced.

#### 13.163.1 The unit is a five-tuple, not a dataset

Two numbers are ordered only when they agree on all of `dataset | variant | answer model | judge |
harness`. The first two say what was asked, the middle two say who answered and who marked it, and
the last says whose pipeline decided what reached the answer model at all.

`harness` is part of the key rather than derived from the other two, because two harnesses can
share an answer model and a judge and still differ in what they retrieve, how they truncate, and
what they call a correct answer. Grouping more coarsely than the truth can split a table that was
in fact comparable; it cannot merge two that were not.

Applied to the 23 entries the ledger currently carries, `--gap 83.0` reports **no comparable
group** and names the three groups that are equally near, each with the fields that differ. That
is the honest statement, and it is the one a ranking would have replaced with a number.

#### 13.163.2 One system, three readings, nineteen points

| system       | readings           | harnesses        | spread   |
| ------------ | ------------------ | ---------------- | -------- |
| Zep          | 90.2 / 79.8 / 71.2 | 3                | **19.0** |
| Supermemory  | 84.6 / 66.07       | 2                | **18.5** |
| Mem0         | 94.4 / 93.4        | 1 (two releases) | 1.0      |
| full context | 62.2 / 60.2        | 2                | 2.0      |

The last two rows are the ones that make the table readable. Mem0's 1.0-point difference is one
author's two releases, so quoting it as evidence that "the harness barely matters" would be the
same error as the one the first two rows demonstrate. The tool labels which is which and sorts
harness differences first, because a reader takes the first row as the largest finding.

The `full context` row is worth its own sentence: a system with no memory at all travels 2.0
points across two harnesses. That is the floor of the effect, and every memory system's spread
should be read against it.

#### 13.163.3 The comparison tables are not comparable either

The ledger's first draft failed its own check, and the failure was the finding:

```
apex-mem-published: members disagree about answerModel (Claude 4.5 Sonnet, unknown)
supermemory-published: members disagree about answerModel (GPT-5, GPT-4o)
```

The APEX-MEM table prints its own row at Claude 4.5 Sonnet and three baselines at an unstated
model; the Supermemory table prints its own row at GPT-5 and its competitors at GPT-4o. A
third-party comparison table is a **collection of conditions**, not one condition, and the vendor
whose row is at the stronger model is the one that compiled it. The repair was to name the
harnesses by their answer model rather than to relax the check -- the check was right.

#### 13.163.4 The injection that proved nothing, which is the entry worth keeping

The eight checks were demonstrated the usual way: break the implementation, confirm the tests go
red. Two defects were injected at once -- `judge` removed from the five-tuple, and the spread
ordering replaced with a plain magnitude sort -- and the suite came back **23 passed**. The
natural conclusion is that the tests are weak. The actual one is worse: the second injection had
silently failed to apply, because the string it searched for had already been rewrapped by
prettier, and `str.replace` on a missing needle is not an error.

Injected properly, each defect fails exactly one test:

| injected defect                       | tests failed                                                    |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `judge` dropped from the key          | `test_a_group_that_differs_only_in_judge_cannot_provide_a_rank` |
| spread ordering replaced by magnitude | `test_harness_differences_sort_above_version_drift`             |

> An injection that does not apply produces the same reading as a test suite that cannot fail, and
> the two are distinguished by nothing except checking that the defect landed.

This is the §13.154 rule one level down. The identity gate exists because a run's output cannot
certify which code produced it; this is the same defect in a five-line fixture. From here, a
negative control is confirmed by reading back the file it edited, not by trusting the edit.

#### 13.163.5 What the ledger refuses and what it prints

| reading                                                       | behaviour                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| an entry with no `source`                                     | refused, listed with every other problem in one run     |
| a group whose members disagree about `answerModel` or `judge` | refused, naming the field and the two values            |
| one system labelled as a same-harness reading                 | refused -- the label is earned by the systems it covers |
| an invalid ledger, with no `--check`                          | refuses to print any table, on stderr                   |
| a system read by two harnesses                                | printed, with the spread and the harness names          |

The last row is the point. A spread is not a defect to be rejected; it is the measurement of how
much of a published score belongs to the pipeline, and the tool's job is to make it impossible to
read a number without it.

### 13.164 The largest opportunity in this arm is twenty questions the memory arm loses to its own control

Every registration since §13.152 has been about a mechanism adding questions: the window ladder
(ceiling 2, §13.161.8), the model fallback (12 reachable-and-wrong, §13.159.1). Both are small.
The reading of `40989420944` contains something an order of magnitude larger, and it was visible
in a table this arm has printed for months without anyone reading the column.

#### 13.164.1 The per-capability table, read against the control rather than against zero

| capability | n       | feature          | reference        | delta    | discordant (ref-only / feature-only) | exact McNemar p |
| ---------- | ------- | ---------------- | ---------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------- |
| IE         | 150     | 141 = 94.0%      | 1 = 0.7%         | **+140** | 0 / 140                              | < 1e-30         |
| KU         | 72      | 62 = 86.1%       | 0 = 0.0%         | **+62**  | 0 / 62                               | < 1e-18         |
| TR         | 127     | 99 = 78.0%       | 84 = 66.1%       | **+15**  | 7 / 22                               | 0.0081          |
| **MR**     | **121** | **84 = 69.4%**   | **104 = 86.0%**  | **−20**  | **26 / 6**                           | **0.00054**     |
| ABS        | 30      | 29 = 96.7%       | 30 = 100.0%      | −1       | 1 / 0                                | 1.0             |
| **total**  | **500** | **415 = 83.00%** | **219 = 43.80%** | **+196** | 34 / 230                             | 6.3e-37         |

The MR row is the finding. The mechanism this arm exists to measure is **significantly worse than
its own reference pipeline on the capability with the second-largest question count**, at
p = 5.4e-4, and that is not a null result being over-read: 26 questions the reference answers and
the arm does not, against 6 the other way.

The same asymmetry holds on the control run (`40751394094`: 87 against 106, −19), so it is a
property of the arm and not of this dispatch.

#### 13.164.2 The 26 are one failure, and it is the failure §13.96 already named

Eight of the twenty-six, read one at a time:

| question                                                                                | gold   | the arm's answer |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------- |
| How many items of clothing do I need to pick up or return from a store?                 | `3`    | `2`              |
| How much total money have I spent on bike-related expenses since the start of the year? | `$185` | `65`             |
| How many movie festivals that I attended?                                               | `4`    | `3`              |
| How many times did I bake something in the past two weeks?                              | `4`    | `3`              |
| How many babies were born to friends and family members in the last few months?         | `5`    | `6`              |
| How many properties did I view before making an offer on the townhouse?                 | `4`    | `5`              |
| How many hours of jogging and yoga did I do last week?                                  | `0.5`  | `30`             |
| What time did I go to bed on the day before I had a doctor's appointment?               | `2 AM` | abstained        |

Seven of the eight are enumerations that come out **one member wrong**: five short by one, two
long by one, and one whose unit was aggregated instead of summed. That is not a reader failure and
not a retrieval failure in the ordinary sense -- the arm reached the sessions and read them. It is
a **membership decision**: which mentions count as instances of the thing being counted. §13.96
named that as the diagnosis three prompt-side attempts failed to move, and moved the arm's effort
to the window mechanism instead. The window mechanism is now closed with a ceiling of 2 (§13.161.8),
and this table says the diagnosis was right and the effort was aimed at the smaller half of it.

#### 13.164.3 Why this dominates everything else on the list

| candidate               | population it could convert                                                  | what it costs                                     |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **MR enumeration**      | **20 net, all 20 already answered correctly by a system in this repository** | one mechanism, measured against the same artifact |
| model fallback (P3c-3)  | 12 upper bound, discounted under 6 (§13.159.2)                               | 68 model calls per run                            |
| window ladder (P3c-2b′) | 2, measured ceiling (§13.161.8)                                              | 0                                                 |
| P1-census               | 0 questions; 17 ledger entries and 4 unexports                               | one `pnpm check`                                  |

The MR row is different in kind from the other three. They are _reachable_ populations -- questions
the arm might convert if a new mechanism works. The MR twenty are **demonstrated**: a pipeline
built from this repository's own components answers them correctly on the same haystack, the same
reader and the same judge. Nothing has to be invented to reach them; what has to be found is what
the reference does that the arm does not.

That is also the reason it is the cheapest to verify. The 26 are named, the 6 are named, and a
repair is separated by whether those ids move.
