```
              the other 473 are identical on both sides (24+/15-)

  attribution (the gain split by whether that record's prompt changed)
  population    n     gained  lost  net
  changed       27    4       0     +4
  unchanged     473   24      15    +9
  attributable +0.80 pt; churn 8.2% of the 473 identical
```

The note is on criterion 4 rather than replacing it because the claim that was registered reads total
accuracy, and a tool that quietly redefined a registered threshold would be doing what `§13.166.6`
refused to do. The verdict stays the verdict; the number beside it says what the verdict is worth.

### 13.173.2 Why `promptChars` and not the classifier

It is the only per-question field that is a property of the **prompt**, so "did the mechanism reach this
question" is decided by the bytes rather than by the shape of the answer. `§13.172.5` is what the other
choice costs: five off-by-one questions changed class with byte-identical prompts, and a classifier-based
guard reads that as a fallthrough when it is churn.

Where the registered population is named by a classifier -- the seven in criterion 1 -- the tool still
reads it from the before state's classifier, which is correct: those seven were named before the dispatch,
and re-deriving them afterwards would let a widened classifier judge itself. Attribution is a different
question and gets the field that answers it.

### 13.173.3 A record missing the field is unmeasured, never unchanged

An artifact from before `promptChars` existed has no prompt comparison at all. Filing those as
"unchanged" would report a population whose prompts were never compared as one whose prompts held, which
is the same collapse `question-record.ts` refuses one field over: absent is not a value. So they are
counted in `unmeasured`, excluded from both populations, and when nothing is measurable the render says
so in one line instead of printing a table of zeros.

### 13.173.4 Why the exit code does not move

The five registered criteria decide `0` and `1`. Attribution is a reading, and a pair that meets every
registered threshold exits `0` even when all of its gain was churn -- because the registered claims _were
met_, and the finding is what they are worth rather than whether they held. A test asserts exactly that,
with every gain on identical prompts.

### 13.173.5 The tests, and the injection that proves they bite

Five tests, `TestWhereTheGainCameFrom` in `tools/__tests__/test_arm_transition.py` -- the file goes from
19 to **24**, and the python tool layer from 891 to **896 passed / 1 skipped**:

| test                                         | what it pins                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a flip on a changed prompt is attributable   | the bucket rule                                                                                                 |
| a flip on an identical prompt is churn       | the same rule from the other side, plus `churnRate`                                                             |
| an unmeasured record is neither population   | the absent-is-not-a-value rule                                                                                  |
| the run this was built from reads as it read | 5 changed +4/-0 over 47 identical +3/-2 → `+7.69` attributable points, and criterion 4 still reading `+2.00 pt` |
| the reading does not move the exit code      | attribution is not a criterion                                                                                  |

The injection: with `attributionOf` filing every record as reached, **three** of the five fail
(`is churn`, `reads as it read`, `does not move the exit code`). The two that survive are the ones whose
input has no unchanged record to mis-file, which is why the fixture has both populations in every case
that matters.

### 13.173.6 What this does not claim

It does not make the +0.80 attributable to the operand contract rather than to the 273-759 extra evidence
characters the shorter instruction block admitted -- `§13.172.9` registers that gap and it needs a third
arm.

It does not turn churn into a correction. Subtracting it would be a model of the noise, and this run is
one pair; what is now mechanical is _measuring_ it, not removing it.

It does not replace criterion 2, which is still registered, still fires on form-class counts, and still
cannot distinguish a fallthrough from churn. Replacing it is a registration decision, and `§13.172.8`
records what the replacement should say.

## 13.174 The two criteria were measuring the instrument, and the repeats were never verified

`41039779987` was read twice. The first reading was the one `§13.166.6` registered and `§13.169` mechanised:
five rows, two of which failed. The second reading is this section: the same artifact, the same pair, judged
by rows that measure the claim instead of a proxy for it. The verdict changes in one place and the change is
the finding.

### 13.174.1 The six rows, as the tool now prints them

| #   | claim                                             | threshold                                   | verdict on `40989420944` → `41039779987`                               |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | named questions stop being reference-only         | at least 4 of 7                             | **pass** — 4 of 7 left, and all four converted to _correct_            |
| 2   | the reached population carries no systematic loss | losses ≤ 5% of it, net ≥ 0                  | **pass** — 0 lost of 27, net +4                                        |
| 3   | no capability loses more than 2; ABS unchanged    | band average                                | **pass** — MR 84.75 → 88.00, TR −1.75, ABS 29 → 29                     |
| 4   | the reached population buys at least 1.0 point    | attributable points                         | **fail** — +0.80 pt on the 27, of a +2.60 headline                     |
| 5   | the mechanism is visible in the prompt column     | moves on the named, equal outside           | **fail** — 20 of 114 outside moved                                     |
| 6   | the repetitions were repetitions                  | ≥ 95% of measured questions sent one prompt | **skipped** — no record carries `promptVariants`; this run predates it |

Rows 1, 3 and 5 are the rows `§13.166.6` wrote. Rows 2, 4 and 6 are not.

### 13.174.2 Row 2 counted a form classifier and called it a leak

The registered row read: _the ten off-by-one questions do not move by more than two_. Five of them moved, the
row failed, and the failure was reported as "3 or more flips among them: they read the control's bytes, so a
movement there is a fallthrough defect".

The premise is false in a way the artifact can check. All five movers have **byte-identical `promptChars`** to
their before-state. Nothing reached them. `off-by-one` is not a property of the request; it is a class the
failure classifier assigns from the pair (gold, answer) — `3` becoming `"3.0"` moves a question from
`off-by-one` to `answered` with no prompt involved. So the row counted form churn and its threshold — 2 of 10 —
sat _below_ the instrument's own churn, which the same artifact measures at 39 flips in 473 untouched records
(8.2%). A count whose threshold is under its noise floor will pass or fail on the draw.

What the row was for is damage where the treatment applies. That is measurable without a classifier: among the
records whose prompt actually changed, how many lost. A prompt that grew can distract a reader, so a band is
honest — 5% — but a **net** loss inside that band is still a net loss on the only questions the treatment can
be blamed for. Both halves are in the row, and neither of them consults the failure taxonomy.

### 13.174.3 Row 4 was satisfied by a variance

The registered row read: _overall accuracy rises by at least 1.0 point_. It rose 2.60 and the row passed. Of
those 2.60 points, **+0.80** came from the 27 questions whose prompt changed and the remaining **+1.80** came
from 24 gains against 15 losses on 473 records that received byte-identical prompts.

That is not a mechanism with a lucky draw attached; it is a draw with a mechanism somewhere inside it. A row
that a variance can satisfy is a row that cannot fail for the reason it exists, and the consequence of the old
reading was worse than a miss: it converted a null result into a pass and made the next dispatch look
justified. The replacement reads the population the treatment reached and divides by the whole run, so the
number is commensurable with the headline and still attributable: `net(changed) / measured × 100`.

### 13.174.4 The run does not clear the amended accuracy gate

|         | registered row 4             | amended row 4                     |
| ------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| reading | `83.00% → 85.60% (+2.60 pt)` | `attributable +0.80 pt on the 27` |
| verdict | pass                         | **fail**                          |

Both numbers come from one artifact and neither is wrong. The difference is what each is a statement about.
The operand ask **does** what it was registered to do — it reaches 27 questions, converts 4, and loses none —
and it does **not** buy the point that would justify calling it a win on the run's own scale. The next
dispatch is therefore a question about reach, not about wording: at 4 conversions in 500 questions the gate is
one conversion away, and at the run's own rate (4 of 27) that one conversion costs 34 reached questions.

### 13.174.5 `promptVariants`: the premise, measured inside one run

`§13.171`'s `promptDigest` compares two **artifacts**: same digest, same bytes. The cache prediction `§13.147.3`
made is about two **passes of one run**, and a digest taken from pass 1 says nothing about what passes 2-4 sent.
That is a defect in the instrument built to test the prediction, and it is the reason three explanations
(requests not byte-identical / provider does not cache across ~25 minutes / the four passes are not the shape
the cache model assumes) survived two artifacts.

`promptVariants` is one integer per question: how many **distinct** prompts that question cost across the
passes. `1` everywhere means the repeats were repeats; `4` means the arm sent four prompts and called them
repetitions. The four hops:

| hop                   | what it does                                                                                     | why there                                                                                            |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `benchmark.ts`        | captures `lastPromptText` on every pass of the **feature** arm                                   | the accessor already exists and the flag that carries it is the one that means "what the reader saw" |
| `ablation.ts`         | folds each pass's text into a per-question set of distinct values, then drops the pass's vectors | the comparison is the only thing that needs the bytes; the artifact must not grow by `runs`          |
| `AblationResult`      | carries `featurePromptVariants`                                                                  | a report shape, not a live evaluation                                                                |
| `bench-memory-arm.ts` | writes `promptVariants` on the record                                                            | the record is where a reader of the JSON looks                                                       |

Three rules, each with a test:

- **absent at `runs: 1`.** A distinct count over one sample is the constant `1`, and printing it would let a
  reader compare a one-pass artifact with a four-pass one as if both had measured repetition. This is the rule
  `featureCorrectByRun` already follows.
- **`null` if any pass declined to report.** A system that says "no prompt" on pass 3 has not shown that pass 3
  matched pass 1, and the count of prompts we happened to see is not the count of prompts that were sent.
- **per question, not per run.** A single run-level flag would erase the shape most likely to be true: a
  handful of questions whose prompt diverges because their evidence assembly is not deterministic.

The hash stays at the arm and the comparison stays in the engine, which is a division of labour rather than a
preference: `cortex-memory` imports no host API and the entry-point graph of `cortex-eval` is host-free today,
so `prompt-digest.ts` remains the only file in the package that imports `node:crypto`. Distinctness needs no
hash at all — `===` on two strings is exact and cheaper than a collision argument.

### 13.174.6 What this section does not claim

- **It does not settle the cache question.** Every artifact in the archive predates the field. Criterion 6 is
  `skipped` on all of them, and it will stay skipped until a run carries `promptVariants` — which the next
  dispatch does at no extra cost, because the capture rides a pass the run already pays for.
- **It does not make the operand ask a success.** Under the amended rows the run fails the accuracy gate. What
  it establishes is narrower and stronger: the treatment does not damage what it touches.
- **It does not separate the mechanism from the 273–759 characters it adds.** Criterion 2 says the reached
  population is unharmed and criterion 4 says it is not yet worth a point; neither says whether the +0.80 is
  the operand wording or the extra text. `§13.172.9` named that gap and this section does not close it: it
  needs a third arm with the wording at the old budget.
- **It does not re-register rows 1, 3 and 5.** They were falsifiable, they were tested, and two of them failed
  on this run for reasons that have nothing to do with the amendment.

### 13.174.7 Verification

- `tools/arm-transition.mjs`: criteria 2 and 4 replaced, 6 added, `criteriaSource` printed so a reading cannot
  be mistaken for the registration it is not. The off-by-one table survives as a diagnostic and no longer
  carries a verdict.
- `tools/__tests__/test_arm_transition.py` 24 → **33**. The new tests pin the two boundaries that matter
  (`1 of 20` passes, `2 of 20` fails; `+1.00` passes, `+0.99` fails), the churn shape of the run that caused
  the amendment (27 changed +4/−0, 473 identical +24/−15 → `+0.80`), and the premise row's arithmetic
  (`38/40` passes, `18/20` fails, `null` counts against).
- Three injections — `CHANGED_MAX_LOSS_SHARE = 0.10`, `ATTRIBUTABLE_MIN_POINTS = 0.0`,
  `REPEAT_PREMISE_MIN_SHARE = 0.5` — fail **5** tests. The tool layer is **905 passed / 1 skipped**.
- `prompt-variants.test.ts` (7 tests) plus one arm-level pairing test: the count is 1 when the passes agree, 2
  when one differs, 4 when none does, `null` when a pass declines, absent at one pass, and the exported text
  vector stays at pass 1 while the count reaches 4.
- `report-write`'s derived-key loop covers `promptVariants`, proved by removing the forward:
  `field promptVariants did not survive the reduction`, 1 failed / 27 passed.
- `cortex-eval` coverage: all files **99.51 / 99.04 / 99.43 / 99.51**; `ablation.ts`, `benchmark.ts`,
  `metrics.ts`, `prompt-digest.ts`, `report-write.ts` all **100**.

### 13.174.8 The next dispatch, registered before it ran

`41090564131` was dispatched at `cac56f1d` with the same payload as `41039779987` — `ask: operands`,
`relevance-hybrid` at `top_k: 256`, `max_prompt_chars: 48000`, `review_pass: bare`, 4 repetitions,
temperature 0, `limit: 0` — and it is a **second draw of the same treatment** rather than a new one. The
reason is the gate this section amended: criterion 4 now reads `+0.80` on the reached population, and a
figure one conversion below a threshold cannot be judged without knowing what the figure's own variance is.
`41039779987` supplies one draw; this run supplies a second, and the difference between them is the noise
the threshold has to clear.

What the run is expected to settle, in order:

| reading            | passes when                                                | fails when                                                                                                        |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| row 6, first ever  | ≥ 95% of measured questions carry `promptVariants == 1`    | the arm sent more than one prompt per question; every cost column in the run is then unreadable rather than wrong |
| row 4, second draw | attributable ≥ +1.0 pt                                     | below, and the two draws together bound how far `+0.80` was a draw                                                |
| row 2              | unchanged: 0 losses on the reached population              | any loss beyond 5% of it                                                                                          |
| row 5              | unchanged: 20 of 114 outside records moved is still a fail | —                                                                                                                 |

Row 5 is expected to fail again and is not a reason to stop: it is the assembly check reporting that the
operand contract moved prompt sizes on records the registration did not name, which `§13.172.3` already
read as the mechanism's true reach being 27 rather than 7. The row is kept because a fail that is understood
and stable is the cheapest possible record of a registration that named the wrong population.

### 13.175 The second draw: the repeats were not repeats, and the noise floor is 2.2 points

`41090564131` ran at `cac56f1d` with a payload byte-identical to `41039779987` and completed `success` at
`18:38:51Z`. It was dispatched as a second draw of one treatment (`§13.174.8`) and it answered a larger
question than the one it was dispatched for.

#### 13.175.1 The reading

| row | verdict | what it said                                                                                                                         |
| --- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1   | skipped | the registered population is 7; this pair has 3                                                                                      |
| 2   | skipped | no question's prompt moved, so the treatment reached nothing to damage                                                               |
| 3   | pass    | ABS 29→29, IE −2 avg, KU −0.5, MR +1.5, TR +0.75                                                                                     |
| 4   | fail    | attributable **+0.00 pt** on 0 changed records; headline 85.60% → 83.40%; churn 14+/25− across the 500 whose `promptChars` are equal |
| 5   | fail    | 0/3 named moved, 0/118 outside moved, named still equal: `d905b33f` `a1cc6108` `c18a7dc8`                                            |
| 6   | fail    | **0/121 sent one prompt**; 121 divergent at 4; 0 unverifiable                                                                        |

#### 13.175.2 Row 6 is the finding, and it invalidates the cost columns

The run reports `4` distinct prompts on **all 500 questions**, not just MR's 121. Its own cost table —
5,653 calls, 31,078,387 prompt tokens, 329,837 completion tokens, 3,222,044 cached (10.37%) — is therefore
**unreadable rather than wrong**, which is the distinction `§13.174.5` registered in advance. A run whose
passes sent four different requests is not a cheaper version of anything: the comparison it invites is
between two prompts, not between two budgets.

#### 13.175.3 The cache premise dies with it, and `§13.168.8` needs an erratum

`§13.147.3` predicted a 60–80% prefix-cache share from the premise that passes 2–4 resend pass 1's bytes.
Two artifacts read 6.47% and 11.16%, and `§13.168.8` framed the gap as three candidates: the provider
declines, the fingerprint measures the wrong thing, or **the passes were never repetitions**. Row 6 says the
third. The immediate consequence is that `§13.168.9`'s comparison of 11.16% against 60–80% is withdrawn: a
10.4% share is roughly what four genuinely different prompts should produce, so it implies no defect at all.
The instrument was measuring a premise, and the premise was false.

#### 13.175.4 Rows 4 and 5 were mis-registered, and the tool says so out loud

This pair has one configuration on both sides, so "the 3 named questions' `promptChars` move" could never
pass and "the reached population buys a point" could never be read. `§13.174.8` registered both anyway. That
is the fourth time in this campaign that a criterion named a population the intervention could not reach, and
the pattern is now stable enough to state as a rule: **a row that compares two dispatches of one payload is a
row about the tool, not about the arm.**

#### 13.175.5 What the second draw did buy: the noise floor

With identical payload, identical carried evidence and identical per-question digests unmeasurable, the
first repetition read **85.60%** on one dispatch and **83.40%** on the other — **−2.20 pt, eleven questions of
five hundred** — while MR's first repetition was identical at 89/121 on both. Two facts follow, and they cost
the campaign more than the run earned:

- **A single dispatch cannot resolve an increment below ~2.2 points.** Every "+X pt" in this document that is
  smaller than that is a redraw until a second dispatch of the same payload says otherwise.
- **The operand ask has no demonstrated effect.** `§13.174.4` read `+0.80` on the reached population and
  called it one conversion short of the bar; the second draw reads `+0.00`, and `+0.80` sits inside a band
  whose width is 2.2. The honest statement of the campaign's `+2.60` / `+0.80` pair is now **one draw of a
  treatment whose effect is not distinguishable from noise.**

#### 13.175.6 The instrument defect behind row 6, and why the arm is not the suspect

Four prompts per question and 500/500 divergent records can be produced by a stateful arm or by inputs that
drift. The artifact rules the first out at one level and cannot rule it out at another, so it was tested:

| comparison                              | result                                           |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| carried turn indices, in order          | **500/500 identical** between the two dispatches |
| `evidenceChars` (the offer)             | 500/500 identical                                |
| `promptChars` (what the prompt carried) | 500/500 identical                                |
| `promptDigest`                          | **0/500 identical**                              |

Equal evidence bytes and unequal prompts leave only the invariant part of the prompt — `QUESTION:` and the
instruction block — and a count cannot name bytes. `prompt-determinism.test.ts` is the arm-level test: one
instance, one question, one evidence set, four passes, on the flat route, the flat route with a constant
relevance signal, and the multi-session route. All three send byte-identical prompts (24,000 / 23,498 /
47,869 bytes). **So the arm does not carry state across passes, and the drift is in what the arm is handed.**
That is a finding about the bench, and `§13.176` builds the instrument that names it.

#### 13.175.7 What this section does not claim

- **Not that the operand wording is wrong.** Nothing here measures the wording; the draw that would have
  measured it is the draw that turned out to be noise.
- **Not that the arm is broken.** It is deterministic given its inputs on the three routes tested.
- **Not that the cost arithmetic is wrong.** It is unreadable: `§13.174.5` said this would happen and this is
  what it looks like.
- **Not that MR regressed.** MR's first repetition is 89/121 on both draws. The 2.2 points moved elsewhere,
  across 14 gains and 25 losses on records whose prompt length did not change.

### 13.176 The witness: one question's prompts, in full

#### 13.176.1 Why a count was not enough

`§13.174` shipped `promptVariants`, and the first run that carried it reported the most useless true answer
available: `4` everywhere. A count answers _whether_ the passes resent one request. It cannot answer _what
moved_, and `§13.175.6` narrowed the answer to the invariant part of the prompt by measurement rather than by
guess. Naming it needs bytes.

#### 13.176.2 What the witness carries, and why so little

`featurePromptRepeatWitness` holds one question's prompt per repetition, plus `commonPrefix[i]`: the number of
leading bytes pass `i` shares with pass 1. Absent at `runs: 1`, because there is no second pass to diff.

- **One question, not a vector.** Four prompts at the registered ceiling are already ~190,000 characters and
  the artifact is 75 MB before anything else is added.
- **The first dataset position whose first pass reported a prompt.** A witness is read by diffing passes
  against each other, so any answered question serves; the first is the only choice that reproduces without a
  seed and can be compared across dispatches.
- **`null`, not a number, at index 0 and wherever a pass reported no prompt.** A pass agrees with itself
  everywhere, and writing that length would read as a measurement of agreement.

#### 13.176.3 The reading, and the one place it refuses to trust the writer

`tools/arm-transition.mjs` recomputes the prefix from the bytes rather than printing the stored figure, and
reports a disagreement as `misreportedPasses` instead of resolving it. The reading is an offset plus 60 bytes
each side of it:

```
prompt repeat witness (§13.176)
  witness `e47becba` (position 0); leading bytes shared with pass 1: 1=— 2=47840 3=47840 4=47840
  pass 2 diverges at byte 47840:
    pass 1: …<the last 60 bytes pass 1 sent>…
    pass 2: …<the last 60 bytes pass 2 sent>…
```

The shape of that output is the whole experiment: an offset near the end of the prompt says the instruction
block moved; an offset near zero says the evidence did, which would contradict `§13.175.6` and reopen the
carried-set question.

#### 13.176.4 The tests, and the injection that proves they bite

- `prompt-variants.test.ts` 7 → **14**: the witness keeps each pass, reports a full-length prefix when the
  passes truly resent one request (10/10), is absent at one pass, witnesses the first question that _reported_
  a prompt rather than the first question, refuses a prefix for a pass with no prompt, and reaches the
  Markdown document (`| 1 | 26 | — |`, `| 2 | 26 | 25 |`).
- `prompt-determinism.test.ts` (new, 3 tests): the arm is a function of its inputs on three routes.
- `test_arm_transition.py` 33 → **39**: the offset is the first byte the passes do not share, identical passes
  report no divergence, a pass with no prompt is labelled rather than prefixed, an artifact without a witness
  says so, the witness is read from the run and not from a top-level record, and a stored prefix the bytes do
  not support is reported rather than trusted.
- Injection: `commonPrefixByPass` forced to return `0` fails **4** tests. Tool layer **911 passed / 1 skipped**.
- `cortex-eval` all files **99.51 / 98.96 / 99.43 / 99.51**; `cortex-memory` **100 / 100 / 100 / 100**.

#### 13.176.5 The next dispatch, registered before it runs

Payload: `maxPromptChars 48000 → 96000`, everything else identical to `cac56f1d` (`ask: operands`,
`relevance-hybrid` at `top_k: 256`, `review_pass: bare`, 4 repetitions, temperature 0, `limit: 0`).

Why this variable, from the artifact rather than from taste: **every one of the 121 MR prompts is at the
ceiling** (`promptChars` min ≥ 45,000, median 46,264, max 46,841 against a 48,000 budget), the median MR
question carries 174 turns of which 16 are truncated at 400 characters, and the median **failing** MR question
delivers 12 of its 17 gold turns. Reach, not ranking, is the binding constraint on that route, and the ceiling
is the cheapest way to test it.

| row                         | passes when                                                                                       | fails when                                                                                      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1 reach                     | median MR `promptChars` ≥ 60,000                                                                  | below 48,000, which would mean the ceiling was never the constraint and the budget was          |
| 2 accuracy (paired, in-run) | MR first repetition ≥ the reference pipeline's MR **on the same run** (103/121 at the draw above) | below it — this row is in-run precisely because `§13.175.5` measured a 2.2-point cross-run band |
| 3 damage                    | no capability's first repetition falls more than 2 questions below the before draw                | beyond, and the 2.2-point band is the reason the bar is 2 and not 0                             |
| 4 cost                      | prompt tokens per question ≤ 2.1× the before draw, read as tokens                                 | above; and **no cache share is quoted while row 6 fails**                                       |
| 5 witness                   | the artifact carries a witness and the tool names the first divergence offset                     | absent, which makes the next reading as blind as this one                                       |
| 6 premise (diagnostic)      | ≥ 95% of questions sent one prompt                                                                | retained and expected to fail; a fail is recorded, not acted on                                 |

Row 2 is the campaign's first genuinely paired accuracy criterion. Every previous accuracy row compared a run
against an archived run, and `§13.175.5` is the bill for that: two dispatches of one payload differ by 2.2
points, which is larger than most of the increments this document has claimed.

### 13.177 The ceiling run: reach bought TR twelve, cost KU eight, and the witness named a defect in the arm

`41144910162` ran at `01a0cf0c` with `maxPromptChars` raised 48,000 → 96,000 and every other field identical to
`cac56f1d`. It completed `success` at `01:34:46Z` in 2h04m. Its six criteria were registered in `§13.176.5`
**before** it ran, and they were chosen so that a null result would be as readable as a positive one.

#### 13.177.1 The reading

| row                        | verdict               | what it said                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1 reach                    | **pass**              | MR `promptChars` min 58,987 / median **67,133** / max 75,356, against a 60,000 bar and a 46,264 median before |
| 2 accuracy (in-run paired) | **fail**              | MR **87/121 (71.9%)** against the reference arm's **100–102/121 (82.6–84.3%)** on the same run                |
| 3 damage                   | **fail**              | KU **64 → 56 (−8)**; MR 89 → 87 (−2, at the bar); IE +1; TR **+12**; ABS 0; overall 417 → 420                 |
| 4 cost                     | **pass**              | 50,301,437 prompt tokens, **1.618×** the before draw's 31,078,387, against a 2.1× ceiling                     |
| 5 witness                  | **pass**              | witness present; the four passes agree on **14 bytes** of 94,674                                              |
| 6 premise (diagnostic)     | **fail, as retained** | 0/500 questions sent one prompt; `promptVariants == 4` on all 500                                             |

Cache share fell 10.37% → **8.70%**, which row 6 says is not a fact about the provider.

#### 13.177.2 The trade the ceiling bought, and why it is not the default

Sixteen of 121 MR questions reached evidence they could not reach before (median prompt 46,264 → 67,133 bytes),
and the temporal route gained **12 questions** — the largest single capability move this campaign has recorded
from a budget change. The bill is 62% more prompt tokens and **eight lost KU questions**, and the net is +3
questions overall (83.40% → 84.00%). That is a bad trade at list price and a _good_ one if the repair in
`§13.177.4` makes the extra bytes cacheable, which is exactly why the next dispatch is registered against it
rather than against the shipping budget.

The KU loss also has a mechanism worth stating before it is re-measured: a larger budget admits more low-value
turns, and `knowledge-update` is the capability whose answer depends on **which** of two contradictory turns is
in the window, so more evidence is not neutral there — it is a chance to deliver the superseded fact as well.

#### 13.177.3 The witness answered its own question, and the answer was not the bench

`§13.176` shipped a witness because a count could only say "the passes were not repeats". The first run carrying
it says:

```
witness `e47becba` (position 0); bytes per pass 94,674 / 94,674 / 94,674 / 94,674
leading bytes shared with pass 1: 1=— 2=14 3=14 4=14
```

Four passes, one length, fourteen shared bytes. The divergence window is the first line of the evidence block:

```
pass 1: EVIDENCE:\n1. [fefd0244-4f1f-4c76-818f-4c492fe652bc] [2023/05/20 (Sat) 03:51] use…
pass 2: EVIDENCE:\n1. [9ad00d6c-2051-4743-9c0c-bb3d0b0d9d55] [2023/05/20 (Sat) 03:51] use…
```

Strip the UUID tokens from the four texts and they are **byte-identical**: 90,628 of 94,674 characters matched,
and every mismatch was a turn id. Fourteen bytes is `EVIDENCE:\n1. [`.

#### 13.177.4 The defect: a turn's identity was drawn, not derived

`createMemory` defaults `id` to `crypto.randomUUID()`, so every admitted turn got a **new identifier every time
it was admitted**. Nothing reads an id by lookup, which is why this survived eleven iterations of cost analysis.
But `formatEvidenceWithSources` renders `${index}. [${turn.id}] ${content}`, and the arms run with
`promptContract: 'abstention-evidence-blocks'` on all six routes — so the ids are **in every prompt**, and the
same turns admitted twice produced two prompts that differed in 4% of their characters.

Three measured consequences, all previously attributed to something else:

- **The cache premise was false, and so was its refutation.** `§13.175` withdrew the 60–80% prediction because
  four prompts "were never repetitions". That was right and incomplete: they were never repetitions _because of
  this_. Four passes of one request share 75% of their prompt tokens by construction; four passes whose first
  evidence line differs share none after byte 14. The 8.70% is the defect, not the provider.
- **`promptVariants == 4` was not a property of the arm's statefulness.** `prompt-determinism.test.ts` was right
  that the arm is a function of its inputs; the inputs included a random id.
- **Admission was not idempotent.** Re-admitting one turn created two identities for one fact. That is the defect
  this project keeps finding in other systems — two rows, one memory — and it was here.

#### 13.177.5 The fix, and the four properties it has to have

`admission.ts` now derives the id: four FNV-1a streams with distinct offset bases over `ordinal\0content`,
avalanched, formatted as a UUID with the **version-8** nibble so it can never be mistaken for a v4 random id. Not
`node:crypto`: `cortex-memory` runs in a browser and its entry graph is guarded against host APIs. An id is not a
secret.

The first version of that hash emitted a leading minus sign for one input in eight — `^` returns a signed int32
and `toString(16)` prints the sign — which turned a fixed-width id into a 30-character one. `turn-identity.test.ts`
caught it on its first run, from the shape assertion.

| property                                       | why the cheap alternative fails             | test                             |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| stable across calls                            | a counter is not stable across processes    | same turn hashed twice           |
| separates equal content at different positions | a content-only hash merges duplicates       | `same words` at 0 and 1          |
| separates different content at one position    | a position-only id merges everything        | `a` vs `b`                       |
| fixed-width, version 8                         | `Math.random` and v4 both look reproducible | pattern **and** `id[14] === '8'` |

- `turn-identity.test.ts` (new, 8): the four properties, a 2,000-turn collision sweep, boundary inputs (empty,
  `"0"`, `"\u0000"`), and admission idempotence. Written through `admitTurns` rather than the private function,
  so the test also proves the derivation is _used_.
- `prompt-determinism.test.ts` 3 → **5**: the sourced rendering on the flat and multi-session routes, four
  passes, one prompt. These are the cases the first three could not reach — they ran without
  `promptContract`, and the sourced renderer is the only one that cites an id.
- Injection: removing `id: turnIdFor(content, ordinal)` fails **exactly those two** and leaves the original three
  green, which is the route distinction stated as a measurement.
- `cortex-memory` 715 → **725 passed**, coverage **100 / 100 / 100 / 100**.

#### 13.177.6 The next dispatch, registered before it runs

Payload: identical to `41144910162` (`maxPromptChars 96000`, `ask: operands`, `relevance-hybrid`, `top_k: 256`,
`review_pass: bare`, contract `abstention-evidence-blocks`, 4 repetitions, temperature 0, `limit: 0`) on the fix
commit. One variable moved — the id derivation — and it moves the _bytes_, which is what makes the predictions
below falsifiable rather than hopeful.

| prediction         | passes when                                                                | falsified when                                                                                      |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| row 6, the premise | ≥ 95% of questions carry `promptVariants == 1`                             | below; the id fix did not reach every route                                                         |
| cache share        | ≥ 60% of prompt tokens report a cache hit                                  | below 60%, and the 60–80% prediction was about the provider after all                               |
| witness            | `commonPrefix` equals the full length on ≥ 95% of passes                   | any pass diverges, and the offset names what else moves                                             |
| billed cost        | `promptTokens × (1 − 0.9 × cacheShare)` ≤ 0.7× the previous draw's 28.18 M | above; then the extra ceiling is not affordable even when cached                                    |
| accuracy           | MR first repetition ≥ 87 and overall within ±2.2 pt of 84.00%              | below either; cosmetic ids should not move accuracy, and if they do the citations were load-bearing |
| within-run spread  | MR's four passes span ≤ 2 questions (they spanned 84–93)                   | above, and the residual variance is the reader rather than the prompt                               |

The last row is the one that costs the campaign something if it passes. If four passes of one request return
near-identical answers, `runs: 4` stops measuring model variance — it becomes a determinism check — and every
future noise estimate has to come from a second dispatch or from a deliberately perturbed prompt. `§13.175.5`
measured a 2.2-point band between two dispatches of one payload; with random ids in every prompt, part of that
band was this defect, and the next two dispatches will say how much.

#### 13.177.7 What this section does not claim

- **Not that 96,000 is the right budget.** Reach passed, accuracy and damage failed; the trade is −8 KU and +12
  TR for 1.62× the tokens, and the correct budget is a question for a cached run.
- **Not that the id fix improves accuracy.** Ids are cosmetic; the prediction is "no change beyond the band", and
  a change would be the interesting outcome.
- **Not that the cache prediction will hold.** It is registered as 60%, derived from "three of four passes resend
  identical bytes" — a provider that declines to cache is still a live explanation for a miss, and this time the
  instrument can tell the two apart.

### 13.178 Gate 2: the persistence has to reproduce on a second engine, and a second Chromium is not one

`§10.2` gate 2 of the execution plan reads: *"`[POC-1]`'s persistence reproduces on **at least two browser
engines** (Chromium + one more)"*. `13.177`'s sibling work closed gate 1 (the size guard, in `pnpm check`, and the
subpaths resolving in a real bundler). Gate 2 is the other half of the same claim, and until it is a reading, the
sentence "the browser tier persists" is a statement about **one** implementation.

#### 13.178.1 Why the second engine cannot be a second Chromium profile

A second Chromium run on a second profile reproduces the *suite* and not the *claim*. The thing that can fail is
`FileSystemSyncAccessHandle`, and Chromium has exactly one implementation of it — the same VFS, the same SQLite
build, the same bug surface, the same quota accounting. Two Chromium profiles agreeing tells you the suite is
deterministic. It cannot tell you the API contract is the one the specification describes.

Firefox is the cheap second implementation and was already installed for this: **Firefox 159.0** at
`/opt/firefox/firefox`. It is also the harder of the two to automate, which is the cost of the answer.

#### 13.178.2 The suite is one module, so the engines can only differ where they really differ

`test/browser/restart-suite.mjs` runs the whole four-phase flow — matrix, deterministic write, **restart**, read,
digest compare — and a caller supplies only `open(origin)`: launch the browser on the profile, navigate, wait for
`window.__ready`, return `{ evaluate, close }`. Which modes run, how many rows, whether the digest matches, and the
24th check are therefore **not** per-engine code. The alternative — a Firefox probe that reimplemented the two-phase
flow — would eventually disagree with the Chromium one about something that is not the engine: the row count, the
digest function, or (the silent one) whether the second launch reuses the origin. OPFS is per-origin storage, so a
second launch on a fresh port reads an empty database and **passes**.

`test/browser/bidi.mjs` is the Firefox half: find the binary, launch headless with `--remote-debugging-port`, speak
WebDriver BiDi over the WebSocket Node already has. No Playwright, for the same reason `cdp.mjs` has none.

#### 13.178.3 The one thing that costs an hour if it is not written down

Firefox removed CDP in 129 and kept the W3C standard. It prints

```
WebDriver BiDi listening on ws://127.0.0.1:PORT
```

and then answers **`200 OK` with an `httpd.js` welcome page** to a WebSocket handshake at that exact URL, because the
root is the HTTP endpoint and the upgrade lives one segment down at **`/session`**. The failure reads as
`non-101 status code`, which looks like a protocol bug and is a path bug. `curl` cannot settle it either: a GET
returns `200`, a POST returns *"the handshake request must use GET method"*. The session is created **inside** the
socket by the first `session.new`, so the connection *is* the readiness test and no HTTP probe can substitute for it.

#### 13.178.4 The criteria, registered before the run

Payload: `CORTEX_ROWS=2000` (the same default the Chromium reading used), the shipped `dist/` served by the same
`server.mjs`, one profile directory across both launches, one origin across both launches.

| # | criterion                | passes when                                                                        | falsified when                                                                                         |
| - | ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1 | the tier                 | Firefox obtains `tier === 'opfs'` (not a fall back to `idb`)                        | `refused` names opfs: Firefox declines `createSyncAccessHandle`, and gate 2 is a **gap**, not a pass     |
| 2 | the check count          | 24 checks, 0 failed — the 23 matrix checks plus the restart check                   | fewer than 24, and a check went missing or was replaced by the "matrix was not run" placeholder         |
| 3 | the names                | the 24 check names are **identical strings** to the Chromium run                    | any renamed, added or absent name: a suite that renames per engine cannot be diffed between engines     |
| 4 | the digest               | 2,000 rows read back as **`4000247205`**, the same integer Chromium produced         | any other value: the rows, or their order, are not preserved across a Firefox restart                   |
| 5 | the refusal path         | `a broken sqlite module falls back to idb, and says why` passes on Firefox as well  | it fails there, and the startup timeout — not the module load — is what closed that path on Chromium    |

Criterion 4 is the load-bearing one and it is deliberately exact: the digest is FNV-1a over
`JSON.stringify` of the rows in query order, pure integer arithmetic with no engine surface, so "same rows, same
order" implies "same integer". A different integer is a **result**, not a tolerance.

Explicitly **not** criteria: the throughput numbers. They move by ~15% between runs on one host and have no shared
meaning across engines; the documents cite them as a range, and a gate on them would fire on a legitimate run
(`§11.4`).

#### 13.178.5 What this will not claim, whichever way it reads

- **Not Safari.** WebKit's OPFS has no persistent profile in the WebDriver session model this suite uses, so the
  third engine needs a real device and a real profile; that stays listed as a boundary in `§10.1.1`.
- **Not multi-tab concurrency, not private browsing, not quota exhaustion.** None is exercised by either probe.
- **Not that Firefox is supported.** Obtaining the tier and surviving a restart is the API contract; a product
  statement about Firefox (quota, eviction, sync-handle contention under many tabs) is a different sentence.
- **Not that the two engines agree on speed.** They do not, and no criterion here reads it.

#### 13.178.6 The reading: gate 2 closed, and the run that closed it was not the run that proved anything

`probe-firefox.mjs` at 2,000 rows, Firefox **159.0** (`rv:159.0`, `Gecko/20100101`), same `dist/`, same
`server.mjs`, one profile, one origin, two launches:

| # | criterion       | reading                                                                     | verdict |
| - | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| 1 | the tier        | `tier === 'opfs'`, engine `sqlite-wasm 3.54.1 on opfs-sahpool (journal: delete)`, `refused: []` — **the same engine string Chromium reports** | **pass** |
| 2 | the check count | 24 checks, 24 passed, 0 failed; digest check row included                    | **pass** |
| 3 | the names       | the 24 names are identical **in order and in string** to `last-run.json`     | **pass** |
| 4 | the digest      | wrote `4000247205`, read `4000247205`, 2,000 rows, `matches: true`           | **pass** |
| 5 | the refusal path| `a broken sqlite module falls back to idb, and says why` passes, reason `error loading dynamically imported module: …/vendor/does-not-exist.mjs` | **pass** |

Row 4 is the one worth the wall-clock: two engines, two implementations of `createSyncAccessHandle`, two
storage backends underneath, and the same 2,000 rows come back in the same order with the same integer.
That is the claim gate 2 was asking about, and it is now a reading rather than an assumption.

Two engine differences that the suite deliberately does not depend on:

| surface        | Chromium                              | Firefox                                  | why it is not a check                                                      |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| failed import  | `Failed to fetch dynamically imported module` | `error loading dynamically imported module` | the check asserts that a refusal is **reported**, not its wording; a text assertion here would be engine coupling |
| speed, 2,000 rows | 120,444 ms commit-per-row (17/s), 208 ms one transaction (9,625/s), read 15.8 ms | 124,949 ms (16/s), 270 ms (7,407/s), read 15.0 ms | within the ~15% run-to-run band; `13.178.4` excludes it on purpose |

#### 13.178.7 The first run failed, and what it proved was not a storage bug

The first Firefox attempt died with

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'hash')
    at runRestartSuite (restart-suite.mjs:40:42)
```

three lines into the **shared** module, on `phases.write.digest.hash`. OPFS on Firefox was fine and had never been
asked. The cause is in the protocol, and it is worth stating in the form it will be met again:

> WebDriver BiDi does not send an object as an object. `script.evaluate` returns
> `{ type: 'object', value: [ ['hash', { type: 'number', value: 4000247205 }], … ] }` — an ordered list of
> `[key, RemoteValue]` pairs. `evaluate` returned `outcome.result.value`, so the suite held the pair list.

Measured, not read off the specification: a live round trip of `({ hash: 4000247205, count: 2000, arr: [1,"a",null],
nested: {ok:true}, u: undefined, nan: NaN, neg: -0 })` also settled the three shapes that would have been "obvious"
guesses — `NaN` arrives as the **string** `'NaN'`, `-0` as `'-0'`, and `undefined` as a type with **no `value` field**.

The conversion is now `deserialize` + `valueOf` in `bidi.mjs`, with `evaluate` reduced to six lines of transport, and
the branch that was wrong is covered without a browser:

- `bidi.mjs --self-test` — **8 cases**, fixtures transcribed from that live round trip: a number, the pair list, an
  array with a null, `undefined` (and that the key still exists), the four numbers JSON cannot carry, an object with
  no pairs, a nested pair list inside an array, and an exception. `8 passed, 0 failed`.
- `tools/__tests__/test_bidi_deserialize.py` — **4 tests**, inside `pnpm check`: the self-test passes, every case is
  reported **by name** (deleting one is a coverage loss, not a smaller count), importing the module runs no test
  (the guard is on which file is the entry point), and a **mutation** that reverts the object branch to
  `return remote.value;` fails **by name** — `4 passed, 4 failed`, the four cases whose result is an object. The
  mutation test is the one that keeps the fix from being tidied away.

Two further facts this cost, both now comments where they are needed: `browsingContext.getTree` is refused with
*"System access is required. Start Firefox with the MOZ_REMOTE_ALLOW_SYSTEM_ACCESS=1"*, so the tab id is exposed as a
read-only accessor (`connection.context`) rather than rediscovered; and the entry-point guard cannot be
`argv[1].endsWith('bidi.mjs')`, because a mutation fixture under another name would then skip the self-test — it is
`import.meta.url === pathToFileURL(argv[1]).href`.

#### 13.178.8 What closing this gate changes, and what it does not

`§10.2` was four conditions on a public sentence. **Now 2 of 4 are closed**: gate 1 (size guard in `pnpm check`, three
browser subpaths resolving in a real bundler) and gate 2 (persistence on two engines, 24/24 each, one digest).

The remaining two are the ones that need something this host does not have: **gate 3**, a false-share upper bound
≤5%, needs a corpus and a reader; **gate 4**, the LongMemEval reading with run id, configuration row and per-question
records, is the accuracy campaign's own output and is the same table `§13.177` reports against. So the sentence
"browser-capable, privacy-safe" is still not publishable, and the reason is now two named rows rather than four.

#### 13.178.9 The gate was measured by hand, which is the shape of gate this repository keeps finding un-attached

Everything above was run by hand on one host, and its evidence is two committed JSON files. That is exactly the defect
`verify.yml` was written to fix for `pnpm check` — *"a gate you have to remember to run is a gate that is not
running"* — reappearing one level up. Three things now attach it:

| where | what it asserts | needs a browser |
| ----- | --------------- | --------------- |
| `pnpm check` → `guard:browser` | the **two committed readings** run the same 24 checks, in the same order, by the same strings, both on `opfs`, both digest-matched | **no** |
| `Verify` → job `browser` | the suite still passes on a real Chromium at 400 rows, and the committed `last-run.json` still describes the tree | yes |
| `tools/__tests__/test_browser_reading_check.py` (6) | the comparator itself: a renamed check, a dropped check, an `idb` reading, an unread digest, and a missing argument each produce a named failure | **no** |

The middle row is the load-bearing one and it is deliberately weaker than the committed reading: 400 rows instead of
2,000, because 2,000 rows at ~60 ms per commit is two minutes of runner time to prove arithmetic the digest already
proves. What it keeps is the restart, the digest and all 24 checks. `CORTEX_RESULTS` sends the fresh reading to `/tmp`
so the committed file survives to be compared with it — writing over it would destroy the comparison on the run that
matters. `CORTEX_RESULTS_BUNDLE` is separate for the bundle suite, because `test:browser` runs both and one shared
variable let the bundle reading overwrite the restart reading, which the comparison then read as 24 checks against 4.
That was measured the obvious way.

Two honest limits: the `browser` job covers **Chromium only** (a Firefox job would double the install and the runtime for
a criterion already enforced offline by `guard:browser`), and it does not re-measure throughput — the job would fail on
a slow runner for a number `13.178.4` excludes from the criteria on purpose.

Reading, on the commit that added them: `Verify` **`41164403077`** at `d8c375b0` — **`Verify library` success** and
**`Verify browser suites` success**. The second job's first run is the only evidence that its own machinery works:
playwright's Chromium installs, the probe finds it through the cache, 400 rows survive the restart, and the comparator
accepts the fresh reading against the committed one.

### 13.179 Four published numbers were computed by a program that is not the one that ships

`§10.2` gate 3 is the last open condition on a release sentence, and the numbers it rests on are
these: **false-share 0/12** and **coverage 31.7%** on 60 hand-labelled utterances, **0/1,467** and
**29.2%** on ten CIMemories personas, **leak 1/3,000** and **coverage 87.5%** on an identifier
corpus. All six are quoted in `docs/04` as properties of the disclosure layer.

None of them was produced by `packages/cortex-core`. They were produced by
`cortex-docs/poc/p04-triage-rules/rules.mjs`, a second implementation of the same table, written so
a probe could run without a build step. That is a reasonable reason to have two tables. It is not a
reason to leave them unwatched, and nothing was watching: checked today, they had drifted in **eight
places**.

#### 13.179.1 The eight differences, and which way each one runs

| field | the probe table said | what ships | direction |
| ----- | -------------------- | ---------- | --------- |
| `credential.retention` | absent | `retention: 'never'` | the probe could not represent "not stored at all" |
| `credential.source` | `…\|ssn\|social security\|\bpin\b\|…` | `…\|social security\|pin\|…` | equivalent in effect; a nested `\b` inside an already-bounded group |
| `strong-pii.source` | no `iban`, no IBAN shape | `\biban\b` and `\b[A-Z]{2}\d{2}…\b` | **probe narrower**: it could not have found the leak described below |
| `strong-pii.policy` | "…postal address" | "…postal address, account" | prose lagged the pattern |
| `money.source` | no named-loan clause | `home/auto/personal/student/car/business loan` | **probe narrower** |
| `health.source` | `\bALT\b`, `\bAST\b`, `\bBMI\b` | `alt`, `ast`, `bmi` behind a value guard | **probe narrower in case, product broader in scope** — the one that hid a defect |
| `health.policy` | "…appointments" | "…measurements" | prose |
| `third-party.source` | `…\|landlord\|doctor` | `…\|landlord` | **probe broader**: a word that has no business in a list of roles |

Two of these are cosmetic. The other six are the interesting kind, and the `health` row is the one
that shows why a parity check is not bookkeeping:

> The probe wrote `\bALT\b`, which matches the letters when they are capitalised. The product wrote
> `alt` inside a `/i` alternation, which matches **"the alt attribute on the logo"**. So the product
> called every accessibility note a health fact, and the probe — the only instrument pointed at the
> *published* numbers — could not see it, because in the probe's table the sentence never matched.

That is a false-private error, so nothing leaked and no safety audit could have found it. It was
found by comparing two implementations of one policy, which is a different instrument from a corpus.

#### 13.179.2 The repair, and the criterion for calling it a repair

The mirror is now generated to match: same ids, same order, same `retention`, same source and flags,
same policy sentences. The criterion was registered as a pair, because either half alone can be
satisfied dishonestly:

| # | criterion | passes when | falsified when |
| - | --------- | ----------- | -------------- |
| 1 | parity | all eight fields equal for all eight rules, in order | any field differs, and the difference is reported by rule id and field name |
| 2 | replication | the four published numbers come back **unchanged** when the probes are re-run under the reconciled table | any of them moves, in which case the document changes rather than the number |

Criterion 2 is the one that decides whether this was an audit or a rewrite. Re-running `p04`,
`p05` and `p06-policy-scale` on the reconciled table:

| probe | metric | before | after | verdict |
| ----- | ------ | -----: | ----: | ------- |
| `p04` (60 rows) | false-share | 0/12 (upper 24.2%) | **0/12 (upper 24.2%)** | unchanged |
| `p04` | coverage | 31.7% | **31.7%** | unchanged |
| `p04` | false-private | 4/8 | **4/8** | unchanged |
| `p06-policy-scale` (1,467) | leak | 0 (NOT MEASURED) | **0 (NOT MEASURED)** | unchanged, and still not a measurement |
| `p06-policy-scale` | coverage | 29.2% (26.9–31.6) | **29.2% (26.9–31.6)** | unchanged |
| `p05` (read side, 60 rows) | all fields | — | — | unchanged |

So the honest headline is not "the numbers were wrong". It is: **the numbers were unverified, and
now they are verified, and they survive.** Six of them did not have to.

One of them nearly did not. The first reconciliation run produced **29.1%**, not 29.2%, and the
difference was a single row:

```
Shawn’s liver enzyme levels (ALT/AST) have returned to normal.
```

The value guard added to fix the `alt` over-match requires a number after the abbreviation, and this
row has none, so a health fact became a card. The fix is not to loosen the guard — it is to name the
clinical phrase (`liver enzyme`) in the table, because that is what the policy says. Coverage went
back to 29.2%. The episode is worth recording as the shape of this trade: **every guard that stops a
false-private error costs recall somewhere, and the cost is measurable, which is the only reason it
can be paid deliberately.**

#### 13.179.3 The two rule defects the reconciliation found

Neither was found by a corpus, and both are now tested by name.

**1. The product over-matched `alt`/`ast`/`bmi`.** Fixed with a value guard: the abbreviation counts
when a number follows within a clause (`\b(?:alt|ast|bmi)\b(?=[^.;!?\n]{0,20}\d)`), and the clinical
phrase `liver enzyme` is named for the rows where no value appears. Three traps are pinned
(`the ast node in our parser`, `my bmi tracker app`, `the alt text on the hero image`), and three
positives (`my ALT came back at 62`, `the blood test put my AST at 40`, `my BMI is 31`).

**2. The single recorded leak is now caught.** `p06` published one row in three thousand:

> In our latest Quality Assurance meeting, we decided to conduct an audit of all our transactions,
> paying special attention to those from Home Loan Account with IBAN LV96INJD0N7MZO8346877.

`strong-pii` wanted `account number`, `money` wanted an amount, and `org-knowledge` wanted nothing
more than the words "we decided". Two clauses were added — `\biban\b` plus the IBAN shape in
`strong-pii`, and a named loan in `money` — chosen so that the **truncated** capture still
classifies: the report cut the row at "Home Loan A", and a rule that only fires on a 22-character
string would have left that row unjudgeable forever. Measured on the recorded text: `strong-pii`
with the identifier, `money` without it, both private.

The accepted cost is stated in the table and in a test: *"The Auto Loan Account segment performs well
in our business model canvas"* is organisational speech that now becomes a card. A card is
recoverable; a published account is not, and the policy's asymmetry is the reason the trade is made
in that direction rather than tuned away.

What is **not** claimed: that the corpus now measures 0/3,000. The corpus lives behind a Hub the
authoring host cannot reach, so the corpus-level re-run is owed. What is claimed is narrower and
checkable: the one row the corpus ever published is now classified private by the shipped table, on
the text as recorded.

#### 13.179.4 The guard, so this cannot drift again

`tools/triage-parity.mjs`, in `pnpm check` as `guard:triage`:

| comparison | what it catches | needs a second checkout |
| ---------- | --------------- | ----------------------- |
| shipped vs `tools/triage-table.json` | a rule change that was not accompanied by a decision about the published numbers | no |
| mirror vs shipped | the drift above, at the moment it appears | yes (skipped otherwise, **loudly**) |
| `--write` | manual, so the snapshot is a statement rather than a side effect | — |

The snapshot is the sentence *"these are the rules the published numbers describe"*. It is compared
field by field — id, scope, policy, pattern source, flags, `retention` — **in order**, because
reordering keeps the set of rules identical while inverting the fail-closed boundary, and a
comparison keyed on ids alone would call that no change.

Eight tests drive it, each with a one-field mutation of the real snapshot: policy text, `retention`,
pattern source, a dropped rule (counted before it is named), a swapped pair (ordering is a
difference even when every rule survives), a missing snapshot (the failure names the command that
fixes it), an absent mirror (reported as `SKIPPED`, and the summary then refuses to say "tables
agree"), and `--write` reproducing the committed file byte-for-byte so that running it without a
change is a no-op rather than a diff nobody reviews.

#### 13.179.5 What this does not close

Gate 3 asks for a false-share upper bound ≤5% on **workplace scope**, and that number still does not
exist: 0/12 gives 24.2%, the persona corpus never fires the publishing rule (0/1,467 is a bound over
a mechanism that did not run), and the one corpus that does fire it fires once. The parity audit
makes the numbers that *do* exist trustworthy; it does not manufacture the missing one, and
`§14.1` keeps gate 3 open for the same reason it was open this morning — the corpus, not the code.

What it does change is the cost of the next measurement: a probe now imports the shipped table's
counterpart that provably equals it, so a re-run of any of these probes describes the product, and a
future drift fails a test instead of quietly rewriting a document.

### 13.180 The false-share bound finally has a denominator: 211 publications, read one by one

`§10.2` gate 3 has been open since it was written, and the reason is arithmetic rather than caution.
The two numbers behind it could not carry a 5% bound:

| corpus | what it gave | why it cannot bound a rate |
| ------ | ------------ | -------------------------- |
| 60 hand-labelled utterances | 0/12, upper **24.2%** | twelve private rows; one in four is compatible with zero observed |
| 1,467 persona facts | 0/1,467, **NOT MEASURED** | the publishing rule never fired, so the bound is over a mechanism that did not run |
| 3,000 identifier rows | leak 1/3,000 | the denominator is *facts*, not *publications*; the rule fired once, and that once was wrong |

The quantity the gate is actually about is a conditional: **of the rows this layer publishes, how many
carry something the policy calls private?** A publication is the only route by which anything leaves
the device, so the denominator has to be publications. No corpus in this repository had more than a
handful.

#### 13.180.1 The corpus was already on disk

Every benchmark artifact this project publishes contains the turns the memory arm was given: 363,191
turns across six reports, **47,927 distinct user utterances** after keeping only the user's side and
deduplicating exact text (`tools/extract-user-turns.py`). That is personal-assistant conversation —
the distribution in which "sprint", "the board", "the project", "we decided" and "our team" actually
occur, including the senses nobody writes down.

Running the shipped table over it: **0.44% published** (211 of 47,927). That publication rate is
itself a product number worth having — 99.56% of what a user says never leaves the device, and 211
rows is a denominator a bound can stand on.

#### 13.180.2 The criterion, and the procedure written down before the repair

The gate's own criterion, unchanged: **Wilson 95% upper bound on the false-share rate ≤ 5%**, with
**every** publication read — a census, not a sample.

The adjudication procedure was written into `tools/triage-publications-adjudicated.json` before any
rule was touched:

> A row is private when it carries a circumstance the published policy names as private
> (`docs/02` §5.3: credentials, regulated identifiers, money, body/health including exercise, family,
> employment status, other people). Otherwise it is an organisational object a colleague could act
> on, which is the shared rule's own policy sentence.

Two properties make this hard to steer. First, every verdict belongs to a **policy class**, so a
disagreement is an argument about the policy rather than about taste. Second, the repair may only
**add private rules**: adding a private rule can move a row out of the publishing set (shrinking the
denominator) but can never turn a private row into a published one, so the direction of every fix is
fail-closed by construction. If the repair had instead loosened the publishing rule, the number would
have been steerable and would not have been worth computing.

#### 13.180.3 The reading, before and after

| | publications | errors | false-share | Wilson 95% upper | verdict |
| - | -----------: | -----: | ----------: | ---------------: | ------- |
| **before** | 211 | **20** | 9.48% | **14.19%** | fails |
| **after** | 189 | **0** | 0.00% | **1.99%** | **passes** |

The twenty errors, by policy class, and what each one cost:

| class | n | example | what the rule missed |
| ----- | -: | ------- | -------------------- |
| health | 15 | "I'm training for a sprint triathlon on November 1st" | `sprint` matched as a software cadence; **exercise** is a private class and the sport vocabulary was absent |
| third-party | 3 | "I also got a gift card to Starbucks for our team lead, Rachel" | `team lead` was not in the role list, and `our` was not a determiner |
| family | 1 | "a little jam session with my siblings" | `sibling` was not in the family list |
| career-status | 1 | "I'd like to explore more about my career growth" | the rule only knew about *changes* of employment, not progression |

The repair is six vocabulary additions, each justified by the policy sentence rather than by the row
that revealed it: sport and training in `health` (including `time off work`, `resting at home`),
`siblings` in `family`, `career growth|path|progression|advancement|move` in `career-status`, and
`friends`/`team lead`/`mentor`/`buddy`/`our` in `third-party`.

Two numbers move as the price, and both are reported rather than smoothed: coverage on the 60-row set
**31.7% → 33.3%**, on the 1,467 persona facts **29.2% → 30.0%**. More rows become cards. That is the
recoverable direction, and it is what "fail-closed" costs when it is actually paid.

#### 13.180.4 What 1.99% means, and the three things it does not

The claim it supports is narrow and, for once, quantitative: **on 47,927 real user utterances, the
layer published 189 rows and a reader found none that the published policy calls private; 0/189 has
a 95% upper bound of 1.99%.**

What it does not support:

1. **Not a second reader.** One reader, one pass, from the sentence and the policy, exactly like the
   60-row set. The rows are committed, so a second reader can re-audit — their reading would *replace*
   this rate, not confirm it. Inter-annotator agreement here is unmeasured and the honest label on
   1.99% is "single-reader".
2. **Not workplace email.** The corpus is personal-assistant conversation. It contains the trigger
   words in their natural senses, which is what the sample could not do, but it is not a random
   sample of an office, and the publication rate in an office would be higher.
3. **Not every private thing.** Rows whose privacy carries no policy class — a hobby, a plan, a legal
   case, an immigration status — are published and are *not* counted as errors, because the policy
   names no class for them. Four such rows were seen and are named in the adjudication file as
   `shared` with their reasons; they are the boundary of this number, not a part of it. If the policy
   later names a class for personal plans, this census has to be re-read, and the number will go up.

#### 13.180.5 The gate, and why it is now a script rather than a paragraph

`tools/triage-publish-census.mjs` recomputes the two rates from a corpus and an adjudication file, and
its exit code *is* the gate: 0 when the upper bound is at most 5% and every publication has been
read, 1 otherwise. Six tests hold it: the committed reading's arithmetic (20/211 → 14.19%, 0/189 →
1.99%), the completeness of the adjudication file (211 verdicts, 20 private, each with a class and a
reason), a synthetic corpus that passes, one that fails at 10%, one with ten unread publications
which reports **NOT MEASURED** instead of a smaller denominator, and a corpus with no publications at
all, which is also not a pass.

The last two are the same lesson `p06` taught about the persona corpus, now enforced in code: a bound
over rows nobody read is not a bound, and a zero over a mechanism that never ran is not a zero.

### 13.181 The coverage gain from 13.180 was not a gain: `gym`, `bike`, and a number that rises as the classifier gets worse

13.180 reports, as the price of the repair, that coverage on the 60-row labelled set moved
**31.7% → 33.3%** and on the 1,467 persona facts **29.2% → 30.0%**. Both of those readings were
wrong, and the way they were wrong is worth more than the numbers were.

#### 13.181.1 The twentieth row

Adding the census vocabulary moved exactly one row of the 60-row set from `defer` to decided:

> I have a production facility on Poland that can produce high end climbing walls, climbing wooden
> volumes and holds, so I know exactly what a climbing or bouldering gym needs.

Gold label: **shared**. A supplier describing their own business. The word that caught it was `gym`,
which 13.180 added to `health` as sport vocabulary. So the classifier got *worse* — a shared
sentence became private — and the coverage number got *better*, because coverage counts decisions and
does not ask whether they were right.

`bike` is the same defect one step quieter. On the 47,927-utterance corpus it matches "bike trails",
"bike shops and models", and "I spent 300 dollars on a bike": nouns and purchases, not a user's
exercise. Neither word is a fact about anybody's body, and neither is load-bearing for the census —
every row that mentions a bike is caught by `triathlon`, `volleyball`, or the transfer to `money`.

Both are removed from the shipped table and from the mirror.

#### 13.181.2 What the numbers are, and what the census actually bought

| reading | after 13.180's repair | `gym` and `bike` removed | delta |
| ------- | --------------------: | -----------------------: | ----: |
| 60-row coverage | 20 (33.3%) | **19 (31.7%)** | −1 |
| persona coverage | 30.0% (27.7–32.4) | **29.5% (27.2–31.9)** | −0.5 pp |
| publications over 47,927 | 189 | **189** | **0** |
| false-share upper bound | 1.99% | **1.99%** | 0 |

The last two rows are the point. Removing two wrong words returns coverage to the value it had before
the census and leaves the measured false-share at zero. **The census bought no coverage at all.** It
bought a denominator, and that is the only thing 13.180 ever claimed for it — a claim that only
survives because the coverage number is now allowed to go back down.

No row of the 60-row set is decided by any word the census added. That is checked by enumeration, not
by assertion: every decided row in that set is matched by `health` (10), `org-knowledge` (4), `money`
(4), or `family` (1), and none of those matches involves a word from the census list.

#### 13.181.3 The A4 ablation finally has a denominator

`p05` asserts that the `defer` default is load-bearing by moving one predicate — a deferral lands in
the shared store instead of the private one — and requiring that the ablation leak. On the 60 rows it
now passes for the wrong reason: widening `health` made the rules decide all twelve gold-private rows,
so the ablation moves nothing and the old `leak > 0` assertion went red. That red was correct.

Deleting the assertion would have been the easy repair. Instead the assertion now states the
precondition (`deferredPrivate === 0 && leak === 0`), so that a rule which later stops deciding a
private row flips the row back to red and the ablation has to be re-read. The claim itself moves to
the corpus where deferrals exist:

| policy | publications over 47,927 utterances | share |
| ------ | ----------------------------------: | ----: |
| shipped | 189 | 0.39% |
| **`defer` → shared (A4)** | **40,822** | **85.18%** |

Two hundred and sixteen times as many rows leave the device, from one predicate. `tools/triage-publish-census.mjs --defer-shared`
computes it, prints no rate on purpose (most of those rows have never been read, and a rate over an
unread denominator is the thing this tool refuses to print anywhere else), and exits 0 by
construction because an ablation is a measurement and not a gate.

#### 13.181.4 The three mechanical forms of the lesson

1. **A number that rises when the rule gets worse is not a metric.** The assertion is back to
   `19 / 31.7%`, and it sits beside private recall (12/12), false-share (0/12), and false-private
   (4/8). Four numbers moving together is a change; one moving alone is a bug report.
2. **The defect is a test block, not a comment.** `triage-rules.test.ts` gains `an activity is
   private; the place that sells the equipment is not`, five cases: the supplier's sentence must
   `defer`; buying equipment must `defer`; the same sentence must be private via `money` when it
   carries an amount; `sprint triathlon` must reach `health` because `sprint` is a trigger in the
   publishing rule; and `sprint review` must still be shared.
3. **The ablation's silence is itself asserted.** See 13.181.3: the precondition is the assertion, so
   silence cannot be mistaken for a pass.

#### 13.181.5 What this does not change

None of the four numbers 13.179 reconciled moves: `p04` still reads 0/12 and 31.7%, `p05` still reads
0/12 end to end, `p06-policy-scale` still reports zero publications it can price, and the census still
reads 189 publications with a 1.99% upper bound. Gate 3 of the execution plan stays closed, and the
two limits on it — single reader, non-office corpus — stay attached to it.

What changes is the reason the widening is defensible. It was never "coverage went up". It is that
twenty rows a reader called private stopped being published, and the price was paid in cards rather
than in loosened publishing.

### 13.182 The judge is the instrument, and nobody has checked it: a false-accept audit registered before it runs

`§10.1` compares arms by counting questions the judge called correct. The effects the campaign is
chasing are two or three questions on a 121-question capability — 1.7 to 2.5 points. The published
audit of LoCoMo's gold answers puts about 6.4% of them at risk of a scoring error and reports that a
standard judge (`gpt-4o-mini`, official prompt) **accepted 62.81% of answers that were topical but
wrong**. This repository has never measured its own judge. That gap is registered as P1 in the
execution plan and is closed here, before the reading rather than after it.

#### 13.182.1 The population is answers the judge already accepted

A rejected answer cannot produce a false accept — the judge already called it wrong — so the audit
draws from `correct: true` rows of an artifact. Each is perturbed so that it is wrong **by
construction**, and re-submitted with the same template the artifact was graded under:

| kind | what moves | example |
| ---- | ---------- | ------- |
| `number-swap` | a number the gold states, replaced with a value absent from the conversation | "18 days" → "139 days" |
| `entity-swap` | a name the gold states, replaced with another real name from the corpus, absent from this conversation | "Rachel moved to Berlin" → "Marcus moved to Berlin" |
| `cross-gold` | the answer replaced by a different question's gold of the same capability | topically adjacent, entirely wrong |

Two invariants make a "yes" unambiguous, and both run on every planned case rather than in a test:

1. the perturbed answer no longer **mentions** the gold;
2. the introduced token appears **nowhere in the conversation the model read**, so a swapped name
   cannot be another true fact about the user that the instrument simply cannot see.
