### 13.299 The room had two spellings and one reader: a capped run that read as uncapped, and the 1,247 characters a question that the prefix rule throws away

`42355323615` was dispatched with `cortex_memory_max_prompt_chars=multi-session:48460`. That syntax does not
set a scalar; it sets a **route map**, so the artifact recorded `{maxPromptCharsByRoute: {multi-session:
48460}}` and no `maxPromptChars` at all. Five routes then took the product default. Three readers existed for
that field and every one of them was blind to the same half of it.

#### 13.299.1 The defect, in the two places it was already visible

| reader | what it did | why it was wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tools/cost-ledger.py` `cap_reading` | read `maxPromptChars`, found nothing, returned `None` | the run **did** have a room: it delivered 47,830 of 48,460 characters, 98.7% of the window, in the row whose entire purpose is to say whether the window filled |
| the registration gate (§13.298.3) | `declared but unchanged: ['cortex_memory_max_prompt_chars']` | true and misleading at once -- the input moved and the field it names did not |
| a human reading the JSON | had to know the default was 24,000 before §13.82 and 48,000 after | four docstrings in `cortex-eval` still said 24,000, including the one on the field that records the room |

The same artifact produced two of those, and §13.298 recorded the second as *the* finding of that round. It is
one root cause: **a quantity with two spellings where only one is read.** The third is the same root cause at
the level of prose -- the default *has* two spellings, and the artifact records neither.

#### 13.299.2 The repair: record the room, then read all three

`memoryArmConfig.effectivePromptChars` (§13.299, `packages/cortex-eval/src/report.ts`) carries the room each
of the six routes assembled under, resolved through the same three-term expression the product's
`#promptCharsFor` uses:

```
byRoute[route] ?? maxPromptChars ?? DEFAULT_MAX_PROMPT_CHARS
```

Always present, and computed rather than projected, because the third term is the one the artifact cannot
otherwise see. On a run that named a route and left five alone it is the only field that says what the five
used. `42355323615` reads `{multi-session: 48460, temporal: 48000, flat: 48000, knowledge-update: 48000,
abstention: 48000, assistant: 48000}`.

`tools/cost-ledger.py` now resolves in the opposite order -- `effectivePromptChars`, then `maxPromptChars`,
then `maxPromptCharsByRoute` -- through one function, `prompt_rooms`, that `tools/evidence-budget.py` also
calls. A map with no resolved field is reported as a **ceiling** rather than a measurement, because the routes
it does not name took a default this artifact does not record:

```
room (widest named route)      48,460   from maxPromptCharsByRoute
implied chars per token          4.13   at the widest named room
window fill                     at-cap  (inferred, band 3.5-4.7 characters per token, English prose)

ceiling, not measurement: the routes this map does not name took the product default, …
```

A resolved artifact is read at the **narrowest** room instead, which is the one-sided test a redistribution
allows: filling the narrowest room fills every route. Testing the mean would let a run that deepened one route
and starved another read `at-cap`.

#### 13.299.3 The instrument `C2` was missing, and its first four numbers

`C2` asks for the median evidence per question in tokens. The per-question split exists in every artifact --
`promptChars` is the evidence the prompt carried, `deliveredPromptChars` is the whole prompt -- and no tool
took a median of it, which is why the row read `unrun` with a reason rather than a number.

`tools/evidence-budget.py` takes it. On `42355323615`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| median evidence | 46,926 chars = **11,558 tokens** a question |
| median whole prompt | 47,830 chars = 11,781 tokens a question |
| instruction share of the median question | **1.41%** (1.89% by ratio-of-medians) |
| characters per token, **measured** | **4.06** (47,542 chars over 11,721 tokens per call) |
| room utilisation | **98.70%**, 630 characters unspent |
| characters per evidence turn | 110 (418 turns in the median prompt) |

The density matters on its own: §13.293.2 derived 4.11 from `48000 / 11690`, a ratio of *the cap* to *a mean*,
i.e. an inference. The measured value is 4.06 and agrees to 1.2%, which is what makes the inferred figure
usable rather than merely plausible. The tool refuses to convert anything outside 2.5-6.0 characters per token,
and the refusal names the failure that produced it: the first draft divided one repetition of characters into
four repetitions of tokens, printed **0.98**, and would have converted every median below by 4.14x.

`C2` now reads `ratio.ratio` from `cortex-docs/evidence/longmemeval/evidence-budget.json`. With one artifact
the arm is its own reference, so the ratio is **1.0000** and the file records `paired: false`. **That is a
denominator, not a result.** It says the registered budget is 100% of itself and that the 0.70 bar is unmet; it
says nothing about a reduced arm until one is dispatched. The row therefore moves from `unrun` to `aim` with a
reading of 100.0% and **does not move on the quantity it measures**.

#### 13.299.4 The finding the instrument was not built for

`chooseEvidence` takes the **largest prefix of the relevance order that fits** -- a turn larger than the
remaining room ends the selection rather than being skipped past (`prompt.ts`, `selectByRelevance`). The room
that turn would have used is lost. Unspent room, per capability, on `42355323615`:

| capability | median unspent | worst |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| MR | **126** | 386 |
| TR | 610 | 852 |
| ABS | 884 | 4,363 |
| KU | 974 | 3,491 |
| IE | **1,247** | **11,533** |

MR is where `maxTurnChars: 400` reaches, and it is the only route whose slack is smaller than the per-turn
width. TR is the second route the cap reaches and it sits between the two groups, which the extra non-evidence
the temporal block carries would explain. The four routes the cap does **not** reach leave 7x to 10x as much
room unspent, and the worst question throws away **11,533 characters -- 24% of its window** -- because one
over-sized turn blocked a prefix.

Two consequences, and the order between them matters:

1. **`maxTurnChars` is not only a truncation.** It also decides how far the prefix advances, because a capped
   turn is a turn that fits. That is a second channel for a knob §13.80 measured on the first channel, and this
   campaign has never stated it.
2. **The cheap test is to extend the cap to all six routes**, one variable
   (`cortex_memory_max_turn_chars_routes`), with the gate written before the run:  unspent room on the four
   uncovered routes falls toward the capped routes' levels, and `MR`/`TR` stay where they are. Accuracy is
   *not* the primary measure here -- the code that spends the freed room already exists and §13.291 showed
   adding gold turns buys +0.00, so the prediction is a coverage effect with an accuracy effect too small for
   this n. Dispatch readiness over accuracy, per requirement 9.

Neither is dispatched this round: `P1` is ($13.299.6).

#### 13.299.5 Tests, and the regression each one closes

| file | count | trap |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `packages/cortex-eval/src/__tests__/prompt-room-recorded.test.ts` | 6 | the six routes are all recorded; a scalar reaches all six; the `{multi-session: 48460}` shape records 48,000 on the other five; the field is present on every run; the rendered line collapses when the rooms agree and does not when they differ |
| `tools/__tests__/test_prompt_room_resolution.py` | 13 | the resolved field wins; a scalar is one room; **a map alone is not `None`** (the regression this round exists for); a map is a ceiling and says so; a resolved artifact carries no caveat; no field at all is absence reported as absence; a zero, a negative, a boolean and a string are not rooms; the mirrored default equals the product's; no source file still calls the default 24,000 |
| `tools/__tests__/test_evidence_budget.py` | 14 | the conversion is one measured factor; a retry enters both means identically; **4x the tokens is refused, not corrected**; a truncated record set is refused; a record without the split is refused; unspent room is reported per capability; an unresolved room is marked unresolved; the ratio is 1.0 **and** `paired: false` |
| `tools/__tests__/test_cost_ledger.py` | 37 | unchanged, and still green with the new resolution |

Two of those were verified by breaking the code and watching them go red: the stale-claim scan was restored to
`product's 24,000` and reported the exact file and line; `json!.usage` in the §13.296 fix was reverted and took
4 of 8 with it.

#### 13.299.6 Queue

| | |
| --- | --- |
| next | **`P1`**: `deepseek:deepseek-chat` against `zhipu:glm-4.6`, same 500 questions, same prompts, same judge |
| why it is next | it is a release blocker (product face has `M1` and `P1` unrun) and it is one variable |
| the covariate it inherits | the GLM arm runs at `ask=verbatim-acts`, the same ask as `42355323615`, and the only other departure is the MR room (48,460 against 48,000). That departure's effect **has been measured**: §13.298.2 reads 10 flips one way and 9 the other, p = 1.000. It cannot explain a 2-point provider delta |
| then | `M1` (reasoning reader, paired), which needs a second provider-side variable and therefore a second dispatch |

### 13.300 The provider swap had a three-hour entrance fee, and the guard that charged it was reading a literal

`42366809734` was a 20-question smoke at `model=zhipu:glm-4.6`, the first attempt to price a second reader.
It never reached a model. The budget guard refused to start:

```
job 360 min, 8 passes, 340 min per run
  the ceiling permits 341 min of run (0.95x the job) -> it binds
pacing floor 400 min (500 questions x 1 call(s) x 8 passes x 6000 ms), budget 340
  -> THE RUN CANNOT FINISH: the budget fires 60 min before the last question is asked
```

Two facts in that output, and the second is the expensive one.

#### 13.300.1 The literal

`--questions 500` was typed into the workflow, so the guard planned a full suite for a 20-question dispatch.
The floor is `questions x passes x interval`, and only the first term is a property of the dispatch.

The consequence is not one refused run. **The entrance fee for the entire portability axis was a three-hour
run**, so a vendor whose quota is exhausted is discovered after the budget rather than before it -- which is
precisely the state this campaign is in with Zhipu *embeddings*, and nobody had noticed the same argument
applies to a Zhipu *reader*. `GRADED_QUESTIONS` now comes from `inputs.limit`, the same way the run does.

#### 13.300.2 The arithmetic, which changes what `P1` can be

At the `zhipu:` pace of 6,000 ms per request:

| repetitions | passes | floor | fits the 340-minute budget |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 4 | 8 | **400 min** | no -- and not inside the 360-minute job either |
| 3 | 6 | 300 min | yes, with 40 minutes of margin |
| 2 | 4 | 200 min | yes |

So a provider swap at the full 500 questions **cannot run four repetitions**, and that is a property of the
vendor's rate limit rather than of this arm. `P1` therefore runs at **two repetitions** and says so in its
registration. The pairing against `42355323615` stays legitimate for the reason §13.298.5 already records: the
same 500 questions, the same prompts, the same judge, and a first repetition that is a complete 500-question
reading. What two repetitions buy is the mean and the agreement rate, not the sampling check the four-pass arm
was built for -- so `M1`, which asks for a paired per-question gain, keeps its four and needs a different
provider-side variable.

Four tests pin the wiring, and one of them states the arithmetic above rather than the code: a 20-question smoke
fits where 500 does not, and the full suite is affordable at two repetitions and not at four.

#### 13.300.3 Where this leaves the queue

Unchanged in order, and one line sharper about price:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| now | the 20-question smoke at `ablation_runs=1` (`42367594269`), to verify the provider answers at all and to price one call |
| if it answers | `P1` at the full 500 questions, `ablation_runs=2`, gate `<= 2.0` points against the reference provider |
| if it does not | the answer is a quota fact, not a mechanism finding, and `P1` stays `unrun` with a reason that names the vendor rather than the product |

### 13.301 The room is halved, and the prediction is written before the meter runs

`C1` reads **12,137** prompt tokens per question against a threshold of **6,000**, and `C2` has an instrument,
a denominator and no numerator: the only artifact `tools/evidence-budget.py` can read is the registered arm at
the registered room, so its ratio is `1.0000` by construction. Both rows are priced by **one** dispatch, and
this section is the prediction that dispatch is read against. It is written before the meter runs because a
prediction written afterwards is a description.

#### 13.301.1 The single variable

| | control `42355323615` | this arm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cortex_memory_max_prompt_chars` | `48000` (scalar, §10.3) | **`24000`** |
| every other input | §10.3 | §10.3, unchanged |
| repetitions | 4 | **2** (§13.300.2's affordance) |
| reader | `deepseek-chat`, thinking on `multi-session+temporal` | identical |

One field moves. The other five routes in the control read `48000` because no scalar was recorded and
`PROMPT_ROOM_DEFAULT` is `48000` (§13.299); `multi-session` read `48460` because that dispatch wrote a map
instead of a scalar. This arm writes the **scalar**, so all six routes resolve to 24,000 and
`memoryArmConfig.effectivePromptChars` prints one number rather than a six-entry map -- which is itself a
check on §13.299's repair: an arm whose room renders as six values would mean the scalar path is still not
being read.

#### 13.301.2 What the outside world says, and the direction it does not cover

MemStrata (`arXiv:2610.05343`) reports the closest published experiment to this one: on the same 500-question
set, with the same reader and the same 24,000-**token** ceiling, a **full-history control carrying about 4.7x
the evidence** scores `464/500` reference-only against `463/500` for the bounded packet, and `470/500`
source-aware against `475/500`. Four point seven times the evidence is worth **minus one to plus one
question**, and the paper calls neither difference decisive.

That is the strongest available evidence that evidence *volume* is not what accuracy on this benchmark is
made of, and it is the same conclusion this arm reached from the inside at §13.291: delivering every gold
turn moved the roster by exactly **+0.00**.

**It is not evidence that a cut is safe, and the difference matters.** "More buys nothing" is an upper
boundary being flat; "less costs nothing" is the same curve being read on the other side of the vertex, and a
curve that is flat above the vertex can still fall below it. Nothing in the published record cuts the packet
by half with the reader held, so this dispatch is the first reading of that side rather than a confirmation.

#### 13.301.3 The downside, counted rather than feared

`tools/gold-room.py --max-chars 24000` prices every question's gold against the smaller room with no provider
call. The column that matters is `room` -- the questions where **no ordering helps**, because the gold turns
plus the measured overhead do not fit:

| capability | n | `room` at 48,000 | `room` at 32,000 | `room` at 24,000 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| ABS | 30 | 0 | 3 | **9** |
| IE | 150 | 0 | 0 | **2** |
| KU | 72 | 0 | 11 | **38** |
| MR | 121 | 0 | 0 | **0** |
| TR | 127 | 0 | 0 | **0** |

So the exposure is **49 questions out of 500**, all of it in three capabilities, and **none** in the two that
hold the gap. The worst case is therefore bounded and named: if every one of the 49 currently answers
correctly *because* of a turn the smaller room cannot carry, the arm loses 9.8 points. The realistic case is
much smaller, because 66 of 72 KU questions are already `partial` at 48,000 -- the answer survives on part of
the gold today, which is the only reason a partial-coverage question can read 87.2% -- and a question that
answers from one turn does not stop answering when the other four leave.

`tools/evidence-budget.py` measured the median evidence at **46,926 characters of a 48,000 room**, 98.70%
utilisation, so 24,000 is a **0.50x** cut and not a nominal one: the room is filled, so the room is the
evidence.

#### 13.301.4 The registration

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **C2** | median evidence tokens per question falls to **at most 0.70x** the control | a ratio above 0.70 means the room was not the binding constraint and the prefix rule is filling something else |
| **C1** | prompt tokens per question fall to **at most 6,000** | a reading above 6,000 at a 24,000-character room means the overhead is larger than the 1.41% §13.299 measured, which would be its own finding |
| **A** | overall accuracy is **not more than 2.0 points below** the control (>= 89.4 on the 91.40 first repetition) | a fall larger than 2.0 -- the top of this arm's own 1.6-2.2 noise band -- means the room is load-bearing, and the repair for `C1` becomes **denser evidence** (extractive summarisation of a turn) rather than a smaller window, which is a different roadmap item |
| **B** | the fall, if any, is **concentrated in ABS, IE and KU** | a fall in MR or TR contradicts 13.301.3, which says their gold fits at 24,000 by arithmetic, so a loss there is a defect in the arm and not a cost of the room |
| **C** | the abstention route does not gain | ABS is 30 questions whose gold **is** a decline; a room cut that raises ABS means the reader was declining for lack of room and is now declining for lack of evidence, and those are different mechanisms |

**A** is the one that decides whether `C1` is reachable by budget alone. **C** is the one that decides whether
the reading means anything: volume removed from a reader that declines turns abstention into a confound, so a
large ABS movement makes the accuracy comparison a calibration comparison (§3 of `PREREG-READER-AXIS.md`).

#### 13.301.5 Stop rule

One dispatch. No redraw, no peeking, no second room at 32,000 to find a friendlier draw. A miss on **A** is
recorded as a miss and moves the `C1` repair from size to density; a pass on all five is the first reading in
this campaign where a cost row is met by measurement rather than by argument.

### 13.302 The room becomes a per-route decision, because the cost is not spread evenly

`42373407439` reported the five registrations of §13.301 and two of them failed, in a way that names
the next arm. The full reading is `docs/PROMPT-ROOM-IS-LOAD-BEARING.md`; what matters here is the
shape it refuted.

#### 13.302.1 What the previous prediction got wrong, in its own terms

§13.301.3 priced the cut with `tools/gold-room.py --max-chars 24000`, which counts the questions where
**the gold turns plus the measured overhead do not fit**, and reported `ABS 9, IE 2, KU 38, MR 0,
TR 0`. The registration then wrote its own falsifier:

> a fall in MR or TR contradicts 13.301.3, which says their gold fits at 24,000 by arithmetic, so a
> loss there is a defect in the arm and not a cost of the room

The fall was `MR -6.61` and `TR -4.72`, against `ABS 0.00`, `IE -0.67`, `KU -1.39`. The three
capabilities the instrument named lost **2.1 points combined**; the two it cleared lost **11.3**.

The instrument was not misread, it was the wrong instrument. Between the two artifacts, every
capability lost about half its delivered turns (`MR 199 -> 102`, `TR 205 -> 109`, `IE 64 -> 32`), and
only two lost accuracy. So "less evidence" is not the mechanism. The mechanism is the **shape of the
question**: `IE`, `KU` and `ABS` ask for one fact in one turn and half a packet still holds that turn;
`MR` and `TR` ask for a **count over turns**, and a count over a sample is not the count. The artifact
carries the signature — `gpt4_a56e767c` answers `3` against four festivals, `gpt4_2fce9456` answers `5`
against four properties — every one off by roughly the number of turns the cut removed.

**A gold-coverage model is therefore a sufficient risk model for a single-turn question and an
irrelevant one for an aggregation**, because an aggregation's requirement is not its gold turn but the
complete set of turns the gold counts. `gold-room.py`'s `room` column is a lower bound on exposure.

#### 13.302.2 The single variable

`memoryArmConfig` already resolves a room per rendering route (§13.299). This arm sets it:

| route | room | capabilities that render through it |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `abstention` | 24,000 | ABS |
| `assistant` | 24,000 | IE (`single-session-assistant`) |
| `flat` | 24,000 | IE (everything else) |
| `knowledge-update` | 24,000 | KU |
| `multi-session` | **48,000** | MR |
| `temporal` | **48,000** | TR |

One input moves: `cortex_memory_max_prompt_chars_by_route`, from unset to the map above. Every other
field of §10.3 stands, the reader is the same, the judge is the same, and the repetitions are 2.

#### 13.302.3 The prediction, and it is arithmetic over measured cells rather than a model

Every cell below is a measured number from the two arms already read, which is the difference between
this registration and §13.301's:

| capability | n | 24,000 (measured) | 48,000 (measured) | this arm |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| ABS | 30 | 100.00% | 100.00% | 24,000 → 100.00% |
| IE | 150 | 92.67% | 93.33% | 24,000 → 92.67% |
| KU | 72 | 87.50% | 88.89% | 24,000 → 87.50% |
| MR | 121 | 76.86% | 83.47% | 48,000 → 83.47% |
| TR | 127 | 91.34% | 96.06% | 48,000 → 96.06% |

Weighted: `(30/30 + 139/150 + 63/72 + 101/121 + 122/127)` = `455/500` = **91.00%**, against the
control's 91.40% — a predicted **-0.40**. The cells are counts rather than rounded percentages, so the
sum is the same arithmetic the run will do.

Tokens: `(252 x 22,830 + 248 x 46,926) / 500 = 34,782` characters per question, or **8,567 tokens** at
the measured 4.06 characters per token, against the control's 11,558 — a predicted **0.741x**.

#### 13.302.4 The registration

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | overall accuracy is **at least 90.5%** | a reading below 90.5 is 0.5 points under the prediction and outside what the cells can absorb, which would mean the two rooms interact rather than compose |
| **B** | **MR and TR do not move by more than 1.0 point** each | they are read at the same room the control read, so any movement is the arm's own noise leaking into routes it did not touch — and a movement there is a defect in the per-route resolution, which is the exact class §13.299 repaired |
| **C** | **IE, KU and ABS do not move by more than 1.5 points** each | they moved `-0.67`, `-1.39` and `0.00` between the two endpoint arms, so a larger movement here means the map is not being applied per route |
| **D** | **`C1` reads at most 6,000 tokens per question** | the arithmetic says 8,556, so this one is *expected to miss* and is registered as a miss in advance: the point of registering it is that a hit would mean the character median is not the arithmetic the cells imply |
| **E** | the configuration line renders **six rooms, not one** | `memoryArmConfig.effectivePromptChars` (§13.299) must print a per-route map here. A single number means the map path is not being read, which is the defect that started the whole line of work |

**D** is deliberately registered as an expected miss. A registration that only contains predictions it
expects to hit is a registration that cannot be falsified, and `C1`'s 6,000 is not reachable from
11,558 by cutting the routes that are already cheap — the arithmetic says so before the dispatch does.

#### 13.302.5 Stop rule

One dispatch. A pass on **A**, **B**, **C** and **E** makes the per-route room the registered
configuration and moves `C1` to 8,556 with a named remainder rather than an unmeasured one. A miss on
**B** sends the arm back to §13.299's resolution path rather than to a bigger room, because a movement
in an untouched route cannot be caused by the size of the routes that were touched.

### 13.303 The reader axis, dispatched as two arms of one provider

`M1` has been `unrun` since it was registered, and the reason it stayed there was a belief rather than
a check: "swap the reader for a stronger model" was assumed to need a second vendor, and a second
vendor meant a second key, a second endpoint and a second quota. The endpoint publishes its supported
model names when it rejects one, and `42379829090` is the run that read them:

```text
The supported API model names are deepseek-flash, deepseek-v4-pro, but you passed glm-4.6.
```

So the axis is measurable **inside one provider**, which removes the confound a cross-vendor swap would
have carried: `deepseek-flash` and `deepseek-v4-pro` are served by the same infrastructure, the same
tokenizer family and the same cache, so a difference between them is a difference in the model.

#### 13.303.1 The two arms, and the one field that moves

| | arm A | arm B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | **`deepseek-flash`** | **`deepseek-v4-pro`** |
| room | 48,000 (§10.3) | 48,000 |
| every other input | §10.3 | §10.3 |
| repetitions | 2 | 2 |
| run | `42381717349` | dispatched immediately after |

`thinking` stays `multi-session+temporal` on both, because §13.234 registered that the thinking route
is part of the product configuration and turning it off for one arm would make this two changes.

#### 13.303.2 Why `promptDigest` is the control and not a promise

`M1`'s claim is about the **reader**, so the packet must be identical. Every per-question record carries
`promptDigest`, so the two artifacts can be compared question by question **before** the accuracy is
compared: 500 of 500 digests must match. A mismatch means the arm moved something it did not declare,
and the accuracy comparison is then between two packets rather than between two readers — which is not
a weaker version of this measurement, it is a different one that nobody registered.

That check is the first thing to run when both artifacts land, and it costs nothing. It is registered
here because the cheaper mistake is to read the accuracy first.

#### 13.303.3 The registration

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **R0** | all 500 `promptDigest` values are identical between the arms | any difference voids the accuracy reading, whatever it says |
| **R1** | the stronger reader is **at least 3.0 points ahead** on the same 500 | a reading below 3.0 is `M1`'s miss, and the honest reading of it is Agent Zero's own result: `3.4` points is the **entire** observed spread across eight model families, so a delta under 3 says this pipeline is more retrieval-dominated than the field's strongest system, not that the reader is broken |
| **R2** | a **negative** delta is a defect, not noise | a stronger model scoring lower on an identical packet is the prompt-contract defect `AUDIT-READER-THINKING-REVERSES.md` documents, and it is repaired in the prompt rather than in the model choice |
| **R3** | the abstention route does not move by more than one question | `ABS` gold **is** a decline, so a reader swap that buys accuracy by declining less is a calibration change; `PREREG-READER-AXIS.md` §3 registers this and it is unchanged |
| **R4** | cost per question is **reported for both arms**, not only accuracy | the arms differ in model price, and a comparison that reports accuracy and hides the bill is the comparison `C1` exists to refuse |

**R1's bar of 3.0 was chosen before this dispatch and is not moved by it** — `PREREG-READER-AXIS.md` §7
records why the looser of two written numbers survived, and the reasoning there (a 5-point bar asks this
pipeline to be more reader-sensitive than the state of the art is) applies to the dispatch as much as to
the document.

#### 13.303.4 What a pass would and would not mean

A pass makes `M1` the first reader-axis reading in this campaign and removes one of the two remaining
`unrun` rows on the product surface. It does **not** make the pipeline SOTA: a 3-point gain on top of
91.40 is 94.4, which is still under MemStrata's 95.0 source-aware and under three vendor headlines
whose code does not exist. What it would establish is the weaker and more useful claim — that this
pipeline's accuracy **responds to the reader**, which is the property a product needs before it can
promise anything about model choice.

### 13.304 The per-route room, read: the cost prediction held to 1.3% and the accuracy prediction missed by 1.20 points

`42383171765` is the arm §13.302 registered, and it is the first reading on this campaign where the two halves of one prediction can be compared to each other rather than to a previous run.

| id | registered | measured | verdict |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `A` accuracy ≥ 90.5 | 91.00 | **89.80** (89.40 / 90.20, 2 runs) | fail, 0.70 short |
| `B` MR and TR each ≤ 1.0 | — | MR **−6.61**, TR −1.57 | fail |
| `C` IE/KU/ABS each ≤ 1.5 | — | +0.67 / −1.39 / 0.00 | pass |
| `D` `C1` ≤ 6,000 | pre-registered as an expected miss | **9,149** | miss, as registered |
| `E` config line renders six rooms | required | rendered in the order registered | pass |

Cost: feature-side prompt tokens **9,148,866 / 1,000 = 9,149 per question**, against 12,137 for the 48,000 baseline — **0.754x**. The registration said **0.741x**. The error is **1.3%**, and it is the second time a cost prediction has landed inside 2% (the first was §13.301's 0.487 against 0.49).

Accuracy: registered **91.00 (−0.40)**, measured **89.80 (−1.60)**. The direction was right and the magnitude was not, which is the same failure shape as §13.301.4 — the gold-coverage model still understates what a smaller room costs an aggregation capability.

#### 13.304.1 The number that needs an adjudication before it is a finding

`MR` reads **93/121 on both arms**: 24,000 at 13:24 and the per-route arm at 15:34, where the multi-session room is 48,000. The 48,000 baseline read 101.5/121 at 10:00. Two explanations fit the data completely and no third is needed:

| | claim | what it predicts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **H1** | the per-route room does not reach the multi-session assembly path | MR equals the 24,000 arm — observed |
| **H2** | the model name drifted by about six points between 10:00 and 13:24 | both later arms read ~93 regardless of room — also observed |

`TR` does not separate them: 91.34 (24,000) → 94.49 (per-route) → 96.06 (48,000) is monotone in room, which is what H1 would predict for the temporal path and also what H2 would predict if the drift were capability-specific.

So the honest state is that **"the per-route room costs MR 6.61 points" is not yet a finding**, and §13.305 is the cheapest experiment that decides it.

### 13.305 The same-day control, registered before it is dispatched

A run of the registered configuration at the current time, and nothing else. The purpose is to price time rather than to test a mechanism.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **S0** | every config field except the clock matches `42355323615` | any difference makes it a different experiment, not a control |
| **S1** | `MR ≤ 97/121` reads as **drift**, and the MR deltas of §13.302 and §13.301 move from "room" to "time" | `MR ≥ 101/121` refutes H2 and leaves H1 standing as a code defect |
| **S2** | if S1 reads drift, every sentence of the form "the per-route room costs MR 6.61" is **withdrawn from every document**, not annotated | a sentence that survives with a footnote is the §7.3 defect in prose |

Two more conditions, because a control that is read loosely is not a control:

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **S3** | the reading is taken on **the same reader** and the same `thinking` routes | a reader change makes the run an `M1` arm |
| **S4** | `promptDigest` for the first repetition is compared against `42355323615`'s and reported, whatever it says | a prompt that moved means S0 was wrong and the run must be read as a second treatment |

`S4` is the one that costs nothing and is skipped most often: the control's whole value is that the packet is the one the baseline saw, and this campaign has already recorded a run where a "control" differed in a field nobody declared.

#### 13.305.1 The reading, and why `S0` convicted itself before `S1` could be applied

`42387911305` finished `success` at 17:12Z. `S0` is the first thing to check, and it fails:

| field | `42355323615` (baseline) | `42387911305` (called a control) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maxPromptChars` | `default` | **`48000`** |
| `maxPromptCharsByRoute` | `multi-session:48460` | **absent** |
| `room` (rendered) | `48460` on two routes | **`48000` on every route** |
| reader | `deepseek-chat`, `thinking` on `multi-session+temporal` | identical |
| everything else | — | identical |

So this is not the registered control. It is a **different treatment**: the per-route room was collapsed into one room for every route, 460 characters (0.95%) narrower on the two routes that had the larger one and 48,000 wider on the four that had `default`. `S1` therefore has no population to apply to — the two thresholds were written for a run whose only change was the clock.

That is `S0` working as designed. A control whose config moved is not a control, and the campaign has already paid once for reading a run as one (the `§13.305` paragraph above records the class). The finding is that **the judgement, not the run, was under-specified**: `S1` is a two-valued test (`≤ 97` drift, `≥ 101` code defect) on a quantity whose observed value is `97.3`.

| reading | baseline `42355323615` | `42387911305` | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| accuracy (4-run mean) | 91.95% (min 91.40, max 93.20) | 90.75% (min 90.20, max 91.00) | **−1.20 pp** |
| `MR` | 83.47% (101/121), mean 101.5 | 80.99% (95/121), mean **97.3** | **−4.2 questions** |
| `IE` | 93.33% (140/150) | 94.67% (141/150) | +0.7 questions |
| `KU` | 88.89% (62/72) | 87.50% (62/72) | 0 |
| `TR` | 96.06% (120/127) | 95.28% (120/127) | 0 |
| prompt tokens | 27,178,561 | 27,178,563 | **+2** |
| completion tokens | 2,294,764 | 2,214,126 | −80,638 (−3.51%) |
| feature-side prompt tokens | 24,273,758 | 24,252,638 | −21,120 (−0.09%) |
| feature-side completion tokens | 2,223,850 | 2,141,529 | −82,321 (−3.70%) |
| prefix-cache share | 95.97% | 96.09% | +0.12 pp |
| **prompt tokens per correct answer** | **13,199** | **13,362** | **+1.23%** |

Two things in that table are worth registering rather than explaining away.

**The prompt total is identical to two tokens.** 27,178,561 against 27,178,563 over 2,000 question-passes is not a coincidence and not a saving: the two rooms are 48,460 and 48,000 characters, both far above what any prompt in this dataset fills, so the cap was never reached and the treatment changed nothing about what was sent. The −21,120 on the feature side is the same spend attributed differently, not spend avoided. **A room change that never binds cannot be tested by a run whose prompts never reach the room**, and the campaign's own `cap` reading already said so: 4.11 characters per token of the 48,000 window.

**The completion side moved 3.70% without any prompt change**, which is the reader varying between dispatches at `temp=0`. That is the size of the day-to-day noise this campaign has been attributing to configuration, and it is larger than the 0.09% prompt movement it was supposed to isolate.

`S1` is replaced by a three-valued reading, because the two-valued one has a gap exactly where the data landed:

| id | band | reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `S1a` | `MR mean ≤ 97` | **drift**: the §13.301/§13.302 MR deltas are time, and every "the room costs MR 6.61" sentence is withdrawn under `S2` |
| `S1b` | `97 < MR mean < 101` | **unresolved**, and no sentence may cite the room as the cause in either direction |
| `S1c` | `MR mean ≥ 101` | the `H2` refutation stands and `H1` remains a code defect |

`97.3` is `S1b`. The value is one question above the drift threshold and four below the defect threshold, so the honest sentence is that **the room explanation is neither confirmed nor excluded**, and `§13.301`/`§13.302` still say "costs MR 6.61 points" without a control behind them. `S2` fires at `S1a` only, and `S1a` did not happen; what fires instead is a weaker obligation, recorded here: no document may state the 6.61 as a mechanism until `42391516675` (the `M1` arm B) or a genuine `S0`-clean control produces a band.

#### 13.305.2 What the run is, now that it is not a control

It is a legitimate experiment and should be registered as one rather than discarded:

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `S5` | collapsing the per-route room to `48000` documents its own **inertness**, because no prompt in this dataset reaches either room | an artifact whose delivered prompts are at the cap, i.e. a `cap` reading that is a window rather than a selection |
| `S6` | the 1.20 pp accuracy drop and the 4.2-question MR drop are **not** attributed to the room, because `S5` leaves the room with no mechanism | any document that connects the two |

`S6` exists because the numbers invite the wrong reading. A 1.20 pp drop that arrives with a 3.70% completion-token drop and a two-token prompt difference is a reader-variance observation, and the next dispatch that wants to price the room must first produce prompts that reach it.


### 13.306 The reader's deadline stops being a constant, and a loss stops being a pass

`42381840503` (the §13.303 arm B, `deepseek-v4-pro`) is the run that made this a defect rather than a tuning question. It answered 291 of 500 and died on

```text
{"url":"https://api.deepseek.com/v1/chat/completions","attempts":2,"retried":1,
 "rateLimited":0,"elapsedMs":601000,"attemptsMs":[299999,300001],"timeoutMs":300000,
 "retryBudgetMs":420000,"cause":"The operation was aborted due to timeout"}
```

Two facts in that object, and they are the whole registration:

1. **`attemptsMs[i] == timeoutMs` on both attempts.** The bound fired; the network did not fail. A loss of this shape is a fact about one question's latency.
2. **The bound was 300,000 ms because the thinking mode is `enabled` on two of six routes and that is what the module constant says.** Nothing in a dispatch could move it, and nothing in the artifact stated it.

#### 13.306.1 Two classes, disjoint by construction

| class | signature | decision | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| deadline loss | **every** attempt reached the deadline within 1% | record `''`, count, keep the pass | the arm has no output for one question, which is one question's cost |
| transport fault | any attempt shorter than the deadline | **throw** | a dead endpoint fails every question; deciding one of them produces a number for a run that did not happen |

The 1% tolerance is not decoration: the recorded pair is `299999` and `300001` against a `300000` bound, so an exact comparison would classify the clearest deadline loss in the campaign as a wire fault.

`''` and not `null`, for the reason §13.303's refusal repair states: `null` is "the arm declined", which `judgeScorer` scores **CORRECT** against an unanswerable gold, so a stall recorded as a decline would hand the abstention column a free pass.

#### 13.306.2 The ceiling, and why one loss is not one loss too many

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `T0` | a pass tolerates up to **2%** of its questions lost to deadlines (10 of 500, floor of 1) | a pass that throws at 10 of 500 is below the registered line |
| `T1` | the 11th loss **throws**, naming the bound to raise | a pass that continues past it and publishes an accuracy is the defect |
| `T2` | the ceiling is printed on the gate line as `deadlineLossCeiling=10` | a ceiling enforced and not printed is §13.306's own complaint about the deadline |
| `T3` | a deadline loss is **never** counted as a provider refusal | a loss that also appears in `providerRefusals()` makes "the filter refused it" a false statement |

The wall clock the ceiling implies is worth stating, because it is the price of a larger bound: a
declared 600 s deadline with its 720 s ceiling allows up to 1,200 s for one question (a full attempt
plus the truncated retry the budget permits), so eleven losses on four workers is **at most 55
minutes** of a pass spent proving the endpoint is dead. The job's own `CORTEX_MEMORY_BUDGET_MINUTES`
is the outer guard; this number is why it does not need to be lowered.

`T3` exists because the first implementation of this repair violated it. The catch was a guard clause followed by the refusal body, so a deadline loss fell through: it was recorded twice and counted as a moderation decision. **Mutation testing found it** — changing `record('', index)` to `record(null, index)` broke no test, because the second write overwrote the first. The catch is now `if`/`else`, and a test asserts `providerRefusals()` does not move when a pass loses a question to a deadline.

#### 13.306.3 The bound becomes declared, and the declaration becomes evidence

`CORTEX_READER_TIMEOUT_MS` overrides the deadline the thinking mode implies. Three consequences, each registered:

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `D0` | the retry ceiling follows a declared deadline (`deadline + 120 s`), because a ceiling at or below one attempt is a ladder that can never retry | a declared 600 s deadline running under the 420 s ceiling leaves every attempt single-shot — `41393748964` on a new number |
| `D1` | `0` is refused: `AbortSignal.timeout(0)` fires before the request leaves | a run that declares 0 and reports 500 provider failures |
| `D2` | the declared value reaches the artifact as a `/deadline=` clause on the reader line | a bound that lives only in a job log is §13.110 on a new field |
| `D3` | the run prints `reader transport: deadlineMs=… deadlineSource=…` before the first question, for both thinking modes | a bound that first appears in the error object of the question that reached it |

`D3`'s second half is the one this campaign needed: the run that died had **two** deadlines (300 s on two routes, 60 s on four) and its log named neither.

#### 13.306.4 Why the framing is a censoring problem and not a timeout problem

The frontier literature has a name for what happened. A thinking budget is any harness-enforceable bound on inference before a scored answer, and a **wall-clock deadline is the same bound denominated in a second currency** — one that imports the deployment's hardware into the construct. When realized usage presses against the mandate, the item is **censored**: the score at that bound mixes genuine inability with amputation.

| source | finding it contributes |
| --- | --- |
| thinking-budget sensitivity (2026) | token cap, wall-clock deadline, round bound, sample bound and effort parameter are **five different knobs** with five different failure modes; "record the knob, record the realized usage, treat the difference as a first-class finding" |
| `AlphaDiana` (`2610.20675`) | harness is an **experimental condition**; 50.0% of agent failures are budget/call-limit, 28.7% truncation, **5.5% a genuine wrong conclusion** |
| Terminal-Bench harness note (2026) | strict 3-minute timeouts **penalize deep-reasoning models**, which spend compute before emitting |

Under that vocabulary `42381840503` lost its pass to a censor on 1 question of 291 (0.34%), which is far below the 28.7% truncation rate those studies report — and it still destroyed the measurement, because the harness treated a censored item as a fatal error rather than as a censored item.

### 13.307 `M1` re-registered: same reader axis, one instrument on both arms

§13.303 registered `M1` with arm A at `deepseek-flash` and arm B at `deepseek-v4-pro`, and arm B never produced a number. The axis is unchanged; what changes is that **both arms now run under the same declared deadline**.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `R0` | all 500 `promptDigest` values agree between the two arms, checked before any accuracy is compared | one disagreement means the arms differ in the packet and the accuracy difference is not the reader's |
| `R1` | arm B ≥ arm A + **3.0** points | a smaller gap leaves requirement 12's upper half unproven at this size |
| `R2` | arm B's per-question deltas are **not** systematically negative on `ABS` or `IE` | a negative sign on the capabilities a stronger reader should not hurt is a wiring defect, not a model property |
| `R3` | the gate line of both arms names `readerTimeoutMs=600000` | an undeclared asymmetry makes the comparison an instrument comparison |
| `R4` | `deadline losses: 0` on both, or the count is disclosed beside the accuracy | a loss recorded as wrong is a conservative bias against the arm that took it |

`R3` is the one this round bought: the previous attempt compared arms whose bounds could not be read from the artifacts, so the difference between an arm that died and an arm that was never given the room would have been indistinguishable from a model property.

`R4`'s asymmetry argument is deliberate: one lost question costs at most 0.2 points, so it cannot manufacture `R1`'s 3.0, but it can shave it, and a reader is entitled to the number.

#### 13.307.1 Arm A's reading, and the two criteria that are already decided

`42391635411` finished `success` at 17:18Z, 48 minutes after dispatch, on `deepseek-flash` with `ABLATION_RUNS=2`. Two of the five criteria are settled and neither needed the other arm:

| criterion | evidence | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `R3` | `cortex-memory gate: ... readerTimeoutMs=600000, deadlineLossCeiling=10` on the gate line, and `reader transport: deadlineMs=600000 retryBudgetMs=720000 minIntervalMs=none deadlineSource=CORTEX_READER_TIMEOUT_MS` printed twice, once per thinking mode | **holds**, for arm A |
| `R4` | `=== deadline losses: 0 ===` and `=== provider refusals: 0 ===` | **holds**, for arm A |

`R3`'s second half is the one `§13.306` registered as `D3` and it is satisfied literally: the transport line appears **before the first question**, so a run that dies on its bound no longer carries a bound nobody can name.

Arm A's numbers, with the same reading the baseline gets:

| capability | accuracy (first repetition) | total | min | mean | max |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IE` | 96.00% | 150 | 144 | 144.0 | 144 |
| `MR` | 77.69% | 121 | 94 | 94.0 | 94 |
| `KU` | 87.50% | 72 | 62 | 62.5 | 63 |
| `TR` | 96.06% | 127 | 122 | 122.5 | 123 |
| `ABS` | 100.00% | 30 | 30 | 30.0 | 30 |

- Overall accuracy: **90.60%** on both repetitions (`min 90.60%, max 90.60%`).
- `MR` against the baseline's 83.47%: **−4.4 questions**, the same order as the `§13.305` pair's −4.2 — which is the second independent sign that the `MR` delta of this week is not the reader model.
- prompt tokens **14,508,996** over 2,000 question-passes; completion **1,182,360**; prefix-cache share **95.78%**.
- `prompt tokens per correct answer`: feature side **12,102,818 / 1,000 / 0.9060 = 13,359**.

That last figure is the one this arm was dispatched to produce, and it says something the `M1` hypothesis did not predict: **the cheaper model is not cheaper per correct answer.** Against the `deepseek-chat` baseline's 13,199 at 91.95%, `deepseek-flash` spends **1.2% more** token per correct answer **and** answers **1.35 pp fewer** correctly — a double loss, not a trade.

The reason is worth registering because it bounds what this instrument can ever say. A weaker reader does not send shorter prompts: the packet is the same 48,000-character window with the same evidence, and `perQuestionPerRun` is a property of the packet rather than of the model. What a cheaper model buys is a lower **rate per token**, and this repository measures tokens, not currency — `cortex-ai/src/usage.ts` states the reason a price would need a rate card it does not own. So the honest reading is: **token efficiency does not improve with a weaker reader, and the case for a stronger one has no cost headwind on this instrument.** Whether the rate card makes `deepseek-flash` cheaper in money is a question this campaign cannot answer and must not imply.

`R0`, `R1` and `R2` need arm B, and arm B arrived while this section was being written.


**One observation that must not become a finding**: the two repetitions produced the *same* total correct count (453 of 500) while `KU` and `TR` swapped one question each (62/123 and 63/122). `featureAggregate.min == max` here is therefore not a stability claim — it is two capability-level moves that cancelled, and the per-capability spread columns are what say so. A renderer that printed only the total would have reported a perfectly stable run.

#### 13.307.2 Arm B: the strong reader is worse, and the shape of the loss names the cause

`42391516675` finished `success` at 18:06Z after 5 h 37 min — 1 h 37 min inside its
`CORTEX_MEMORY_BUDGET_MINUTES=340` guard, so the guard did its job and the declared 600 s deadline
never fired (`deadline losses: 0`, `provider refusals: 0`, prefix-cache share 95.18%).

| criterion | measurement | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `R3` | `reader transport: deadlineMs=600000 retryBudgetMs=720000 deadlineSource=CORTEX_READER_TIMEOUT_MS` printed for both thinking modes before question 1 | **holds** |
| `R4` | `deadline losses: 0` | **holds** |
| `R1` | arm B **85.90%** against arm A's 90.60% — a **−4.70 pp** gap where the registration required **+3.0** | **refuted**, and in the opposite direction |
| `R2` | `IE` −15 questions (144 → 129), `KU` −5 (63 → 58), `TR` −3 (122 → 119), `MR` −2 (94 → 92), `ABS` 0 | **fires**: the sign is systematically negative on the capability a stronger reader must not hurt |

| capability | arm A (`deepseek-flash`) | arm B (`deepseek-v4-pro`) | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IE` | 96.00% (144/150) | 86.00% (129/150) | **−15** |
| `MR` | 77.69% (94/121) | 76.86% (92/121) | −2 |
| `KU` | 87.50% (63/72) | 80.56% (58/72) | −5 |
| `TR` | 96.06% (122/127) | 93.70% (119/127) | −3 |
| `ABS` | 100.00% (30/30) | 100.00% (30/30) | 0 |
| overall | 90.60% | **85.90%** (min 85.80, max 86.00) | **−4.70 pp** |
| per correct answer | 13,359 | **14,084** | **+5.4%** |

`R2` was written for exactly this: *"a negative sign on the capabilities a stronger reader should
not hurt is a wiring defect, not a model property"*. `IE` at −15 of 150 is the largest movement
this campaign has recorded on a capability, and it moved **down** when the reader got stronger.

The three counters that localise it:

| counter | arm A | arm B | reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exact` channel | 525 | **476** | **−49** deterministic matches |
| `structural` channel | 567 | 536 | −31 |
| `judge` channel (fallback) | 741 (37.0%) | **815 (40.8%)** | +74 |
| `unjudged` | 0 | 0 | the judge finished every fallback |
| `llm` abstentions | 69 | 71 | +2, i.e. **not** a refusal difference |
| feature-side completion tokens | 1,131,636 | **1,598,096** | **+41.2%** |

**−47 questions of accuracy against −49 lost `exact` matches.** The loss is not the model
answering worse; it is the model answering in a shape the deterministic channels no longer
recognise, falling to the LLM judge, and being scored wrong there. A reasoning reader emits more
text (+41% completion at a *smaller* prompt budget: 12,098 against 12,103 prompt tokens per
question), and this harness's `structural` and `exact` matchers are the first two rungs.

So `R1`'s refutation is **not** evidence that `deepseek-v4-pro` is a weaker reader, and it must
not be reported as one. It is evidence that this pipeline has a **contract defect**: the answer
shape a reasoning model produces is outside what the scorer accepts without a judge.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `R5` | the loss is in the **scorer contract**, not in the reader: normalising the answer shape before `structural`/`exact` restores arm B's deterministic-channel count to arm A's (~525 of 2,000 calls) | a normalised arm whose `exact` count stays near 476 |
| `R6` | if `R5` holds, arm B's accuracy rises by at least **4 of the 4.70 points** it lost, because −47 accuracy against −49 lost `exact` matches is 0.96 of the gap | a post-normalisation gap smaller than 4 points |
| `R7` | the judge is **not** stricter on arm B: for the fallback population, exact and judge agree at the same rate on both arms | a judge that rejects arm B's fallbacks more often on the same gold |

`R5` is the cheapest experiment in the queue. It is also the one requirement 12 needs: the
requirement says a stronger reader must score better, and the honest current state is that **the
harness cannot see the stronger reader's answer**. `R7` guards the other explanation — a judge
that is right and an `exact` matcher that is too generous on arm A — which would make the finding
a scorer-fairness result rather than a contract result.

`R5`/`R6`/`R7` are registered, not run. Nothing in this section may be quoted as "the strong
model is worse" until either `R5` is measured or the scorer contract is shown to be sound.

### 13.308 A correct answer's price, and the population its denominator came from

`§13.305.1`'s last row is where this started. `prompt tokens per correct answer` was being computed by `tools/cost-ledger.py` as `perQuestionPerRun / accuracy`, and the two operands describe different populations:

- `perQuestionPerRun` = `usageBySide.feature.promptTokens / (questionCount × runs)` — a sum over **every repetition**.
- `accuracy` = `feature.metrics.accuracy` — **one repetition**, which `report.ts` renders as *"accuracy (first repetition)"* for the reason `§13.122` records at length.

On the `§13.305` pair the two arms' first repetitions sit on opposite sides of their means: the baseline's is its worst (91.40% against 91.95%) and the treatment's is its best (90.80% against 90.75%). The shipped division therefore charged the baseline 0.60% more than it spent and the treatment 0.06% less, and read a **1.20 pp** accuracy gap as a **0.57%** cost gap where the matching denominator gives **1.23%** — the arm that answered fewer questions correctly looked 54% cheaper than it was.

Repetition order is arbitrary, so the sign of that error is arbitrary too. That is what makes it a defect rather than a tuning choice, and it is why the repair is not "divide by the better number in the tool".

#### 13.308.1 The reading moves into the artifact, with its denominator named

A ratio every consumer recomputes is a ratio every consumer can get differently right, so the run writes it down. `AblationReport.costEfficiency` carries four fields, and the third one is the fix:

| field | why it is a field and not something a reader derives |
| --- | --- |
| `perCorrectAnswerPromptTokens` | the reading itself |
| `promptTokensPerQuestion` | the numerator, so the division can be rechecked without the artifact's other blocks |
| `accuracy` | the denominator, because the ratio is a function of it and a price quoted alone is a product of two numbers with one hidden |
| `accuracySource` | **`all-runs` or `first-repetition`** — the two coincide on a one-repetition arm and differ on a four-repetition one, and a reader comparing two artifacts is entitled to know which population it is holding |

The computation reads `ablation.featureAggregate.avg`, the unweighted mean of each repetition's accuracy. Every repetition grades the same questions, so it equals the pooled proportion the numerator is built from. When the field is absent — an artifact written before the spread existed, or one that only ever had a single repetition — the fallback is `feature.metrics.accuracy` and `accuracySource` says `first-repetition` rather than letting a coincidence pass for a measurement.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `E0` | the price is invariant to **which repetition ran first**: reordering four repetitions changes `feature.metrics.accuracy` and nothing else in the artifact, so the reading must not move | two prices for one run |
| `E1` | a report with `featureAggregate` prices from `all-runs`; one without prices from `first-repetition` and says so | an artifact that picked one silently |
| `E2` | the ratio is **absent**, never `0`, `Infinity` or a thrown error, for four states: no side split, no question count, no repetition count, a run that spent nothing | a number where the division is undefined |
| `E3` | a run that answered nothing right is **absent** and not enormous | `inf` rendered as a price |
| `E4` | a side split that does not close cannot price an answer | a ratio computed from a column the renderer itself calls `SPLIT UNAVAILABLE` |
| `E5` | the rendered line names the population `all-runs | first-repetition | artifact` beside the accuracy | a ratio quoted without its denominator |
| `E6` | the correct-answer count is **not** quoted beside an all-runs mean, because it is one repetition's count | `(454 correct, all-runs)` against 90.75% -- two populations in one parenthesis, and 454/500 = 90.80% describes no run |

`E0` is the one a code review cannot check, because both divisions look correct in isolation. It is asserted directly: two artifacts differing only in `feature.metrics.accuracy` must return the **same** float.

#### 13.308.2 The same defect, second instance: a split that does not close

`E4` exists because the numerator is a column of `usageBySide`, and that block carries two independently accumulated tallies. When `baseline + feature` claims more prompt tokens than `llmUsage` reported, `residualUsage` refuses to name a residual and `render.ts` prints `SPLIT UNAVAILABLE` instead of a per-arm column. A price computed from that column inherits the doubt, and an absent ratio reads as "not measured" while a wrong one reads as a measurement — the `null`-versus-`0` rule this campaign applies to retry counters and to token columns, one field further out.

The guard is conditional on the total existing, because `llmUsage` and `usageBySide` attach independently and requiring one to check the other would make a report that carries only the split unpriceable for no reason. The `tools/cost-ledger.py` side implements the same rule for artifacts it reads rather than wrote.

#### 13.308.3 Two readers, one rule

`tools/cost-ledger.py` now prefers the artifact's own `costEfficiency` and adopts it only when its shape can be divided — a percentage, a boolean or a missing ratio is refused rather than trusted, because a field a future build writes is not a field this build may assume. When the artifact has no such field the tool computes the ratio itself, with the same denominator selection and the same `accuracySource` label.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `V0` | an authored reading wins over recomputation | a consumer that disagrees with the run that produced both inputs |
| `V1` | an authored reading of the wrong shape is refused, and the tool falls back to computing | `accuracy: 92` adopted as a fraction |
| `V2` | the tool's fallback picks the same denominator the run would have | two artifacts, one with `costEfficiency` and one without, read as two different prices for one run |
| `V3` | the rendered line names the population in all three cases (`artifact`, `all-runs`, `first-repetition`) | a text reading that cannot say which population it used |

#### 13.308.4 A reader that survives an old artifact must not crash on one

Writing the `first-repetition` case exposed a live defect in the renderer. `formatAblationReport` read `ab.featureAggregate.min` unguarded, so an artifact written before the spread existed — the exact artifact `E1`'s fallback exists to price — threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` instead of rendering. The spread table now renders `—` per row and the dash is documented as "the repetitions were never spread", which is a fact about the run and not a stability result.

This is the third time in this campaign that a rule about absence lived in a conditional whose absence case was never executed. It is now covered by the same file that covers the rule.

#### 13.308.5 The reading, on two real artifacts

Two artifacts from this week still predate the field, so both exercise the fallback path — which is the path a reader of an old file actually takes.

| artifact | `feature.metrics.accuracy` (first) | `featureAggregate.avg` | old division | new division |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `42387911305` | 90.80% | 90.75% | 13,355 | **13,362** |
| `42391635411` | 90.60% | 90.60% | 13,359 | **13,359** |

`42391635411` cannot distinguish the two — its repetitions happen to agree — and that is exactly why the pair was worth running both halves of. `42387911305` moves by 0.05 pp on the denominator and 7 tokens on the price, and the tool now prints

```text
  per correct answer              13,362   prompt tokens
  at accuracy                     90.75%   (no count, the mean spans runs, all-runs)
```

#### 13.308.6 A third field in the same parenthesis, and a third population

`42387911305`'s first rendering attempt read `(454 correct, all-runs)` against a denominator of 90.75%. `454/500` is 90.80% — the first repetition's count, printed beside the all-runs mean. A reader who divides the two numbers in one bracket gets a third number that describes no run at all.

That is the same defect as `E0`, one field over, and it is registered as `E6`: the count is withheld when the denominator is a mean over repetitions, because the artifact holds no count for that population. The rendered line says so rather than printing `n/a`, since "the mean spans runs" is a reason and `n/a` is a shrug.

The Python side withholds it; the TypeScript side never carried it, because `costEfficiency` was designed with four fields and a count is not one of them. The two readers therefore agree on the sentence as well as on the number.


---

## 13.309 A quota that runs out is one question's loss, and the ladder's measurements were being discarded

### 13.309.1 The run, and the 1.7% that cost everything

`42381702081` is `P1`, the second-provider arm: `glm-4.6` through Zhipu, 500 questions, four workers, a 340-minute budget. It ran 5 h 42 min and ended `failure` with **no report at all**. The record it left is a partial measurement that cannot be graded, and the whole of it is one call:

```text
LLM request failed: 429 Too Many Requests — {"error":{"code":1302,
  "message":"您的账户已达到速率限制，请您控制请求频率"}}
  — not retried (attempts-exhausted) after 9 attempt(s) and 160 s was left
```

The transport accounting from the same run, taken minutes earlier, reads `attempts: 1613, rateLimited: 28`. **Twenty-eight of sixteen hundred requests** — 1.7% — and one call collected nine of them in a row, which is more than its ladder allowed.

The counting matters because it rules out the obvious repair: the arm was not throttling itself, the pacing floor was 6,000 ms, and 1.7% is not a quota problem at the process level. It is one question's weather, and it destroyed 500.

### 13.309.2 What the catch classified, and the family it left out

§13.306 taught this layer that an exhaustion which happens **on every attempt** is a fact about the endpoint rather than about the system under test, and that such a loss is one entry scored as unanswered rather than the end of the pass. That repair classified exactly one shape:

| class | predicate | disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| moderation refusal | `ProviderContentRefusal` | record `''`, continue |
| deadline exhaustion | every attempt reached `timeoutMs × 0.99` | record `''`, continue, count against a 2% ceiling |
| everything else | — | **throw** |

A retry ladder that ends with every attempt answered `429` satisfies **neither** of the first two: `429` returns immediately, so no attempt reaches the deadline. It fell into "everything else" and ended the pass. The two are one family — the endpoint's allowance ran out, on the clock or on the rate — and the predicate is structurally identical: *did every attempt fail for the same external reason?*

`rateLimitExhaustion` is therefore the twin of `deadlineExhaustion`, reading the same `retryExhausted` object with `rateLimited === attempts` in place of the duration test. The mixed case still throws: one attempt throttled and one dead on the wire has two causes and neither explains it, and classifying it per question would let a broken network be reported as a busy provider.

### 13.309.3 The defect underneath: the ladder's measurements were thrown away with the outcome

The first implementation of the classifier matched nothing, and the reason is a real defect one layer down rather than a mistake in the predicate.

`retryableFetchWithStats` has two ways to end badly. A transport failure is **thrown**, with a `RetryExhaustion` attached. An exhausted retry count is **returned** — the loop hands back the last response and a `RetryRefusal` whose reason is `attempts-exhausted`. `post` then sees `!res.ok`, renders the refusal into a message, and raises a bare `Error`. The `RetryOutcome` — attempts, retried, rate-limited, and inside it the per-attempt durations — went out of scope with the stack frame.

So the adapter could not attach an exhaustion object even if it wanted to, and reconstructing one there was refused: `attemptsMs`, `timeoutMs` and `elapsedMs` live only in the retry loop, and filling them with placeholders would fabricate the three numbers a reader would then reason from.

`RetryOutcome.exhausted` now carries the measured object on the `attempts-exhausted` path, and the adapter attaches it with the same `withExhaustion` helper the thrown path uses.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Q0` | a call whose every attempt was `429` is recorded as one entry, and the pass continues | a pass that dies on the first throttled question |
| `Q1` | that entry is counted against **one** ceiling with deadline losses, not a second ceiling of its own | a pass that could lose 4% while each counter stayed under its own bound |
| `Q2` | a mixed exhaustion still throws | a run that reports a network fault as a quota |
| `Q3` | the record names which kind it was, and the advice names the knob that answers it | a message that sends a reader to `CORTEX_READER_TIMEOUT_MS` over a quota |
| `Q4` | `lostToTransport(kind?)` partitions rather than overlaps: the parts sum to the whole | a third kind arriving without a name |

`Q3` is not cosmetic. §13.306's message named `CORTEX_READER_TIMEOUT_MS` because that was the only kind; advice that is wrong half the time is worse than none, because it is a dispatch someone makes twice.

### 13.309.4 One dead branch removed rather than covered

`benchmark.ts`'s refusal branch read `err instanceof ProviderContentRefusal ? err.providerCode : null`. The guard above it is `err is ProviderContentRefusal`, so the `null` arm was unreachable **by construction** — it showed up as the last uncovered branch in the file, which is what an unreachable arm looks like when it is written as a fallback. Removed. A branch that cannot execute is not defence in depth; it is a coverage hole that reads like safety.

---

## 13.310 The M1 gap, decomposed — and the retraction of `R5`

### 13.310.1 A marginal count cannot say what happened to the questions it counted

§13.307.2 concluded from two numbers that the strong reader's loss was a **scorer-contract defect**: `exact` verdicts fell from 175 to 134 while accuracy fell from 90.60% to 85.80%, so the matcher had "stopped seeing" arm B's answers. The arithmetic is right and the inference is wrong, and the way it is wrong is worth a registration of its own.

Both artifacts carry the per-question records, so the two arms can be joined on `questionId`. That join says:

| | A right | A wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **B right** | 419 | 10 |
| **B wrong** | 34 | 37 |

Of the **53** questions where arm A matched exactly and arm B did not, **arm B was still scored correct on 47**. The judge rescued them. The migration was real — `exact` did fall 41 on the margin — and it cost **six** questions net, not twenty-four.

The marginal readings are not wrong; they answer a different question. *"How many verdicts left by the exact door"* is a property of one arm. *"What happened to the questions that moved"* requires both. A decomposition read off marginal counts is a decomposition of nothing.

### 13.310.2 The 24 questions, by cause

| cause | questions | share | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| preference questions | **10** | 42% | the judge disagrees with itself about a gold that is a criterion |
| `exact` migration not rescued | **6** | 25% | arm B's answer shape moved a question to the judge and the judge said no |
| genuine answer-quality difference | **8** | 33% | arm B counted wrong, dropped a qualifier, or declined |

The last row is not a defect and must not be reported as one: `gold 2` against arm B's `1` on a question whose own `rawOutput` enumerates two bicycles, `gold 99` against `100`, `gold Dark Souls 3 DLC` against `Dark Souls 3`. Those are answers that are wrong.

**§13.307.2's `R5` is withdrawn.** Its claim was that normalising the answer shape before the deterministic matchers would restore arm B's `exact` count to arm A's and recover at least four of the 4.70 points. The migration is 53 questions and the judge already rescued 47 of them, so the ceiling on that repair is **6 questions, 1.2 points** — a quarter of what the registration predicted, and it would not have been the mechanism that mattered.

### 13.310.3 The preference column: 5.8% of the dataset, 42% of the gap

| population | questions | A correct | B correct | A only | B only |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| preference golds | **29** | 23 (79.3%) | **13 (44.8%)** | 10 | 0 |
| everything else | 471 | 430 (91.3%) | 416 (88.3%) | 24 | 10 |

The preference gold is written as `The user would prefer responses that acknowledge and build upon their existing efforts…` — a description of what a good answer should do, not an answer. It can never be matched, so it always reaches the judge, and the judge is the only instrument on it.

Two explanations were tested and **both were refuted**:

| hypothesis | test | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| length bias — the judge prefers long answers | arm A's answer length against arm B's on the ten questions A won | B was **shorter** on two, longer on one, within 8% on one. No direction |
| noise — the same content judged twice | Jaccard overlap of the two arms' answers on those ten | **0.372** mean, none above 0.75. The answers genuinely differ |

So the honest state is that **the cause of the preference gap is not established**, and §13.311 registers how to establish it. What is established is its size, which is the part an accuracy number cannot show.

### 13.310.4 The instrument, and why it must be able to refuse

`tools/arm-delta-decomposition.py` performs the join, the matrix, the migration count and the preference split. It reimplements `metrics.ts`'s four-channel decision in Python, which makes it a second opinion that can be wrong — so for every verdict derivable without a judge it compares its own answer with the artifact's `correct` and **raises** on any disagreement. A decomposition over two graders that disagree is a number about nothing, and the failure without the check is silent: the table would look exactly like the last one.

On the two M1 artifacts it reproduces the numbers above, and both arms' self-checks agree on all 500 questions each. Its `judgeDependence` line — 50.4% for arm A, 57.2% for arm B — is the share of each arm this tool cannot verify, and it is printed because a decomposition over a mostly-judged arm is a statement about the judge rather than about the arm.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `D0` | a re-derived verdict that disagrees with the artifact raises, naming the question | a table printed over a disagreement |
| `D1` | the join is on `questionId`, so a re-ordered artifact is the same comparison | a resort read as a regression |
| `D2` | two arms over different question sets are refused | a comparison of two datasets reported as a comparison of two arms |
| `D3` | the migration count reports how many the judge rescued, not only how many moved | a migration reported as a loss |
| `D4` | the preference split is computed, because the gold's opening is a property of the dataset | a preference question counted with the rest |

### 13.310.5 What this retracts, stated plainly

- §13.307.2's sentence *"it is evidence that this pipeline has a contract defect: the answer shape a reasoning model produces is outside what the scorer accepts without a judge"* is **wrong**. The scorer accepted 47 of the 53.
- §22.48.6's conclusion that the same-backbone comparison against Reglos now carries a shape condition is **withdrawn**: the shape effect is 1.2 points at its ceiling, not a plausible explanation of a 3–5 point difference.
- The requirement-12 finding **stands and is sharper**: a stronger reader scored **4.70 points worse** on this harness, and the largest single cause is a question type where the judge is the entire instrument. That is not a harness bug in the matcher; it may be one in the rubric.

The lesson is the one this campaign keeps paying for: **a change was inferred from a distribution rather than measured on the pairs.** §13.306's method — build the object that makes the claim checkable — was available and was not used, and the cost was a round of work aimed at the wrong mechanism.

---

## 13.311 The remaining explanation for the preference gap, and how to measure it

### 13.311.1 Why this is now the only path left

§13.310 refuted length bias and refuted same-content-different-verdict, and confirmed that the two arms' answers on the ten questions arm A won genuinely differ (Jaccard 0.372). Two explanations survive:

1. **arm B's answers are worse on preference questions** — they address the criterion less well, and 44.8% is the true reading;
2. **the judge's verdict on a preference question is unstable** — the same gold and answer can be scored either way, so 79.3% against 44.8% is a comparison of two draws from a noisy instrument rather than two abilities.

These are distinguishable with one measurement, and it is not the one that was attempted: **re-judge the same recorded answers several times and count how often the verdict moves.** The first explanation predicts a low flip rate at both arms' accuracies; the second predicts a flip rate large enough to manufacture a 34.5-point difference.

### 13.311.2 What the literature says the answer might be, and what it says about the instrument

Two 2026 audits make this a measurement with a published prior rather than a fishing expedition.

**`All Verdicts are Not Equal`** (arXiv:2610.12083, AACL IJCNLP 2026 Main) stress-tests six frontier judges across four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two presentation orders, three temperatures and ten repetitions per condition. Three findings bear directly here: verdicts change **across identical replications at temperature zero**; the most deterministic judge achieves perfect consistency by trivially repeating incorrect verdicts, agreeing with ground truth **51%** of the time; and **reliability is item-specific rather than model-level**. The last is the one that matters for this campaign: a judge-level agreement figure cannot say whether *this* question type is the unstable one.

**`Reliability without Validity`** (arXiv:2606.19544) evaluates 21 judges from nine providers over ~541,000 judgments and reports two numbers that cut in opposite directions. Exact agreement overstates quality by **33–41 pp** against Cohen's κ, and high test–retest reliability (**>0.95**) coexists with severe position bias (**>0.10**) in judges already in production — a judge that repeats the same mistake on every pass reads as perfectly reliable. But **verbosity bias is small (<0.011)** under a single pairwise rubric, which is the published form of what §13.310 measured directly: length was not the mechanism.

Neither paper measures a pointwise judge on preference golds, which is the cell this section fills. What they supply is the metric and the discipline: `T`, the trustworthy verdict rate, is the joint probability that a verdict is reproducible, order-invariant and accurate. **This harness's judge is pointwise** — one gold, one answer, no order — so the order dimension is not applicable and `T` degenerates to the product of the other two, which this section can measure.

### 13.311.3 The criteria

The instrument is `tools/judge-regrade.mjs`, which re-judges recorded answers `--passes` times and reports the flip rate by capability; it now also takes `--preference-only`, so the population whose golds are criteria can be measured apart from the population whose golds are answers. `judge-audit.yml` gains a `population` input forwarded to both the plan step and the reading step through one derived variable, because two steps that derived it separately could grade different populations into one artifact.

| id | claim | falsifier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `J0` | the flip rate over preference golds is **higher** than over answer golds, on the same judge, the same arm and the same five passes | preference flip rate at or below the answer-gold rate |
| `J1` | if `J0` holds, at least half of the preference gap is attributable to instability: the 34.5-point difference is larger than one flip-rate's worth of noise could produce on a stable instrument | a gap that survives the measured flip rate |
| `J2` | the judge's **test–retest agreement is high while its agreement with the gold on preference questions is low** — the consistency-without-validity paradox, measured on this repository's own judge rather than borrowed from the paper | an unstable judge (low retest) or a stable-and-correct one (high both) |
| `J3` | `T` = retest agreement × gold agreement, reported for the preference population and for the rest, is **lower on preference** | `T` equal across the two populations |

`J2` is the one that decides which repair is available. A judge that is stable and wrong needs a **better rubric** — the preference golds have to be graded against stated criteria rather than by asking an LLM whether an answer "reflects" a description. A judge that is unstable needs **more passes and a majority verdict**, because a single draw from a noisy instrument cannot separate two arms whose true difference is smaller than the noise. The two repairs cost different things and only one of them is right, which is why the round that has the reading must not skip it.

### 13.311.4 Dispatched, not read

Two dispatches, one per M1 arm, `mode=regrade`, `passes=5`, `population=preference`, `limit=500`: 29 questions × 5 passes × 2 arms = 290 judgments. The reading is not in this registration; §13.312 will carry it, and until then **nothing in §13.310 may be read as "arm B is worse on preference questions"**. What §13.310 establishes is the size and the location of the gap, and where it is not.

## 13.312 The preference gap was the instrument: three silent substitutions in the judge

§13.311 dispatched two re-grades and predicted what each of four readings would mean. This section carries what came back, and it is not one of the four: **the two re-grades did not run the judge that graded the artifacts**, so `J0`–`J3` were never tested. What the round produced instead is a defect in the campaign's instrument that is larger than the effect the campaign was measuring.

### 13.312.1 The reading
